﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book has been sent down to you, so let there be no tightness in your breast about it﴾: "A Book" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a Book." "Sent down to you" is its adjective. By "the Book" is meant the Surah. "So let there be no tightness (ḥaraj) in your breast about it" means doubt about it. [Mahmud said: "Ḥaraj means doubt... etc." Ahmad said: The verse ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ supports this. For this subtle point, Imam al-Haramayn distinguished between knowledge (ʿilm) and sound conviction (iʿtiqād): "ʿaqd" (binding) is tying thought to a belief, and "iʿtiqād" is a derived form of it, while knowledge indicates the untying of knots, which is expansiveness, clarity and confidence. How excellent is his remark, "iʿtiqād is a derived form of it."

He means: if ʿaqd is opposed to knowledge, then what do you think of iʿtiqād, since the form iftiʿāl is more emphatic in meaning. From the same root come iʿtimād (reliance) and iḥtimāl (bearing).

Hence it is reported in the hadith "kasaba" (earned) and, for its opposite, "iktasaba" (acquired), because souls are more inclined to desires, transgressions and following whims than to obedience and restraining appetites. On this pattern comes ﴿It has what it earned, and it has what it acquired﴾. Although "ʿilm" (knowledge) derives from "aʿlam" (the one who has a mark), which comes from "ʿalama," meaning the splitting and parting of the lip, the point the Imam made is then the ultimate in its kind. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] ; like His saying ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. He called doubt "ḥaraj" because the one in doubt has a constricted breast, just as the one who is certain has an expanded and open breast. That is: do not doubt that it is sent down from Allah, and do not be distressed about conveying it. [He resumed his speech: "Or: and do not be distressed about conveying it, because he feared his people, their denial of him, their turning away from him and their harm to him, so his breast would tighten at delivering it and would not open to it. So Allah strengthened him and forbade him to care about them." Ahmad said: The verse ﴿Perhaps you will leave out part of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be strained by it, because they say, "Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?"﴾ supports this interpretation.] Then Allah commanded him to warn with it, as in ﴿that you may warn with it, and as a reminder to the believers﴾.

Question: What does "li-tundhira" (that you may warn) relate to? Answer: to "unzila" (was sent down): that it was sent down to you so that you may warn with it, or with the prohibition. For if he did not fear them, he would warn them. Likewise, when he is certain that it is from Allah, the certainty encourages him to warn, because the one with certainty is bold, relies on his Lord, and depends on His protection.

Question: What is the position of "dhikrā" (a reminder)? Answer: it may take the three vowel cases. In the accusative, it is governed by an implied verb, as if it was said: "that you may warn with it and remind (tudhakkir) a reminding," since "dhikrā" is a noun meaning "tadhkīr" (reminding). In the nominative, it is conjoined to "Book," or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. In the genitive, it is conjoined to the position of "an tundhira" (that you warn), meaning for warning and for reminding.

Question: The prohibition in ﴿So let there not be﴾ is directed at "ḥaraj" (tightness); what is its meaning? Answer: it is like their saying, "I will not see you here" (lā ararannaka hāhunā). [Ahmad said: He means that "ḥaraj" is apparently the thing forbidden in the verse, and the intended meaning is the prohibition of it, and Allah knows best.]

Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, which is the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and do not follow, apart from Him (min dunihi, i.e., apart from God), any awliya' (protectors, patrons). That is: do not take as your allies (lit. "do not take as protectors") apart from Him the devils of the jinn and of mankind, who would then lead you to worship idols, to follow desires, and to innovations (bid'a, a matter newly introduced into religion), and lead you astray from the religion of God and from what was sent down to you, and from following it, which He has commanded.

It is related from al-Hasan: "O son of Adam, you have been commanded to follow the Book of God and the Sunnah of Muhammad (ﷺ). By God, no verse was ever revealed except that he loved for you to know about what it was revealed and what its meaning is."

Malik ibn Dinar recited it as "wa-la tabtaghu" (and do not seek), from the verb ibtigha' (seeking): "wa-man yabtaghi ghayra al-Islami dinan" (And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion) [Qur'an 3:85].

It is also permissible that the pronoun in min dunihi refers to "what has been sent down," meaning: "and do not follow, apart from the religion of God, the religion of awliya'." 

*Qalilan ma tadhakkarun* (Little is it that you remember), where you abandon the religion of God and follow other than it. It is also read as *tadhkurun* (with the tā' elided), and as *yatadhakkarun* (with the yā'). *Qalilan* is in the accusative as an adverb of *yatadhakkarun*, meaning: you remember only a little. The *ma* is an added particle used to emphasise the paucity.

The Qur'anic phrase fa-jā'ahā (﴿فَجاءَها﴾) and the word bayātan (﴿بَياتاً﴾) are a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning "while they were spending the night." It is said: bāta bayātan ḥasanan, and bayta ḥasanah. His words "they are at midday rest" (﴿هُمْ قائِلُونَ﴾) are a circumstantial clause coordinated [[his speech ends. He said: "His words 'they are at midday rest' are a circumstantial clause coordinated with bayātan, as if it were said: 'the punishment came to them while they were spending the night or at midday rest'..." etc.]] with bayātan, as if it were said: "Then Our punishment came to them, spending the night or at midday rest." If you ask: should the omitted noun ("the people," ahl), which is before "town" (qaryah) or before the pronoun in ﴿أَهْلَكْناها﴾, be supposed? I answer: a noun is supposed to be omitted only out of necessity, and there is no necessity, for the town is destroyed just as its people are destroyed. We supposed it before the pronoun in ﴿فَجاءَها﴾ because of His words ﴿أَوْ هُمْ قائِلُونَ﴾. If you say: one does not say "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman" without a conjunction (wāw), so what about His words ﴿هُمْ قائِلُونَ﴾? I answer: some grammarians supposed that the conjunction wāw was omitted, but al-Zajjāj rejected this and said: if you said "Zayd came to me on foot, or he is a horseman," or "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman," no conjunction would be needed, because the reference has returned to the first term. The correct view is that when a clause is coordinated with a preceding circumstantial clause, the conjunction is omitted for the sake of lightness, to avoid two coordinating particles coming together, because the circumstantial wāw is the coordinating wāw, borrowed for connection. So your saying "Zayd came to me on foot, or he is a horseman" is eloquent speech that fits its rule. As for "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman," it is faulty. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿أَهْلَكْناها فَجاءَها بَأْسُنا﴾, given that destruction is only after the coming of punishment? I answer: its meaning is "We intended to destroy it," like His words ﴿إِذا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلاةِ﴾. These two times were singled out, the time of spending the night and the time of midday rest, because they are times of heedlessness and ease, so the descent of punishment in them is more severe and terrible. The people of Lot were destroyed at night, at the time of dawn, and the people of Shu'ayb at midday rest.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 5:

Then their claim (da'wahum) was nothing but what they used to call upon and profess of their religion and adhere to of their creed, except their acknowledgment of its falsehood and corruption. And their saying: ﴿Indeed, we were wrongdoers﴾ concerning what we used to follow.

It is also permissible: their appeal for help (istighathatahum) was nothing but this saying of theirs, because there is no one from whom help is sought from God other than Him. And among their appeals is their saying: "O Ka'b!" (ya li-Ka'b).

It is also permissible: their calling upon their Lord (da'wahum rabbahum) was nothing but their acknowledgment, knowing that supplication would not benefit them, and that "it is not the time for supplication" (lat hin da'a'), so they add nothing beyond blaming themselves and lamenting what they had done.

Da'wahum is the accusative as the predicate of kana (khabar kana), and an-qalu is the nominative as its subject (ism lahu), and the reverse is also permissible.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 6–7:

﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾. "Were sent" (أُرْسِلَ) is here a verb whose subject is the prepositional phrase "to them" (إِلَيْهِمْ), and its meaning is:

"We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, namely the nations, and He will ask them about what they answered their messengers with, as He said: ﴿And on the day He calls to them, He will say, "What answer did you give the messengers?"﴾ And He will question the messengers about what they were answered with, as He said: ﴿On the day when Allah gathers the messengers and says, "What was your response?"﴾ ﴿Then We will surely relate to them [their deeds] with knowledge, on the basis of [Our] knowledge of them﴾, on the part of the messengers and of those to whom they were sent, what had come from them, ﴿and We were not absent﴾, [being] those who know their outward and inward conditions, their words and their deeds, and We were not absent from them, nor from what occurred among them.

If you say: since He knows all of that and will relate it to them, what is the point of questioning them? I say: its meaning is reproach, rebuke and affirmation, when they confess it with their own tongues and their prophets testify against them.

The weighing on that Day is the truth (al-Haqq). That is, the weighing of deeds and the distinguishing between their heavy and light. It is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "that Day" (yawma'idhin). "Al-Haqq" is its attribute (sifah). That is: the weighing is on the Day when God questions the nations and their messengers [[His saying "that is, the weighing is on the Day when God questions the nations" applies only if yawma'idhin is connected to "the weighing" and "al-Haqq" is the predicate. As for what he has said, the implied meaning is: "and on the Day when He questions..." It is possible that his intention is: "the weighing exists on the Day when God questions the nations and their messengers, that is, the true weighing." The closer reading would be: "that is, the true weighing is on the Day when He questions..." (ʿAlam)]] — the true weighing, that is, the just weighing. It has also been read as al-qist (the equity).

Concerning the manner of the weighing, it has been said: the scrolls of deeds are weighed on a scale that has a tongue and two pans, which the creatures look at, as confirmation of the proof, a display of fairness, and a cutting off of excuses. Just as He questions them about their deeds, and they acknowledge them with their tongues, and their hands, feet and skins bear witness against them, and the prophets, angels and witnesses testify against them, so too are the deeds recorded in their books, which they read at the place of reckoning. It has also been said that this is a metaphor for the equitable judgment and the just ruling.

﴿Then as for him whose scales are heavy﴾: the word is the plural of mizan, or of mawzun, meaning those whose deeds that have weight and measure are heavy, which are the good deeds, or that by which their good deeds are weighed. It is related from al-Hasan: "It is fitting that a scale in which good deeds are placed should become heavy, and it is fitting that a scale in which evil deeds are placed should become light."

﴿by Our signs they used to wrong﴾: that is, they denied them, wronging themselves, like His saying: ﴿so they wronged themselves by them﴾.

We established you firmly in the earth: We made for you in it a place of settlement and residence. Or: We gave you dominion over it and empowered you to act freely in it. And We made for you in it means of livelihood (ma'ayish), plural of ma'ishah, which is what one lives by, such as food, drink and other things, and whatever one uses to attain these. The correct form is with a clear yā' (ya'). It is related from Ibn ʿĀmir that he pronounced it with a hamzah, by analogy with ṣaḥā'if (scriptures/pages).

And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you. That is: We created your father Adam from clay, not yet fashioned, and then We fashioned him after that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾? [He was not] among those who prostrated to Adam.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 12:

The "lā" in ﴿أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ﴾ is an extra (ṣila) particle, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I created with My hands?﴾ Similar to it is ﴿لِئَلَّا يَعْلَمَ أَهْلُ الْكِتابِ﴾ in the sense of "so that" the People of the Book would know. If you ask: what is the benefit of its addition? I say: it emphasizes and confirms the meaning of the verb it precedes, as if it were said: "so that the knowledge of the People of the Book may be realized." And [the meaning of] ﴿What prevented you from realizing the prostration and binding yourself to it, when I commanded you?﴾ is that My command to you to prostrate obligated it upon you, making it incumbent on you and necessary, something you must do. If you ask: why did He ask him about what prevented him from prostrating, when He already knew what prevented him? I say: it was for reproach, and to manifest his obstinacy, his disbelief, his arrogance, his boasting of his origin, his contempt for the origin of Adam, and that he disobeyed his Lord's command, believing it was not obligatory upon him, since he saw that the prostration of the superior to the inferior is outside the realm of what is correct. If you ask: how can His saying ﴿I am better than him﴾ be an answer to "what prevented you," when the answer should be "such-and-such prevented me"? I say: he has begun a narrative in which he informs about himself as being superior to Adam, and about the reason for his superiority over him, which is that his origin is from fire while Adam's origin is from clay. Thus the answer is understood from it, with something added to it, namely a denial of the command and a claim that it is far-fetched that one like himself should be commanded to prostrate to one like Adam. It is as if he says: whoever is of this description would be unlikely to be commanded to do what he was commanded.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 13:**

﴿So descend from it﴾ from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient, humble angels, ﴿to the earth﴾, which is the abode of the disobedient, arrogant jinn and humans (*al-thaqalan*). ﴿It is not for you﴾, meaning it is not proper for you, ﴿to be arrogant therein and disobedient, so go out. Indeed you are among the humbled﴾, meaning among those who are abased and disgraced before God and before His friends, because of your arrogance. This is like saying to a man, "*Qum saghiran*" (stand up in humiliation) when you wish to shame him, and its opposite is "*Qum rashidan*" (stand up as one rightly guided). This is because when he displayed arrogance, he was clothed in abasement.

It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever humbles himself before God, God raises his *hukmah*" (the *hukmah* is what surrounds the jaw of a bridle, according to *al-Sihah*), "and says: *in'tha'sh, yunʿishka Allah*" (rise up, may God lift you up). "And whoever becomes arrogant and oversteps his bounds, God presses him down into the earth" (*wahasahu*: he pressed him down; *al-wahs* is breaking something soft and stamping hard upon the ground, according to *al-Sihah*).

[Ibn Abi Shaybah reported it in his *Musannaf*. He related to us: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, ʿAbd Allah ibn Idris, and Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, from Ibn ʿAjlan, from Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, from Maʿmar ibn Abi Hayyah, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Khiyar, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, when the servant humbles himself before God, God raises his *hukmah* and says: *in'tha'sh, yunʿishka Allah*. So he is small in himself and great in the eyes of people. And indeed, when the servant magnifies himself and oversteps his bounds, God presses him down into the earth and says: *ikhsa', khasa'aka Allah* (be silent, may God silence you). So he is great in himself and small in the eyes of people; he is more despicable to them than a pig." Al-Bayhaqi reported it in *al-Shuʿab* through the chain of ʿAli ibn al-Madini from Sufyan.

Part of it has also been transmitted as a saying traced to the Prophet. Al-Daraqutni reported in *al-ʿIlal* from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "There is no human except that an angel holds him by his *hukmah*. When he raises himself up, it is said to the angel: 'Lower his *hukmah*.' And when he lowers himself, it is said to the angel: 'Raise his *hukmah*.'" He said: it is not established, for in its chain is ʿAli ibn Zayd, who is weak.]

If you say: Why did He grant his request for respite, when he only asked for respite in order to corrupt His servants and lead them astray?

[[Mahmud said: "If you say: Why was he granted his request for respite, when he only asked for respite in order to corrupt His servants... etc." Ahmad said: This question is raised, and its answer is undertaken, only by the al-Qadariyya (the Qadariyya, those who hold that God is obliged to safeguard what is best in His acts). As for Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna, the adherents of the Prophetic tradition and consensus), they have listened with the fullest attention to the words of God Most High, ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ (21:23), so none of them raises this question, nor does anyone who raises it receive an answer from them. And God is the Granter of success.]]

I say: Because in that there is a trial for the servants, and in opposing him lies one of the greatest rewards. His case is like that of what He created in this world of kinds of adornment, varieties of pleasures and diversions, and what He set in souls as desires, so that He may test His servants through them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 16–17:

﴿Because You have sent me astray﴾, that is, because of your leading me astray (ighwa'ika iyya), ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. This is his being charged with a duty (taklif), which is what caused him to fall into error (al-ghayy) and did not keep him steadfast as the angels were kept steadfast, even though they are superior to him and to Adam in essence and rank [[His statement "and superior to Adam in essence and rank" is the view of the Mu'tazila; as for the people of the Sunna, Adam is superior to them. (ʿA.)]]. And from al-Asamm: "You commanded me to prostrate, and pride drove me to disobey You."

The meaning is: because of my falling into error (al-ghayy), I will surely strive to lead them astray, ﴿so that they will be corrupted through my agency, just as I was corrupted through theirs﴾. [[Mahmud said: "The meaning is: because of my falling into error, I will surely strive to lead them astray, so that they will be corrupted through my agency... etc." Ahmad said: Within this statement of al-Zamakhshari there are two subtle Mu'tazili slips:

The first: his distortion of ighwa' (leading astray) into taklif (being charged with a duty), because he believes that God, exalted is He, did not cause him to go astray, that is, did not create error in him, on the basis of the principle of the good and the bad, and of benefit and the optimal (al-tahsin wal-taqbih wal-salah wal-aslah). His belief compels him to read ighwa' as referring to his being charged to prostrate, since that was the cause of his error. He often interprets the actions of God, when he attributes them literally to His essence, as causation (tasabbub), and makes that a figurative use of causality, because an action has relations with the agent, the object, the time, the place and the cause. Attributing it to the agent is literal, and attributing it to the rest is figurative, and he makes the action attributed to God because He is its cause, not its agent. He has argued for this earlier by the saying of Malik ibn Dinar to a man he saw shackled and imprisoned on account of debt: "These fetters were placed on your legs because of this," and he pointed to a basket containing pastries and various foods that he saw with the prisoner, meaning that your concern with these foods was the cause of squandering the wealth which led you to have fetters placed on your legs.

Accordingly, he intends to read this verse, meaning by "what You charged me with" the duty that was the cause of my creating error in myself, so "I will surely sit in wait", making Iblis the actual agent, while the attribution of the act to God is figurative. This is the first of the two slips.

The second: his making the duty one of the acts, because he claims that the speech of God is created, one of His acts, not one of His attributes, and the duty is part of speech. These are two slips which the Qadariyya combined. Iblis, may God curse him, did not accept either of them, because he attributed the leading astray to God, Exalted is He, since He is the creator of everything. So what is to be thought of a group which accepts for itself a hidden shirk that Iblis did not precede? We seek refuge in God from exposing ourselves to His wrath.]]

Some have said that "mā" (what) is interrogative, as if it were said: "By what thing did You lead me astray?", then he began: "I will surely sit in wait". The retention of the alif when the preposition is placed before the interrogative "mā" is rare and anomalous. The root of al-ghayy is corruption. From it: "ghawa al-fasil", when the young camel's stomach becomes distended (bashima). Al-bashm is corruption in the stomach.

﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, that is, I will lie in ambush for them on the path of Islam, as an enemy lies in ambush on the road to cut it off from travelers. Its accusative form is that of an adverb of place (zarf), like the line of poetry:

"...as the fox trod the path (kama 'asala al-tariqa al-tha'lab)" [[Lidan bahzi al-kaffi ya'salu matnahu... fihi kama 'asala al-tariq al-tha'lab. This is by Sa'ida ibn Ju'ayya, describing a spear as supple, whose shaft moves back and forth in the hand from being shaken, so that it does not stay in place, just as the fox ran about on the road. The verb 'asala here means "to move quickly". The object was dropped from the second clause by necessity, and was allowed because it was mentioned in the first.]]

Al-Zajjaj compared it to the saying: "Zayd struck the back and the belly", meaning "on the back and on the belly".

It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Shaytan sat in wait for the son of Adam at his paths: he sat for him on the path of Islam and said to him: 'Will you abandon the religion of your fathers?' He disobeyed him and embraced Islam. Then he sat for him on the path of emigration and said: 'Will you abandon your homeland and go abroad?' He disobeyed him and emigrated. Then he sat for him on the path of jihad and said: 'You will fight and be killed, your wealth will be divided, and your wife will be married,' and he disobeyed him and fought." [[Related by al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Samura ibn al-Fakih and Ibn Abi al-Fakih, and more complete than this. Two notes: first, the word "bi-atriqihi" (at his paths) is vocalized in al-Dala'il with a kasra on the ra' and a damma, with a ha'. Second, the word "bi-atriqihi": it occurs in al-Tibi's text, narrated by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Sayyara ibn Ma'bad, and this is an error.]]

﴿Then I will come to them from before them and behind them, from their right and from their left﴾. The four directions from which the enemy usually comes. This is a figure for his whispering to them and his enticing them as far as he is able and capable, like the verse: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice, and attack them with your horse and your foot soldiers﴾.

If you ask: why was "from before them" and "from behind them" expressed with the preposition of origin (min), while "from their right" and "from their left" with the preposition of passing (ʿan)? I answer: the adverbial object had the verb extended to it just as the verb is extended to the direct object; just as the prepositions of extension differ in that case, they differ in this one, and this is a usage to be accepted and not analogically extended. One only investigates whether its placement is correct. When we heard them say "jalasa ʿan yamīnihi" and "jalasa ʿala yamīnihi" ("sat on his right"), and "ʿan shimālihi" and "ʿalā shimālihi", we said: the meaning of "ʿalā yamīnihi" is that he settled on the right side as one who is high settles over the one above whom he is. The meaning of "ʿan yamīnihi" is that he sat aloof from the companion on the right, turned away from him, not adjacent to him. Then it became common and was used for the aloof and for other than the aloof, as we mentioned under "taʿālā". Similar to this with the direct object are the sayings "ramaytu ʿan al-qaws", "ʿalā al-qaws" and "min al-qaws" (I shot from the bow), because the arrow moves away from it, and rests upon it when it is placed on its middle for shooting, and the shooting begins from it. Likewise they said "jalasa bayna yadayhi" and "khalfahu" with the meaning of "fihi" (within), because both are adverbial places of the act. "Min bayni yadayhi" and "min khalfihi" (from before them and from behind them) because the act occurs in part of both directions, as you say "ji'tuhu min al-layl" (I came to him at night), meaning part of the night. From Shaqiq: "There is no morning but that Shaytan sits in wait for me at four watchposts: from before me, from behind me, from my right, and from my left. As for from before me, he says: 'Do not fear, for God is Forgiving and Merciful,' so I recite: ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to whoever repents, believes and does righteousness﴾. As for from behind me, he frightens me with the loss of those I leave behind, so I recite: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon God﴾. As for from my right, he comes to me from the direction of praise, so I recite: ﴿And the final outcome is for the righteous﴾. As for from my left, he comes to me from the direction of desires, so I recite: ﴿And a barrier is placed between them and what they desire﴾, and ﴿You will not find most of them thankful﴾." He said it as a conjecture, as shown by the verse: ﴿And Iblis indeed confirmed his assumption about them﴾. It was also said that he heard it from the angels through God's informing them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 18:

"Madh'uman" (ﷻ, "reviled, disgraced") is from dha'ama, meaning he reviled him when he blamed him. Al-Zuhri recited it as madhumam (with a lightened pronunciation), like mas'ul in masul (the pattern of lightening the hamza).

The lam in "la-man tabi'aka" (ﷻ, "surely whoever follows you") is the lam that introduces an oath (lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam). "La-amla'anna" (ﷻ, "I will surely fill") is its answer, and it stands in place of the answer of the conditional. "Minkum" (ﷻ, "of you") means "from you and from them," the masculine plural pronoun of address being given precedence over the others, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [27:55].

Isma (Isma) transmitted from Asim: "Liman tabi'aka" with a kasra on the lam, meaning: "for whoever of them follows you, this threat," which is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾, with "la-amla'anna" in the position of the subject (mubtada'), and "liman tabi'aka" as its predicate (khabar).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 19–22:

﴿وَيا آدَمُ﴾ and ﴿وقلنا يا آدم﴾. It is read ﴿هذى الشجرة﴾ (with the ya' elided and the ha' replacing it), though the original form is with the ya'. It is said:

Waswasa (to whisper, to murmur) means to speak a quiet speech and repeat it. From it comes "waswasa al-hulliy" (the ornament made a faint, whispering sound), and this is an intransitive verb, like "waw'alat al-mar'ah" (the woman ululated) and "wa'wa'a al-dhi'b" (the wolf howled). A man is "mawsus" (with a kasra on the waw), and one does not say "mawsus" with a fatha. Rather, one says "mawsus lahu" and "mawsus ilayhi," the latter being one to whom the whisperings are delivered. The meaning of "waswasa lahu" is that he performed the whispering for his sake, and "waswasa ilayhi" means that he cast it to him, so that he would make that a purpose for himself, in order to distress them when they saw what they wished to conceal, and that it not be exposed for them to see. In this is evidence that uncovering the private parts is among the grave matters, and that it has never ceased to be abhorrent in natures and reprehensible to intellects. [[Commentary of al-Zamakhshari's glossator, Ibn al-Munayyir (Ahmad): In these words there is also an inclination toward the doctrine of the Mu'tazila in two matters. The first is his saying that uncovering the private parts has never ceased to be deemed repugnant by the intellects, for this arises from his belief that goodness and ugliness are known by reason. Even if it is permissible for this statement to come from one who holds the creed of the Sunna, he does not intend its apparent meaning, since goodness and ugliness are apprehended only through the Law and revelation, not through reason. The meaning of this general statement, even if it came from a Sunni, is that reason apprehends the reason for which the Law made concealment good and uncovering abhorrent. The second matter is his inference that the angels are superior to the prophets, and it has already passed that this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, although some of the People of the Sunna have leaned toward it. The reply, from one who believes in the superiority of the prophets, is that it does not follow from Iblis's belief and his whispering that the angels are superior that this is so in the knowledge of God Most High. Do you not see that Iblis, may God curse him, reported that God forbade them the tree lest they become immortal or become angels? And he in that was a liar and a deceiver, so there is no proof in it, for there is nothing in the verse that requires God Most High to confirm Iblis in that, nor to affirm his saying. Rather, the verse concludes with what shows that he lied to them and deceived them, for God Most High said of him: ﴿so he brought them down by deception﴾. Perhaps his preference of angelhood over prophethood is among his deceptions, and God knows best.]] And that it has never ceased to be shameful in dispositions and reprehensible to intellects.

If you say: why was the ﻭ with damma in "wa-rawa" not changed into a hamza, as you say in "aw yasil"? I say: because the second is a madda (long vowel) like the alif of "wari". In the reading of Abdullah it occurs as "awrā," with the change. ﴿Except that you become angels﴾, that is, except out of dislike that you become angels. In this is evidence that angelhood is by the highest appearance, and that humanity perceives its rank, neither... And it is read "malakayn" with a kasra on the lam, like His saying ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay﴾. ﴿Of the immortals﴾: of those who do not die and remain in the Garden, dwelling.

It is read ﴿min sawatihima﴾ in the singular, and ﴿sawwatihima﴾ with a doubled waw. ﴿And he swore to them﴾: he made an oath to them, ﴿Indeed I am to you both among the sincere advisors﴾. If you say: al-muqasama is that you swear to your companion and he swears to you, you say "qasamtu fulanan" meaning "I made an alliance with so-and-so," and "taqasama" means they made a mutual oath. From it is His saying, ﴿They said to one another, "Swear by God that we shall surely attack him by night"﴾. I say: it is as if he said to them, "I swear to you that I am among the sincere advisors," and they said to him, "Do you swear by God that you are among the sincere advisors?" So He made that a mutual oath between them. Or: he swore to them upon the advice, and they swore to him upon accepting it. [[Ibn al-Munayyir: This interpretation is complete given the presence of muqasama with mention of what is sworn upon. But where the sworn matter is only the advice and nothing else, the stated interpretation is remote, unless the matter is taken to mean that he called the acceptance of advice "advice" by way of figurative correspondence, as it was said of His saying ﴿and We appointed Moses﴾, that He called Moses' commitment to fulfilment and attendance at the appointment "an appointment," and attributed the expression to the form of mutual action, and God knows best.]] Or the oath of Iblis came out in the form of mufa'ala, because he exerted himself in it as one who swears does. ﴿So he brought them down﴾: he lowered them to eating from the tree ﴿by deception﴾: by what he deceived them with through the oath by God. It is related from Qatada: "And the believer is only deceived through God."

It is related from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, that when he saw in his slave obedience and good prayer, he would free him. So his slaves would act that way seeking manumission. It was said to him: "Indeed they are deceiving you." He said: "Whoever deceives us by God, we are deceived by him." [[Reported by Ibn Sa'd through Nafi' who said: "When Ibn Umar was greatly pleased with something of his property, he drew near to his Lord with it, and his slaves had come to know this about him. So one of them would exert himself and keep to the mosque. When Ibn Umar saw him in that good state, he would free him. His companions said to him..." and so on. Abu Nu'aym also reported it in al-Hilya through this route.]]

﴿So when they tasted the tree﴾: they found its taste, beginning to eat from it. It is said: it was the ear of grain. It is said: the tree of the vine. ﴿Their private parts became apparent to them﴾: that is, the clothing fell away from them, so their nakedness appeared to them, and they did not see it of themselves, nor one of them of the other. It is related from Aisha, may God be pleased with her: "I never saw it of him, nor he of me." [[Reported by Abu Ya'la through the narration of Kamil Abu al-Ala' from Abu Salih, who narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: Aisha said, "The Messenger of God ﷺ never came to any of his wives except while veiled, with his garment let down over his head, and I never saw his private part, nor did he see mine." Its chain is weak. At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Maja, Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shayba narrated through Abdullah ibn Yazid from Aisha's client, who said: "I never saw the private part of the Messenger of God ﷺ at all." ad-Daraqutni narrated in the Gharib of Malik from az-Zuhri, and at-Tabarani in as-Saghir narrated through Anas from Aisha the like, adding: "nor did he ever look at my private part"; in its chain is Zayd ibn al-Hasan from Malik, and it is weak. He said: this is not authenticated from Malik nor from az-Zuhri. At-Tabarani in as-Saghir also narrated through Anas from Aisha something similar, in whose chain is Baraka ibn Muhammad al-Halabi, who is abandoned.]] It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "Their clothing was of the kind of fingernails." It is related from Wahb: "Their clothing was a light that screened between them and sight." It is said: "tafaqa" with an act means "ja'ala yaf'alu kadhha," (he began to do such a thing). Abu al-Sammal read ﴿wa-tafiqa﴾ with a fatha. ﴿They began to stitch together upon themselves leaves of the Garden to cover their private parts﴾, so that they would be concealed by them, as a sandal is stitched, by placing one strip upon another and binding them with thongs. Al-Hasan read ﴿yakhsifan﴾ with a kasra on the kha' and shadda on the sad; its origin is "yakhtasifan." Al-Zuhri read ﴿yakhsifan﴾ from "akhsafa," which is transmitted from "khasafa," meaning they stitched themselves together. It is also read ﴿yakhsifan﴾ from "khasafa" with shadda. ﴿From the leaves of the Garden﴾: it is said it was the leaves of the fig. ﴿Did I not forbid you both﴾: a rebuke from God Most High, a reproach and an alert to the error, since they did not guard against what God had warned them of, the enmity of Iblis. And it is related that He said to Adam: "Did you not have, from what I bestowed upon you of the trees of the Garden, a sufficiency apart from this tree?" He said: "Yes, by Your might, but I did not think that any of Your creatures would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I will surely bring you down to the earth, and then you will not attain life except with toil." So he was brought down, and he was taught the craft of iron, and was commanded to till, so he tilled, watered, harvested, threshed, winnowed, ground, kneaded and baked.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 23:

They named their sin "wrongdoing" (ẓulm) against themselves, even though it was a minor sin that was forgiven. ["Mahmud said: 'They named their sin wrongdoing, even though it was a minor sin that was forgiven... etc.' Ahmad said: This is also a hidden Mu'tazilism, for they claim that avoiding the major sins necessitates the expiation of the minor sins even if the servant does not repent from them. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words: 'even though it was a minor sin that was forgiven.' I have labelled this Mu'tazilism as hidden because this statement may be accepted as coming from the People of the Sunna, but they mean by its being forgiven that God Most High graciously pardoned it, and if He willed He could have held them to account for it, even though the prophets are protected from major sins. It is not as the Mu'tazila claim, that His forgiveness is obligatory. And God is the Granter of success."]

And they said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers﴾, in keeping with the habit of the saints and the righteous of magnifying small misdeeds and belittling great good deeds.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 24–25:

﴿Go down﴾. The address is to Adam, Eve and Iblis (Satan). ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: hostile to one another, Iblis being hostile to them both and they being hostile to him. ﴿A dwelling-place﴾ (mustaqarr) denotes settlement, or a place of settling. ﴿And provision for a time﴾ means benefit from livelihood until the end of your appointed terms.

On the authority of Thabit al-Bunani: When Adam was sent down and his death drew near, the angels surrounded him, and Eve began to circle around them. He said to her: "Leave the angels of my Lord alone, for what has befallen me is because of you." When he died, the angels washed him with water and lote-leaves an odd number of times, perfumed him with camphor, and shrouded him in an odd number of garments. They dug a grave for him, made a niche in its side (laḥd), and buried him at Sarandib in the land of India. And they said to his descendants: "This is your sunnah after him."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 26:

He made what is on the earth a descent (*manzil*) from the sky, because He decreed and wrote it. From the same root is ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ (39:6). The *rish* (ريش) is the garment of adornment, used metaphorically (*isti'ara*) from the feathers of birds, because it is their garment and their adornment. That is, "We sent down to you two garments: a garment that covers your private parts, and a garment that adorns you, because adornment is a legitimate purpose, as He said: ﴿that you may ride them and as adornment﴾ (16:8). ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ (16:6)."

Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) recited *wa-riyashan* (ورياشاً), the plural of *rish*, like *sha'b* and *sha'ab*.

﴿And the garment of righteousness﴾ means the garment of piety, awe and fear of Allah the Exalted. It is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence) is either the clause ﴿that is better﴾, as if it were said: "And the garment of righteousness, it is better," because demonstratives come close to pronouns in referring back to a previously mentioned noun. Or the predicate is the singular *khayr* with *dhalika* as an adjective of the subject, as if it were said: "And the garment of righteousness indicated is better." The demonstrative must either intend to glorify the garment of righteousness, or refer to the garment that covers the private parts, because covering the private parts is part of righteousness, giving it precedence over the garment of adornment. It has also been said that ﴿the garment of righteousness﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "and it is the garment of righteousness," and then "that is better" follows.

In the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy (Ibn Ka'b), it is read: ﴿And the garment of righteousness is better﴾.

It has also been said that the intended "garment of righteousness" is what is worn of armour, coats of mail (*jawashin*) and helmets (*maghafir*) and other things by which one protects oneself in battles. [[His words "the jawashin and the maghafir": the jawashin are what is woven of armour to the size of the chest. The maghafir are what is woven of it to the size of the head, worn beneath the cap. (E.)]]

It was also read as ﴿and the garment of righteousness﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with *libasan* and *riyashan*.

﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾, which indicate His grace and mercy toward His servants, meaning the sending down of clothing, ﴿that they may remember﴾, so that they recognize the great blessing in it.

This verse comes as a digression (*istitrad*) following the mention of the exposure of private parts and the placing of leaves upon them. It is to show the favour in what He created of clothing, and because of the humiliation and disgrace in nakedness and the uncovering of the private parts, and to indicate that concealment is a great gate among the gates of righteousness.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 27:

﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾: he will not test you by preventing you from entering Paradise, just as he tested your two parents by causing their expulsion from it. ﴿Stripping them of their garments﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he expelled them while stripping off their garments, in that he was the cause of their garments being removed from them. ﴿Indeed, he sees you﴾ is a justification for the prohibition and a warning against his temptation, since he is like an enemy who conceals his hostility (al-'adu al-mudaji), who plots against you and ambushes you ﴿from where you do not see﴾. It is related from Malik ibn Dinar: "Indeed, an enemy who sees you while you do not see him is severe in his burden, except for those whom God protects." ﴿And his tribe and his hosts﴾, that is, from the devils. In this there is clear evidence that the jinn do not see [humans] and do not appear to humans, and that their ability to make themselves visible is not within their power, and that the claim of anyone who asserts that he sees them is falsehood and fabrication.

﴿Indeed, We made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾: that is, We left them to them and them to them, We did not restrain them from them, until they took them as allies and obeyed them in what they urged upon them of disbelief and sins. This is a second warning, more emphatic than the first. If you ask: upon what is "and his tribe" conjoined? I say: it is conjoined to the pronoun in "he sees you," which is emphasized by "huwa," while the pronoun in "innahu" refers to the matter/statement (lil-sha'n wal-hadith). Al-Yazidi read "wa-qabilahu" in the accusative, and in this there are two possibilities: that it be conjoined to the noun of "inna," or that the waw be in the sense of "ma'a" (with). When it is conjoined to the noun of "inna," which is the pronoun in "innahu," then it refers back to Iblis.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 28:**

*Al-fāḥisha* (the abomination): that which is most extreme in ugliness among sins. That is, when they committed it, they offered two excuses: that their fathers used to do it, so they followed them, and that Allah the Exalted had commanded them to do it. Both are invalid as excuses. [[Mahmud said: "Both are invalid as excuses, because one of them is ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This too is a hidden Mu'tazilism (*al-i'tizal al-khafi*). His aim is to lay the groundwork for the principle of *al-taḥsin wa al-taqbīḥ* (that acts are morally good or bad in themselves), the observance of *al-ṣalāḥ wa al-aṣlaḥ* (what is best for the servant), and the impossibility of Allah acting contrary to that. This purpose is not achieved by it, because what is condemned in them is their claim that Allah commanded them to commit abomination, and they are lying in this claim. Negating the command does not entail negating the will, because Allah commands what He does not will and wills what He does not command.]] The first is imitation (*taqlīd*), and imitation is not a path to knowledge. The second is a fabrication against Allah and a distortion of His attributes. They used to say: "If Allah disliked what we do, He would have prevented us from it."

It is related from al-Ḥasan: "Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to the Arabs, and they were Qadariyyah-Mujbirah, attributing their sins to Allah." [[His saying "they were Qadariyyah-Mujbirah" means they were like the Mujbirah, meaning the Ahl al-Sunna, because they say that Allah wills evil just as He wills good. For the Mu'tazilah, will is command, but for the Ahl al-Sunna will is other than command. So the abomination is by His will, but He does not command it. Its full discussion is in the book on *tawḥīd*.]]

The confirmation of this is the saying of Allah: ﴿When they commit an abomination, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to do it." Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command abomination."﴾

Because doing what is ugly is impossible for Him, owing to the absence of any motive and the presence of a deterrent, how could He command its performance? ﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ This is a denial of their attribution of ugliness to Him, and a testimony that the basis of their saying is extreme ignorance. [[His saying "doing what is ugly is impossible for Him" means that Allah does not will the performance of ugliness, which is the creed of the Mu'tazilah. As for the Ahl al-Sunna, Allah wills both the ugly and the good: "What Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be." (ʿ)]]

It was also said: the abomination here refers to their circumambulating the House naked.

Bil-qist: with justice, and with what is established in souls as upright and good to every discerning person. It is also said: with monotheism (al-tawhid).

Wa-aqimu wujuhakum: and "Set up your faces" (wa-qul: aqimu wujuhakum), meaning: direct your intentions to worship Him, upright toward it, not inclining to anything else. 'Inda kulli masjid: at every time of prostration, or in every place of prostration, which is prayer (al-salat).

Wa-du'uhu: and worship Him, mukhlisina lahu al-din: sincere in obedience to Him, seeking thereby the face of God, purely. Kama bada'akum ta'udun: as He originated you, you will return; as He brought you into being at the start, He will bring you back. He argued against them in their denial of resurrection by the beginning of creation. The meaning is: He will restore you and then recompense you for your deeds, so devote your worship to Him sincerely.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 30:

﴿فَرِيقاً هَدى﴾: that is, those who submitted (aslamu); meaning, He granted them success (wafqahum) in faith. ﴿وَفَرِيقاً حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ الضَّلالَةُ﴾: that is, the word of misguidance (kalimat al-dalala) was decreed upon them, and God knew that they would go astray and not be guided. The accusative of the phrase ﴿وَفَرِيقاً﴾ is governed by a hidden verb which its following words explain, as if it were said: "And He abandoned a party upon whom misguidance was decreed." ﴿إِنَّهُمُ﴾: indeed, they, i.e. the party upon whom misguidance was decreed, ﴿اتَّخَذُوا الشَّياطِينَ أَوْلِياءَ﴾ ("they took the devils as protectors"): that is, they submitted to them (tawallaw-hum) in obedience to what they commanded them. This is evidence that God's knowledge has no effect on their misguidance, and that they themselves are the ones who go astray by their own choice and by their taking the devils as protectors instead of God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 31:

"Take your adornment" means your feathers (rish) and the clothing of your adornment, "at every masjid," that is, whenever you pray or circumambulate. They used to circumambulate the House naked. It is narrated from Tawus that He did not command them to wear silk and brocade; rather, one of you would circumambulate naked and leave his clothes behind the masjid. If he circumambulated while still wearing them, he would be struck and they would be taken from him, because they said:

"We will not worship God in garments in which we have sinned." It is also said that they did this as an omen, so that they would be stripped of sins just as they were stripped of clothes.

It is said that the adornment is the comb. It is also said that it is perfume. The Sunnah is that a man should take his best appearance for prayer. The Banu Amir, during their pilgrimage days, did not eat food except in small measure, and did not eat fat, glorifying their pilgrimage by this. So the Muslims said: "We are more deserving of doing this." It was said to them: "Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant." And it is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Eat what you wish and wear what you wish, as long as two qualities do not elude you: extravagance (israf) and conceit (makhilah)." [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it: Sufyan related to us from Ibrahim ibn Maysarah from Ata and Tawus from him, with this, but he said "two qualities" (khaslatan). Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ahmad and al-Hakim narrated it from the narration of Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Eat and drink, give in charity, and wear, as long as you do not mix in extravagance or conceit."]]

It is related that al-Rashid had a skilled Christian physician, and he said to Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid: "There is no knowledge of medicine in your Book." Knowledge is two kinds: knowledge of bodies and knowledge of religions. He said to him: "Allah has gathered all of medicine in half a verse of His Book." He asked: "What is it?" He said: the words of the Exalted: "Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant." The Christian said: "Is nothing from your Messenger transmitted concerning medicine?" He said: "Our Messenger (ﷺ) gathered medicine in brief words." He asked: "What are they?" He said: his saying: "The stomach is the house of disease, and restraint is the head of medicine, and give every body what it has been accustomed to." [[I did not find it. Al-Uqayli narrated in al-Du'afa' from the narration of Ibrahim ibn Jurayj al-Rahawi from Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah from al-Zuhri from Abu Salamah from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "The stomach is the pool of the body, and the veins come to it; when the stomach is sound, the veins issue health, and when the stomach is corrupt, the veins issue sickness." He said: a false hadith with no basis. Al-Daraqutni said: it is not authentic and is not known as a saying of the Prophet (ﷺ); for the chain of Ibrahim ibn Jurayj, apart from this, is not known, and he was a physician, so he fabricated a chain for it.]] The Christian said: "Neither your Book nor your Prophet left Galen any medicine."

Zīnat Allāh (the adornment of God) refers to clothing and whatever one beautifies oneself with; and al-ṭayyibāt min al-rizq (the good things of sustenance) refers to delicious foods and drinks. The interrogative sense in man (who?) is a denial of the prohibition of these things. It has been said: when they entered the state of iḥrām, they would forbid the sheep and what comes from it, its meat, its fat and its milk.

﴿Say: They are for those who believe in the life of this world, not exclusively for them, since the polytheists are their partners in them, but exclusively for them on the Day of Resurrection, when no one shares them with them.﴾

If you ask: why was it not said, "They are for those who believe and for others"? I answer: this is to draw attention to the fact that they were created for those who believe in the primary sense, and that the disbelievers are subordinate to them, like the verse ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy briefly, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire﴾.

It is also read as khāliṣatan (exclusively), in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and in the nominative as a predicate following a predicate.

The fawahish (gross indecencies): *ma tafahasha qubhuh*, meaning that its ugliness increased. It was also said that they are what relates to the private parts. Al-ithm (sin) is general to every sin. It was also said that it refers to drinking wine. Al-baghy (oppression, transgression) means injustice and arrogance. He singled it out for mention, as in His words ﴿He forbids indecency, wrongdoing and oppression﴾. ﴿For which He has sent down no authority﴾ contains *tahakkum* (mockery). This is because it is not possible for Him to send down proof that one should associate others with Him. [[Mahmud said: "In this there is *tahakkum*, because it is not possible for Him to send down proof that one should associate others with Him." Ahmad said: He means by *tahakkum* that the speech follows the pattern of "that which has an authority, except that it was not sent down," because it only negates the sending down of authority for it and does not negate that it has an authority. The original wording would have been: "and that you associate with Allah what has no authority for it, so that it is sent down," making it follow the manner of the poet's verse: "On a love-struck path whose landmark is not guided by."]] ﴿And that you say about Allah﴾, meaning: and that you invent and fabricate lies against Him, such as prohibitions and other things.

And for every nation there is a term. This is a warning to the people of Makkah of the punishment that will descend at a known term with God, as it descended upon the earlier nations. It is also read: "فإذا جاء آجالهم" (fa-idha ja'a ajaluhum, "when their terms come"), a variant recitation (qira'a).

He said "ساعة" (sa'a, "an hour") because it is the shortest unit of time in people's usage. The one who is hastening says to his companion, "In an hour," meaning the shortest and nearest time.

Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 35–36:

"Imma ya'tiyannakum" (إِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ): here "in" (إن), the conditional particle, has had "ma" (ما) joined to it, emphasizing the meaning of the condition. For this reason its verb is obligatorily followed by the heavy nun or the light nun. If you ask: what is the response (jaza') of this condition? I say: the fa' (فاء) and what follows it of the condition and response. The meaning is: "Whoever among you fears God and makes amends, and those among you who deny..." Also read: "ta'tiyannakum" (تأتينكم), with a ta' (تاء).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 37:

"So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs?" Fa-man aẓlamu, fa-man ashna‘u ẓulman mimman taqawwala ʿalā Allāh mā lam yaqulhu, aw kadhdhaba mā qālah. Ulāʾika yanāluhum naṣībuhum mina al-kitāb, ay mimmā kutiba lahum mina al-arzāq wa al-aʿmār ("their portion from the Book," i.e., what has been decreed for them of provision and lifespans), ḥattā idhā jāʾat-hum rusulunā, ḥattā ghāyatun li-naylihim naṣībahum wa-istīfāʾihim lahu, ay ilā waqt wafātihim, wa-hiya "ḥattā" allatī yubtadaʾu baʿdahā al-kalām, wa-al-kalām hāhunā al-jumla al-sharṭiyya, wa-hiya idhā jāʾat-hum rusulunā qālū. Yatawaffawnahum ḥāl min al-rusul, ay mutawaffīhim. Wa-al-rusul Malak al-Mawt wa-aʿwānuh. "Mā" waqaʿat mawṣūlatan bi-ayna fī khaṭṭ al-muṣḥaf, wa-kāna ḥaqquhā an tufṣal, li-annahā mawṣūla bi-maʿnā: ayna al-ālihat alladhīna tadʿūn ḍallū ʿannā, ghābū ʿannā fa-lā narāhum wa-lā nantafiʿu bihim, iʿtirāfan minhum bi-annahum lam yakūnū ʿalā shayʾin fīmā kānū ʿalayh, wa-annahum lam yaḥmadūhu fī al-ʿāqiba.

Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah al-A'raf, verses 38–39:

﴿He will say: "Enter"﴾. That is, God Most High says on the Day of Resurrection to those about whom He said ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God or denies His signs?﴾, meaning the idolaters of the Arabs. ﴿Among nations﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), meaning: you are among a group of nations, and within their multitude, accompanying them. That is, enter the Fire along with nations ﴿that passed away before you﴾, whose time preceded your time. ﴿Each nation curses its sister﴾, the one that went astray by following it. ﴿Until, when they have all gathered together therein﴾: adrakū means taddārakū, that is, they caught up with one another and assembled in the Fire. ﴿The last of them says of the first of them﴾, that is, the followers and the lowly, ﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment in the Fire."﴾ The phrase li-ūlāhum (of the first of them) means "on account of the first of them," because their address is to God, not to them. He says: ﴿He says: "For each there is double, but you do not know."﴾ This is read with the yā' and with the tā'. ﴿The first of them says to the last: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you earned."﴾ They joined this statement to God's words to the lowly: ﴿For each there is double﴾, meaning: it has been established that you have no superiority over us, and that we are equal in deserving the double punishment. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾ is either the words of the leaders, or the words of God to all of them.

﴿He will say: "Enter"﴾. That is, God Most High says on the Day of Resurrection to those about whom He said ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God or denies His signs?﴾, meaning the idolaters of the Arabs. ﴿Among nations﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), meaning: you are among a group of nations, and within their multitude, accompanying them. That is, enter the Fire along with nations ﴿that passed away before you﴾, whose time preceded your time. ﴿Each nation curses its sister﴾, the one that went astray by following it. ﴿Until, when they have all gathered together therein﴾: adrakū means taddārakū, that is, they caught up with one another and assembled in the Fire. ﴿The last of them says of the first of them﴾, that is, the followers and the lowly, ﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment in the Fire."﴾ The phrase li-ūlāhum (of the first of them) means "on account of the first of them," because their address is to God, not to them. He says: ﴿He says: "For each there is double, but you do not know."﴾ This is read with the yā' and with the tā'. ﴿The first of them says to the last: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you earned."﴾ They joined this statement to God's words to the lowly: ﴿For each there is double﴾, meaning: it has been established that you have no superiority over us, and that we are equal in deserving the double punishment. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾ is either the words of the leaders, or the words of God to all of them.

﴿Their gates of heaven will not be opened, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of a needle.﴾ No righteous deed of theirs ascends to Him; ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾, ﴿No! Indeed the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin.﴾ It has been said: since Paradise is in heaven, the meaning is that they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven, nor will a path to it be made for them, so that they may enter Paradise. It has also been said: their spirits will not ascend when they die, as the spirits of believers ascend.

It has been said: blessing will not descend upon them, and they will not be given relief, ﴿so We opened the gates of heaven﴾. It is recited as ﴿لا تُفَتَّحُ﴾ with the doubled ta (tashdid).

﴿لا يُفَتَّحُ﴾ with ya'. ﴿لا تُفَتَّحُ﴾ with ta', in the active voice, with ﴿الأبواب﴾ in the accusative, on the basis that the verb refers to the signs (āyāt). With ya' it is read with the verb referring to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn ʿAbbas read al-Jamal (الجمل) on the pattern of al-qaml (القمل). Saʿid ibn Jubayr read al-Jamal on the pattern of al-naghr (النغر). It is also read al-Jamal (الجمل) on the pattern of al-qafl (القفل), al-Jamal on the pattern of al-nasab (النصب), and al-Jamal on the pattern of al-ḥabl (الحبل). Its meaning is a thick rope (al-qals al-ghalīẓ), because it is ropes gathered together and made into a single unit. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah is too exalted in comparison to be likened to a camel. He means that a rope is suitable to the thread that passes through the eye of a needle, whereas a camel is not suitable for it. However, the common recitation is more fitting, because the eye of a needle is a metaphor for narrowness of passage. It is said: "narrower than the hole of a needle" (akhrat al-ibra). And they called a skilled guide kharrīt (خريت), because he is guided by him through narrow passages likened to the holes of needles.

The camel is a metaphor for the bulk of a body. A poet said:

Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, do not the dreams of the lowly restrain you from us,
while you are, from within, hollow and puffed-up?

There is no harm in the people for their height and their size:
the bodies of camels and the dreams of sparrows.

As if they were reeds, hollow at their bases,
perforated, into which the whirlwinds have blown.

These are by Ḥassān. "Ḥārith" is a truncated form of Ḥārith, built on ḍamm because it is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been dropped. "Al-aḥlām" is the plural of ḥilm, meaning intellects. "Al-jawf," with ḍamm, is the plural of ajwaf, meaning having a wide hollow. "Al-jamākhīr" is the plural of jamkhūr, meaning of great body.

He says: how could you not have intellects, when you are great in bulk? Then he explained this by saying: "there is no harm" or damage that befalls these people from their height and bulk, meaning: there is no deficiency in them because of that. In this there is mockery of them. Or: they do not disdain that, for they deserve it. Or: there is no harm that befalls you because of the people, on account of their height and bulk, for their bodies are like the bodies of camels, and their intellects are like the intellects of sparrows, if sparrows have intellects, meaning that they have no intellect. When their lower hollows are split, their upper parts are more numerous.

He likened the openings of their senses to its perforations, empty of beauty. "Al-aʿāṣīr" is the plural of iʿṣār, which is a wind blowing in a circular motion, going toward the sky. He used the metaphor of blowing for the entry of air into it with force, like blowing. In the rhyme there is iqwāʾ (إقواء, an inconsistency of vowel in the rhyme-letter), because the vowel of the rawī (rhyme-letter) varies between kasra and ḍamma.

Al-mukhayyat is like al-ḥizām and al-miḥzam: that with which one sews, which is the needle.

﴿And thus﴾, that is, such a dreadful recompense, ﴿We recompense the criminals﴾, to indicate that criminality is the cause that leads to punishment, and that everyone who commits crime is punished. He repeated it, saying ﴿And thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, because every criminal is a wrongdoer to himself.

﴿Their gates of heaven will not be opened, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of a needle.﴾ No righteous deed of theirs ascends to Him; ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾, ﴿No! Indeed the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin.﴾ It has been said: since Paradise is in heaven, the meaning is that they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven, nor will a path to it be made for them, so that they may enter Paradise. It has also been said: their spirits will not ascend when they die, as the spirits of believers ascend.

It has been said: blessing will not descend upon them, and they will not be given relief, ﴿so We opened the gates of heaven﴾. It is recited as ﴿لا تُفَتَّحُ﴾ with the doubled ta (tashdid).

﴿لا يُفَتَّحُ﴾ with ya'. ﴿لا تُفَتَّحُ﴾ with ta', in the active voice, with ﴿الأبواب﴾ in the accusative, on the basis that the verb refers to the signs (āyāt). With ya' it is read with the verb referring to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn ʿAbbas read al-Jamal (الجمل) on the pattern of al-qaml (القمل). Saʿid ibn Jubayr read al-Jamal on the pattern of al-naghr (النغر). It is also read al-Jamal (الجمل) on the pattern of al-qafl (القفل), al-Jamal on the pattern of al-nasab (النصب), and al-Jamal on the pattern of al-ḥabl (الحبل). Its meaning is a thick rope (al-qals al-ghalīẓ), because it is ropes gathered together and made into a single unit. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah is too exalted in comparison to be likened to a camel. He means that a rope is suitable to the thread that passes through the eye of a needle, whereas a camel is not suitable for it. However, the common recitation is more fitting, because the eye of a needle is a metaphor for narrowness of passage. It is said: "narrower than the hole of a needle" (akhrat al-ibra). And they called a skilled guide kharrīt (خريت), because he is guided by him through narrow passages likened to the holes of needles.

The camel is a metaphor for the bulk of a body. A poet said:

Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, do not the dreams of the lowly restrain you from us,
while you are, from within, hollow and puffed-up?

There is no harm in the people for their height and their size:
the bodies of camels and the dreams of sparrows.

As if they were reeds, hollow at their bases,
perforated, into which the whirlwinds have blown.

These are by Ḥassān. "Ḥārith" is a truncated form of Ḥārith, built on ḍamm because it is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been dropped. He says: how could you not have intellects, when you are great in bulk? He repeated it, saying ﴿And thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, because every criminal is a wrongdoer to himself.

The Qur'an verse, quoted in full: ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tariḍa) placed between the subject (al-mubtada') and the predicate (al-khabar). Its purpose is to encourage the acquisition of the everlasting bliss that no describer can fully characterise, while reassuring the reader through the word wus'uhā (capacity), which means the broad scope of possibility, not a narrow constraint, in faith and righteous deeds. Al-A'mash read it as لا تكلف نفس (la tukallifu nafs, with the verb in the second person and the noun unmarked), which is a variant recitation.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 43:**

Whoever had rancour (*ghill*) in his heart toward his brother in this world, it will be removed from him. Thus their hearts will be sound and purified, and there will be among them nothing but mutual affection and sympathy. And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "I truly hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr will be among them."[[Ibn Saʿd narrated it through the transmission of Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad from his father, and al-Ṭabarī through the transmission of Maʿmar from Qatāda from ʿAlī, but both are disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*). In Ibn Abī Shayba it is narrated through the transmission of Ribḥī from ʿAlī, and it is connected (*muttaṣil*).]] ﴿Who guided us to this﴾, that is, who granted us success in what necessitates this great triumph, namely faith and righteous action. ﴿And we would not have been guided﴾: the *lām* here is for emphasizing the negation.[[Maḥmūd (al-Zamakhsharī) said: the *lām* is for emphasizing the negation, meaning "it would not be proper..." etc.

Aḥmad (ibn al-Munayyir) said: This refutes the faces of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) with a decisive answer, for it bears complete witness, emphasized by the *lām*, that the one who is guided is one for whom Allah created guidance, and that anything else is impossible, so no one is guided except by Allah's guidance, and had He not guided him, he would not have been guided. As for the Qadariyya, they claim that every guided person created guidance for himself, and so he is guided even if Allah did not guide him, since Allah's guidance of the servant would consist in creating guidance for him. In their view, Allah Most High did not create guidance for any of the guided, and this does not depend on His creation—exalted is Allah above what they say. When al-Zamakhsharī perceived this, he followed his habit of distorting guidance from Allah Most High into the subtle grace (*luṭf*) by means of which the servant creates his own guidance. So be just with yourself, and set before yourself the statement of the speaker: "The one who is guided is the one who is guided by himself, without Allah guiding him—that is, creating guidance for him." Compare it with the Qur'anic statement reported about the speech of the monotheists in the abode of truth: "We would not have been guided had Allah not guided us." Observe the contrast between these two sayings: the words of the Muʿtazilī in this world, and the words of the monotheist in the Hereafter, "in a seat of truth." Choose for yourself which of the two groups you will follow. I do not think—and the address is to every intelligent person—that you would prefer this statement, reported about the friends of Allah in the abode of peace and noted with honour in the Noble Book, to the statement of a deviant Qadarī who vacillated with his desires and his partisanship in the abode of delusion and transience. We ask Allah for a good return and a good end.]] They mean: it would not have been proper for us to be guided unless Allah guided us and granted us success. In the codices of the people of Syria it reads *mā kunnā linahtadiya* without a *wāw*, making it a sentence that clarifies the first one. ﴿Indeed the messengers of our Lord had come with the truth﴾, and that was a grace for us and an admonition toward guidance, so we were guided. They say this out of joy and gladness at what they attained, and out of delight in speaking it, not as a means of drawing near to Allah or an act of worship, just as we see someone who has been granted some good in this world speaking in similar terms, unable to refrain from saying it because of his joy, not because of seeking nearness (to Allah). ﴿That this is the Garden﴾: *an* is a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, its estimated sense being: "they were called out to, that this is the Garden." The pronoun is a pronoun of the matter and the statement. Or it may mean *ayy* (that is), because calling out is a kind of speech, as if it were said: "It was said to them, that is, this is the Garden, which you have inherited." ﴿You have been made to inherit it﴾ [[His words resumed. He said: "His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they were called out to: this is the Garden, which you have been made to inherit by what you used to do﴾ means: by reason of your deeds, not by way of divine bounty, as the *mubṭila* (those who claim falsely) say." Aḥmad said: by "the *mubṭila*" he means a group who heard the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds, but by the grace of Allah and His mercy." It was asked: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy." They said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke the truth," and these are the People of the Sunnah. It was said to them: "Then what is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been made to inherit by what you used to do﴾?" They said: "Allah bestowed grace by making Paradise a reward for deeds, out of His grace and mercy, not because it is owed to Him as a due, as debts are owed by which the debtor has no choice in discharging them." Thus they combined the two proofs in a way that accords with the proof of reason, which indicates that it is impossible for Allah Most High to have any obligation placed upon Him. So, O just one, consider whether you find in this speech anything false that would warrant calling its adherents *mubṭila*. Judge yourself by it. Then, when it becomes clear to you that they are innocent of this in their righteousness, present it to people who claim that they have a right against Allah Most High through their deeds, deeds which neither benefit Him by their existence nor are harmed by their absence—exalted and sanctified is He above that—and who utter with the tongue of audacity that Paradise and its bliss are their allotment by a right owed by Allah Most High, with no bounty from Him toward them in it, but rather as a debt that some people demand from their debtors. Consider which of the two groups mentioned is more deserving of the title *mubṭila*. And peace.]] ﴿by what you used to do﴾: by reason of your deeds, not by way of bounty, as the *mubṭila* say.[[His saying "as the *mubṭila* say" refers to the People of the Sunnah, who say that entry into it is by grace and its distribution is according to deeds, as in the hadith. (ʿ)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 44–45:

"Anna" in "anna qad wajadna" may be understood as the light (mukhaffafa) form of the heavy "inna," and it may be explanatory (mufassira), like the one that preceded it a moment ago. Likewise "anna la'natu Allahi 'ala al-zalimin." They said that to them out of delight in their own state, gloating over the People of the Fire, and as an increase in their grief, so that its narration would be a kindness (lutf) to whoever hears it. Likewise is the saying of the caller (mu'adhdhin) among them:

"The curse of God be upon the wrongdoers." He is an angel whom God commands, and he calls out among them a call that the People of Paradise and the People of the Fire both hear.

It has been read as "anna la'nata Allah," with tashdid and nasb. Al-A'mash read "inna la'natu Allah," with the kasra of "inna," intending the sense of saying, or treating "fa-adhdhana" as equivalent to "qala."

If you say: why was it not said, "What your Lord promised you," just as it was said, "What You promised us"—[[the text of his speech continues: He said: If you say, why was it not said "ma wa'adakum rabbukum" as it was said "ma wa'adana"... etc." Ahmad said: One may say:

If the object had been mentioned, as in the first instance, and it were said: "Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?", then the verb would also be unrestricted with respect to what was promised, since it was not mentioned, and it would encompass every existing thing: the resurrection, the reckoning, and the punishment, of which the regret over the bliss of the People of Paradise is one kind. So it is not specific to the omission of the object referring to those promised. Rather, the preferable view is that its omission is brevity, lightening, and self-sufficiency through what came before. And God knows best.]] Our Lord?

I say: its omission is for lightening, since "wa'adna" indicates it. One may say: it is left general so as to encompass everything God promised of resurrection, reckoning, reward, punishment, and all other conditions of the Last Day, because they all denied it entirely, and because everything promised was something that distressed them; the bliss of the People of Paradise is nothing but torment for them. Therefore it was left general for this reason.
