And between them is a barrier (ḥijāb), meaning between Paradise and Hell. Or between the two groups, and it is the wall mentioned in God's words: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate﴾ [Qur'an 57:13]. And on the A'raf (al-A'rāf), that is, on the heights of the barrier, the wall struck between Paradise and Hell, and they are its upper parts. A'raf is the plural of ʿurf, a word borrowed from the ʿurf of a horse (its mane) and the ʿurf of a rooster (its comb). Men from among the Muslims, the last of them to enter Paradise because of the deficiency of their deeds, as if they were those held in suspense (murjawn) for the command of God, will be detained between Paradise and Hell until God permits them to enter Paradise. They will recognize each of the companies of the blessed and the wretched by their marks (bi-sīmāhum), by their sign which God has informed them of, God inspiring them with that. Or the angels will inform them.

When they turn their eyes toward the companions of the Garden, they call out to them with greeting ("peace be upon you"). And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, and they see what they are suffering, they seek refuge in God and turn to His mercy, that He not place them among them. And they call out to men from among the leaders of disbelief, saying to them: ﴿Are these the ones about whom you swore that God would not grant them any mercy?﴾, pointing to the people of the Garden, whom the leaders used to belittle and despise for their poverty and their small share of worldly fortune, and they used to swear that God would not admit them to the Garden. ﴿Enter the Garden; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.﴾ It is said to the companions of the Heights: enter the Garden. This is after they have been held back at the Heights and have looked at both groups, recognized them by their marks, and said what they say.

The benefit of this is to make clear that recompense is according to the deeds, that precedence and delay are based on their goodness, and that no one precedes before God except by his precedence in deeds, and no one is held back before Him except by his lagging in them. It is so that the listeners may desire the state of the foremost and strive to attain their rank, and so that they may picture that on that Day everyone is recognized by the mark he deserved to be branded with, of the people of good and of evil; thus the evildoer refrains from his evil, and the doer of good increases in his goodness. And it is so that it may be known that every person rebukes the disobedient, even the least of people in deeds.

His words ﴿And when their eyes are turned﴾ indicate that a turner turns their eyes so that they look, seek refuge, and are rebuked. Al-A'mash read: "And when their eyes are turned (qulibat)." It is also read: "Enter the Garden" (udkhulū), in the passive form. And ʿIkrimah read: "They entered the Garden" (dakhalū). If you ask: how does the saying ﴿No fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve﴾ fit these two readings? I say: its interpretation is, "Enter," or "They entered the Garden," with it being said to them: "No fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve."

If you ask: what is the position of His words ﴿They have not entered it, while they hope﴾? I say: it has no grammatical position, because it is a new sentence (istiʾnaf), as if a questioner asked about the condition of the companions of the Heights, and it was answered: ﴿They have not entered it, while they hope﴾, meaning their state is that their entry into the Garden was delayed behind the entry of the people of the Garden; so they have not entered it because they are held back, while they hope and have not despaired.

It is permissible that it have a position, by being a description of "men" in ﴿What your gathering of wealth availed you, nor your multitude and assembly, nor your arrogance against the truth and against people﴾. It is also read: "your being many" (tastakthirūn), from abundance.

It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿Throw down to us from what God has provided you﴾ of food and fruit. Like the poet's words:

*I fed her chaff and cool water*
*I did not unsaddle her from the riding-gear while she was coming to the water...*
*I fed her chaff and cool water*

He says: when I unsaddled the riding-gear from the she-camel while I was coming to the water, I fed her chaff and gave her cool water, with the verb governing *mā'an* (water) omitted. It is also possible that the meaning is: I handed her chaff and water, using *'alf* (feeding) figuratively, because water is not something one feeds to an animal. It may also be that *tibnan* and *mā'an* are both objects, or that *mā'an* is a *mafʿūl maʿahu* (object of accompaniment), meaning: I fed her chaff accompanied by water, so it does not follow that the water was fed to her. The rejection of this reading, on the grounds that water does not accompany chaff in feeding, is open to question, since it is possible that chaff was placed for her and water was placed beside it so that she could take whatever she wished.

The narration of al-Farrā' reads:

*I fed her chaff and cool water*
*until her eyes became abundantly tearful* (*hamālah*)

*Shatawtu* (I spent the winter) at a place means: I stayed there during the winter season. That is, until she was in the winter season, her eyes were *muḥālah* (streaming), i.e., abundant in tears. *Hamālah* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), and *ʿaynāhā* (her eyes) is its subject. It is also narrated as: *ḥattā ghadat* (until she became), and *ḥattā baddat* (until she appeared).

They make this request only while despairing of being granted it, out of bewilderment in their situation, as one who is in distress and tested does.

﴿He has forbidden both to the disbelievers﴾: He prevented them from the drink and food of Paradise, as a responsible person is prevented from what is forbidden to him and barred from it, like the poet's words:

*Forbidden to my eyes is that they taste sleep*
*and that they be stilled until I meet you, O Hind.*

*Al-karā* is drowsiness, which is the beginning of sleep. It is said: *karā yakrā karan*, from the pattern of *taʿiba*, when one becomes drowsy. It is described as being like food by way of *al-makniyya* (implicit metaphor). *An taṭʿamā* means "that they taste", which is *takhyīl* (imaginative representation). *Raqaʾa* (stilled) with the hamza means: the tears or blood became still. Attributing it to the eyes is a rational metonymy (*majāz ʿaqlī*), since it actually belongs to the tears. It is also possible that he used *tarqaʾā* metaphorically for *tughmiḍā* (closing), because it involves the stillness of the eyelids. The meaning is: drowsiness and dullness are forbidden to my eyes, or weeping is forbidden with emphatic prohibition, just as a forbidden thing is prohibited to a responsible person. In this there is an explicit metaphor (*istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya*). *Ḥattā alqāka yā Hind* (until I meet you, O Hind).

And I obtain from your bounty. In the vocative there is a sense of lamentation.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 52–53:

﴿فَصَّلْناهُ عَلى عِلْمٍ﴾ [We have detailed it with knowledge], ﴿عالمين﴾ [knowing], i.e., how to detail its rulings, its admonitions, its narratives and all its other meanings, ﴿حتى جاء حكيما قيما غير ذى عوج﴾ [until it came as wise, upright, without crookedness].

Ibn Muhaysin read: ﴿فضلناه﴾ [We have favoured it], with the dotted ḍād. The meaning is: We favoured it over all the (other) Books, knowing that it is worthy of being preferred over them.

﴿وَهُدىً وَرَحْمَةً﴾ [and as guidance and mercy] is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause from the accusative object of ﴿فضلناه﴾, just as ﴿على علم﴾ [with knowledge] is a circumstantial clause from its nominative subject.

﴿إِلَّا تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ [except its final outcome (taʾwīl)]: i.e., only its final outcome and what it leads to, namely the manifestation of its truthfulness and the clear validity of what it stated of promise and threat.

﴿قَدْ جاءَتْ رُسُلُ رَبِّنا بِالْحَقِّ﴾ [Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth]: i.e., it became clear and was confirmed that they came with the truth.

﴿نُرَدُّ﴾ [Are we to be returned?] is a clause conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to the clause before it, included with it under the rule of the interrogative, as if it were said: "Do we have any intercessors?" or "Are we to be returned?" Its being in the nominative (rafʿ) is due to its occurring in a position suitable for a noun, just as you say at the outset: "Does Zayd strike?"

No other verb is sought to be conjoined to it, so one should not estimate: "Will an intercessor intercede for us, or are we to be returned?"

Ibn Abi Ishaq read: ﴿أو نُرَدُّ﴾ [or are we returned], with the accusative, conjoined to ﴿فيشفعوا لنا﴾ [so that they intercede for us]. Or "أو" may mean "حتى أنّ" (until), i.e., "that they intercede for us until we are returned and so we act."

Al-Hasan read ﴿نُرَدُّ﴾ with the accusative and ﴿فَنَعْمَلَ﴾ [and we act] with the nominative, meaning: "so we act."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 54:

﴿يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا﴾ It is also read "yughashshī" (with the doubled shadda), meaning: the night overtakes the day, and the day overtakes the night; each of them covers the other. As for the second reading, the proof of it is the reading of Humayd ibn Qays: "yughshī al-layla al-nahāra," with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥa and "al-layl" in the accusative and "al-nahār" in the nominative, meaning: the day overtakes the night and seeks it swiftly. This suits the reading of Humayd well.

﴿بِأَمْرِهِ﴾ means by His will and His direction. It is connected with "musakhkharāt" (subjugated), meaning: He created them running in accordance with His wisdom and His arrangement. And just as He wills to turn them, He calls that "command" by way of analogy, as though they were commanded to do so.

It is also read "wal-shamsu wal-qamaru wal-nujūmu musakhkharātun," with the nominative case.

Then, after He mentioned that He created them subjugated by His command, He said: ﴿أَلَا لَهُ الْخَلْقُ وَالْأَمْرُ﴾ ("Verily, His is the creation and the command"), meaning: He is the one who created all things, and He is the one who turns them according to His will.

Tadarru'an wa khufyatan (تَضَرُّعاً وَخُفْيَةً) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning "in a state of humility and secrecy." The same applies to khawfan wa ṭam'an.

Al-tadarru' is a form of the (tafa''ul) pattern derived from al-ḍarā'a, which means abasement, i.e., humbling oneself and entreating. "Tadarru'" means humility and supplication.

[The author Maḥmūd said: "Al-tadarru' is a tafa''ul form from al-ḍarā'a, which is abasement… etc." Aḥmad said: It is sufficient to determine the secrecy in supplication that the verse links it with tadarru'. Neglecting it is like neglecting humble submission to God in supplication. A supplication without humility or reverence is of little benefit. Likewise, a supplication without secrecy and the dignity that accompanies it is of little value. You will see many people of your time relying on shouting and screaming in supplication, especially in the congregational mosques, until the clamour grows intense, the ears are deafened, and the supplicator sways the people. He does not realise that he has combined two innovations (bid'a): raising the voice in supplication and doing so in the mosque. Sometimes the common people are moved to tenderness by this, which they do not feel when the voice is lowered, dignified bearing is maintained, and the established Sunna (sunna) transmitted by reports is followed. That tenderness is nothing but a softness similar to that which affects women and children; it does not come from the core of the heart. For if it came from a real root, it would be greater, more complete and purer when following the Sunna in supplication and in lowering the voice. How often falsehood is confused with truth in the minds of many people! O God, show us the truth as truth and grant us to follow it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and grant us to avoid it.]

It means humiliation, that is, abasement and flattery.

Wa-qurri'a: "wa khufyatan" (and secretly) [this has been read differently]. [Note: "The statement 'and it was read wa khufyatan' perhaps this is with a kasra. (ʿ)"]

It is reported from al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him): Indeed, Allah knows the pious heart and the hidden supplication. A man may have memorised the Qur'an while his neighbour is unaware of it; a man may have understood much jurisprudence while people are unaware of it; a man may perform a long prayer while the people with him are unaware of it. We have indeed known people who had no deed on earth that they could do in secret without it becoming public, and the Muslims used to strive in supplication while no voice of theirs was heard except a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, and He praised Zakariyya, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. Between the supplication in secret and the supplication in public there is seventy-fold difference.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed what they were commanded in everything, including supplication and other things.

It is reported from Ibn Jurayj that it means raising the voice in supplication. And from him: shouting in supplication is disliked and an innovation. It was also said: it means excessive verbosity in supplication.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will be a people who will transgress in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings me closer to it of speech and deed, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings me closer to it of speech and deed." [Abū Ya'lā reported it through the narration of Shu'ba from Ziyād ibn Mihrān from Qays ibn 'Unān from a client of Sa'd ibn Sa'd, who heard his son saying: "O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and its chambers and such and such, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and its shackles and such and such." Sa'd said: "You have asked Allah for good, and sought refuge in Him from much evil. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'There will be a people who will transgress in supplication.' And it is sufficient for you to say: 'O Allah, I ask You for Paradise…' (the report)." And he said at its end: "I do not know whether his saying 'and it is sufficient for you…' to the end is from Sa'd's words or from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ)." It was also narrated by Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī and al-Bayhaqī in al-Da'awāt through his chain from Sa'd, except that he said: "And it is sufficient for you to say: 'O Allah, I ask You for all good, what I know of it and what I do not know, and I seek refuge in You from all evil, what I know of it and what I do not know.' In this chapter there is also a report from 'Abd Allāh ibn Mughaffal, reported by Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim.]

Then he recited His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, like His saying: ﴿And indeed I am Forgiving to whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds﴾.

He said qarīb (near) in the masculine form, either by interpreting "mercy" as "womb" or "compassion," or because it is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a near thing"; or by analogy with the pattern fa'īl, which carries the meaning of maf'ūl, as that pattern was made like it, so one says qatlā' and asrā' (slain and captives); or because it is in the pattern of the verbal noun (maṣdar), which is the opposite, like ḍaghīb (the sound of a hare). [Note: "'The opposite' refers to the sound of the cry of the eagle (al-naqīḍ) and the sound of the litter (al-maḥmal); al-ḍaghīb is the sound of a hare. (ʿ)"] Or because the feminine marking of "mercy" is not real.

It is read nushran, which is a verbal noun of nashara. Its accusative is either because arsala and nashara are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said: "He spread it, spreading," or it is in the circumstantial accusative meaning "spreading." Nushur is the plural of nashūr.

Nushran is a lightened form of nashr, like rusul and rusl. Masrūq read nushran, meaning "spread out," a fa'l form with the meaning of maf'ūl (passive), like naqḍ and ḥasb. From it comes their saying ḍamm nashrahu (gather its spreading). Bushran is the plural of bashīr (bringer of good news). Bushran is also read in its lightened form. Bushran, with a fatḥa on the bā', is a verbal noun from bashara, meaning bashara (to give good news), i.e., bāshirāt (bringing good news). Bushran bayna yadayy raḥmatihi: before His mercy, which is the rain, which is among the most complete and the most excellent of blessings and the finest in effect. Aqallat: carried and lifted up. The derivation of iqlāl (lifting) is from qilla (lightness), because the one who lifts and is able to lift sees what he lifts as light. Saḥāban thiqālan: heavy clouds laden with water, plural of saḥāba. Suqnāhu: the pronoun refers to the cloud according to its wording; if it were taken according to its meaning, as in thiqāl, it would be feminine. Just as if the adjective were taken according to its wording, one would say thaqīlan. Li-baladin mayyitin: for the sake of a dead land in which there is no life, and so that He may give it drink. It is read mayt. Fa-anzalnā bihi: with it, meaning with the land or with the cloud or with the drive. Likewise fa-akhrajnā bihi: and similarly, kadhālika: like that, i.e., like that bringing out, which is the bringing out of fruits. Nukhriju al-mawtā la'allakum tadhakkarūn: so that the remembrance leads you to realise there is no difference between the two bringings out, since each of them is a return of a thing after its origination.

Wal-baladu al-ṭayyibu: the good land, of good soil and noble earth. Wal-ladhī khabutha: the salt land which does not produce what is beneficial. Bi-idhni rabbihi: by His facilitation, and this is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), as if it were said: "its plant comes out good and abundant," because it stands opposite to nakidan, and nakid is that which has no good in it.

It is read yakhruju nabātuhu, meaning the land brings it out and causes it to grow. His saying wal-ladhī khabutha is an adjective of "land," and its meaning: "The bad land produces its plant only meagrely." The noun that is omitted is "plant," and the genitive noun that is the return to the land is placed in its position, except that it was in the genitive, explicit, so it became nominative, hidden, because it occupies the position of the subject. Or it is estimated as: "and the plant of that which was bad."

It is read nakidan with a fatḥa on the kāf as a verbal noun, meaning "with meagreness." And nakidan with sukūn for lightness, like His saying: nazzih 'ani al-rayb, meaning nazzih. This is an example for those obligated persons upon whom admonition and warning have effect, and for those upon whom nothing of that has effect. [Mujāhid said: Ādam and his progeny: among them is the bad and the good.] Qatāda said: The believer hears the Book of Allah, retains it with his intellect and benefits from it, like the good land which the rain reaches and it produces growth. The disbeliever is the opposite of that. This simile is placed after the mention of rain, its descent on the dead land and the bringing out of fruits by it, by way of digression (istiṭrād), kadhālika: like that, nuṣarrifu al-āyāti: We turn them and repeat them li-qawmin yashkurūn: for a people who give thanks for the blessing of Allah, and they are the believers, so that they may reflect upon them and take lessons from them.

It is read yuṣarrifu, with the yā', meaning Allah turns them.

He does not realise that he has combined two innovations (bid'a): raising the voice in supplication and doing so in the mosque. Sometimes the common people are moved to tenderness by this, which they do not feel when the voice is lowered, dignified bearing is maintained, and the established Sunna (sunna) transmitted by reports is followed. That tenderness is nothing but a softness similar to that which affects women and children; it does not come from the core of the heart. ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾: the answer to an implied oath. If you ask: why do they only use this lam with *qad*, and rarely otherwise? Consider the line of Imru' al-Qays:

[[حلفت لها بالله حلفة فاجر ... لناموا فما إن من حديث ولا صالى
فقالت سباك الله إنك فاضحى ... ألست ترى السمار والنار أحوالى
فأصبحت معشوقا وأصبح يعلها ... عليه قتام كاسف الظن والبال
يغط غطيط البكر شد خناقه ... ليقتلني والمره ليس بقتال
أيقتلنى والمشرفي مضاجعى ... ومسنونة زرق كأنياب أغوال]]

He says: his beloved Salma grew impatient when he watched for her at night, although the watchers were around her. *As-Summar* is the plural of *samir*, meaning one who talks at night; *ahwal* is the plural of *hawl*, meaning side, so it indicates the large number of people and their spread around her sides. It is reported that it has the form of a plural but is not one; likewise its dual, because *hawl* of a thing, *hawlayhi*, *ahwalhu*, *ahwalayhi*, *hawalahu*, *hawalayhi* all mean its surrounding side. The singular may be used metaphorically to mean any side, so it takes the dual and plural form in actual usage. The common practice, when the past tense verb is the answer to an oath, is to join it with *qad*. Indeed, some say that if it is absent, *qad* is assumed to be present, because the answer is expected to be anticipated, which is the meaning of *qad* when the listener first hears the oath. *In* and *min* are added for emphasis. *Al-hadith* means the speaker, so that it matches what follows. *As-sali* means one who warms himself by the fire. Here there is an omission indicated by the context, meaning: "So she was accommodating and I obtained my desire from her, and she was pleased, so I became her beloved, while I had been a lover." Her husband had dust upon him, which is dust and blackness of the face; *kasif az-zann* means dejected in expectation, which is a metaphor; *kasif al-bal* means grieved of heart, or in bad condition. *Al-ghatit* is the rise of the sound of breath during choking, drowsiness, and the like. *Al-bakr* is a young camel. *Al-khanaq* is a rope used to choke, like a belt for what is girded, and a binding for what a prisoner is tied with. His saying *laysa bi-qattal* means: as he claims to be brave. *Al-mashrafi* is the sword, a nisba to Mashariq, the plural of Mashraf, like Ja'far; they are villages in the land of the Arabs near the countryside. He compared it to bedfellows because it stretches beside him and stays with him. *Al-masnunah* of the arrows means those with sharpened points. *Az-zurq* is the plural of *zarqa'*, meaning clear in colour. He compared them to the fangs of ghouls in the sharpness of their points and in the loathing that every soul feels for them. This does not require the existence of the ghoul or the sight of its fang, although the Arabs claim it.

I say: that was only because the oath clause is not used except as an emphasis of the clause it swears to, which is its answer. So it was expected to carry the sense of anticipation, which is the meaning of *qad*, when the addressee hears the word of oath.

The hamza is for disapproval (inkar), and the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf), and the element conjoined to (al-maʿtuf ʿalayhi) is omitted. This is because they used to wonder at the prophethood of Nuh, peace be upon him, and they would say: "We have not heard of this among our first fathers," meaning the sending of a human being. And those who were with him—it is said they were forty men and forty women. And it is said: nine, his sons Sam, Ham and Japheth, and six of those who believed in him. If you ask: "in the ship" (fi al-fulk) — what does it relate to? I answer: it relates to "with him," as if it were said: "and those who settled with him in the ship, or accompanied him in the ship." It is also permissible for it to relate to the verb of deliverance, i.e., "We delivered them in the ship from the flood," ﴿blind﴾, blind of heart, not perceiving. It has also been read ʿāmīn (ʿāmīn). The difference between ʿammā (ʿamā, blindness) and ʿāmī is that ʿamā indicates a blindness that is established, whereas ʿāmī indicates a blindness that is newly arisen. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿and your breast is constricted by it﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 7, verses 70–72:

﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾ They denied and found it implausible that God alone should be worshipped and that the religion of their fathers should be abandoned in favour of taking idols as partners with Him, out of love for what they had been raised upon and attachment to what they found their fathers practising as religion.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "coming" (*al-majī'*) in His words, ﴿Have you come to us?﴾ I say: there are several possibilities. It may be that Hud, peace be upon him, had a place apart from his people where he would seclude himself in worship (*yatahannath*), as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to do at Hira before the prophethood. [Agreed upon (*muttafaq 'alayh*), from the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, on the beginning of revelation: "He used to seclude himself in the cave of Hira, practising worship in it, until the revelation came upon him while he was in the cave of Hira."] Then, when revelation came to him, his people came to him calling them (to God). Or they may have meant it as mockery, because they believed that God sends only angels; so it is as if they said: "Have you come to us from heaven as the angel comes?" Or they did not mean the literal act of coming, but rather a approach and intent, as one says "he went to abuse me" (*dhahaba yashtimunī*) without meaning the literal going. It is as if they said: "Have you intended us, that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with imposing that?"

﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with﴾: this is a request by them for the punishment (to hasten it). ﴿It has already fallen upon you﴾: that is, it has become due and is necessary, or it has already descended upon you. He treated what is expected and must inevitably descend as though it had already occurred. A similar usage is your saying to someone who has asked you for something: "That has already happened." It is related from Hassan that his son 'Abd al-Rahman was stung by a wasp while he was a child, and came crying. He (Hassan) said to him: "My son, what is wrong with you?" He said: "A little insect stung me, as if it were wrapped in two striped Yemeni garments" [Its wording "in two striped garments": *ḥibra*, like *ʿanaba*: a Yemeni cloth. (Ṣiḥāḥ)]. So he embraced him to his chest and said to him: "My son, you have composed poetry!"

*Al-rijs*: punishment, from *al-irtijās*, which is agitation/trembling.

﴿Names that you have named﴾: these are things which are merely names with no named realities beneath them, because you call them gods, while the meaning of divinity is non-existent in them and impossible for them to have. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿what you worship besides Him is nothing but names﴾. The meaning of ﴿you named them﴾ is "you named them with," as in "I named him Zayd."

*Qat' dabirahum*: their uprooting, their total annihilation down to the last of them.

The story of them is that the 'Ad had spread throughout the lands between 'Uman and Hadramawt. They had idols which they worshipped: Sada', Sammud, and al-Habba'. God sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was among the most noble and excellent of them in lineage. They denied him and increased in insolence and arrogance. So God withheld rain from them for three years until they were afflicted with hardship. Whenever calamity befell people, they would ask God for relief at His Sacred House, both Muslim and polytheist. At that time the people of Mecca were the 'Amalīq, descendants of 'Umlīq ibn Lāwadh ibn Sām ibn Nūh, and their chief was Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr. The 'Ad sent seventy of their notable men to Mecca, among them Qayl ibn 'Anz and Martha ibn Sa'd, who had been concealing his Islam. When they arrived, they stayed with Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca beyond the Sacred Precinct (*haram*). He lodged them and honoured them, as they were his maternal uncles and in-laws. They remained with him for a month, drinking wine while two singing girls, al-Jaradatān, who were Mu'āwiya's, sang to them. When he saw how long they stayed and how they were absorbed in amusement and had forgotten what they came for, it troubled him, and he said: "My maternal uncles and in-laws are perishing, and these people are as they are." He was too shy to speak to them, fearing they would think his hosting them had become a burden. So he mentioned that to the two girls. They said: "Compose a poem for them to sing, so they will not know who composed it." So Mu'āwiya said:

Ah, Qayl, woe to you, stand up and make a murmured supplication,
perhaps God will give us rain as clouds.

So that He waters the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad
have become unable to speak clearly,

From severe thirst; we do not hope for it
(for it), the old man nor the boy.

Their women were once in goodness,
but now their women have become widows (*ayāmā*),

And wild beasts come to them openly,
and do not fear the arrows of the 'Adites.

And you are here, in what you desire,
your day and your night in complete pleasure.

Evil is your delegation, of a people
who neither greet nor give salutation.

[This is what is said for Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr. It is reported that 'Ad sent from among their people: Qayl ibn 'Anz, Nu'aym ibn Hazāla, Martha ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, Julhuma ibn al-Hals, maternal uncle of Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr, and Luqmān ibn 'Ad, each with a group of their kin, to supplicate God for rain at the Ka'ba. They lodged with Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr, who honoured them and sent the two girls to sing for them, the two being singing girls, the first to sing among the women of the Arabs. They forgot their people through excessive amusement and merriment. Mu'āwiya said: "My maternal uncles are perishing, and if I say something to them they will think me stingy." So he composed this and ordered the two girls to sing it to them. *Al-hay'ama*: a faint sound that is not understood. Its meaning is supplication to God for rain. *Yasqīnā ghamāman*: meaning water of clouds. *Mā yubayyinūna al-kalām*: because of their weakness from thirst. "*Fa-laysa narjū*" means "we do not hope for her," that is, for 'Ad. It is also narrated as "*bihi*," meaning because of thirst. The correct transmission is "*bihā*," meaning in the land of 'Ad. *Al-shaykh wa-lā al-ghulām*: *al-'ayma* is intense desire for milk. Its meaning is absolute destitution. *Al-'ayāmā*: plural of *ʿayyim* (with shadda), meaning one of weak condition; its root is *ʿayāʾim*, changed to *ʿayāmā*, as *ayāmā* is reported, which is the plural of *ayyim*, originally *ayāʾim*, meaning women who have lost their husbands. The meaning is thus by way of comparison. It is also possible that the intended meaning is your women whom you left behind, as if they were without husbands there. The repetition of "women" is for the purpose of eliciting compassion for them. *Al-ʿādī*: a relative adjective from 'Ad, and they were the harsh and mighty. *Al-wahsh*: a collective noun of plurality, singular *wahshī*, like *kānis* and *insī*, *turk* and *turkī*. It is treated as masculine in terms of its form and as feminine in terms of its collectivity. It is also reported as "*bihimā*." *Nahārakum*: accusative as an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*). *Min wafd qawm*: the specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Al-salām* is conjoined to *al-taḥiyya*, and it contains a double meaning (*tawriya*), because it points to the cessation of speech, just as those who meet bring it at parting. When the people heard this, they set off for the Ka'ba. Martha ibn Sa'd, who was a believer, caught up with them and reproached them. He supplicated God for himself, not for the people. Qayl said:

"O God, if Hud is truthful, give us water."

So He produced a white cloud, a red cloud, and a black cloud. Then a voice called: "O Qayl, choose whichever you wish." He said: "As for the white, it is a sudden cloud (*jafl*); as for the red, it is a passing cloud (*ʿāriḍ*); as for the black, it is a heavy-pouring cloud (*hayṭal*)." He chose it, and then the voice called: "You have chosen ashes, scorching ashes, which will leave none of 'Ad, neither parent nor child." The black cloud moved against 'Ad and destroyed them. Luqmān ibn 'Ad came after they had finished their supplications and said: "O God, I have come to You alone, so give me what I ask." He asked for seven vultures (*ansur*), and the age of the vulture was eighty years. He would take a vulture from its nest and keep it with him until it died. The last of his vultures was named Labad, and when it died, he died.]

Then, this (story) happened before Mecca and Zamzam existed, for they were only found in the time of Abraham and Ishmael. So perhaps Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr lived close to the place of Mecca, not in the place itself, because at that time there was neither pasture nor water there. When the two girls sang it, the people said: "Your people are seeking relief from the calamity that has befallen them, and you have been slow to help them. Enter the Sacred Precinct and ask for rain for your people." Martha ibn Sa'd said to them: "By God, you will not be given water by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and repent to God, you will be given water." He had made his Islam apparent. They said to Mu'āwiya: "Hold back Martha, so that he does not come with us to Mecca, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion." Then they entered Mecca. Qayl said: "O God, give water to 'Ad as You used to give it to them." So God produced three clouds, white, red, and black. Then a caller called to him from heaven:

"O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people."

He said: "I choose the black, for it is the most abundant in water." It came out upon 'Ad from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. They rejoiced at it and said: "This is a cloud that will bring us rain." But there came from it a barren wind, which destroyed them. Hud and the believers with him were saved; they came to Mecca and worshipped God there until they died.

If you ask: what is the benefit of denying belief to them in His words ﴿and they were not believers﴾, together with affirming that they denied the signs of God? I say: it is an allusion (*taʿrīḍ*) to those among them who believed, such as Martha ibn Sa'd and those who were saved with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: "We cut off the last of those among them who denied, and they were not like those among them who believed," to make clear that destruction was specific to the deniers, and God saved the believers.

He chose it, and then the voice called: "You have chosen ashes, scorching ashes, which will leave none of 'Ad, neither parent nor child." The black cloud moved against 'Ad and destroyed them. Luqmān ibn 'Ad came after they had finished their supplications and said: "O God, I have come to You alone, so give me what I ask." He asked for seven vultures (*ansur*), and the age of the vulture was eighty years. He would take a vulture from its nest and keep it with him until it died. The last of his vultures was named Labad, and when it died, he died.]

Then, this (story) happened before Mecca and Zamzam existed, for they were only found in the time of Abraham and Ishmael. So perhaps Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr lived close to the place of Mecca, not in the place itself, because at that time there was neither pasture nor water there. When the two girls sang it, the people said: "Your people are seeking relief from the calamity that has befallen them, and you have been slow to help them. Enter the Sacred Precinct and ask for rain for your people." Martha ibn Sa'd said to them: "By God, you will not be given water by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and repent to God, you will be given water." He had made his Islam apparent. They said to Mu'āwiya: "Hold back Martha, so that he does not come with us to Mecca, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion." Then they entered Mecca. Qayl said: "O God, give water to 'Ad as You used to give it to them." So God produced three clouds, white, red, and black. Then a caller called to him from heaven:

"O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people."

He said: "I choose the black, for it is the most abundant in water." It came out upon 'Ad from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. They rejoiced at it and said: "This is a cloud that will bring us rain." But there came from it a barren wind, which destroyed them. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 7, verses 70–72:

﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾ They denied and found it implausible that God alone should be worshipped and that the religion of their fathers should be abandoned in favour of taking idols as partners with Him, out of love for what they had been raised upon and attachment to what they found their fathers practising as religion.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "coming" (*al-majī'*) in His words, ﴿Have you come to us?﴾ I say: there are several possibilities. It may be that Hud, peace be upon him, had a place apart from his people where he would seclude himself in worship (*yatahannath*), as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to do at Hira before the prophethood. [Agreed upon (*muttafaq 'alayh*), from the hadith of 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, on the beginning of revelation: "He used to seclude himself in the cave of Hira, practising worship in it, until the revelation came upon him while he was in the cave of Hira."] Then, when revelation came to him, his people came to him calling them (to God). Or they may have meant it as mockery, because they believed that God sends only angels; so it is as if they said: "Have you come to us from heaven as the angel comes?" Or they did not mean the literal act of coming, but rather a approach and intent, as one says "he went to abuse me" (*dhahaba yashtimunī*) without meaning the literal going. It is as if they said: "Have you intended us, that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with imposing that?"

﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with﴾: this is a request by them for the punishment (to hasten it). ﴿It has already fallen upon you﴾: that is, it has become due and is necessary, or it has already descended upon you. He treated what is expected and must inevitably descend as though it had already occurred. A similar usage is your saying to someone who has asked you for something: "That has already happened." It is related from Hassan that his son 'Abd al-Rahman was stung by a wasp while he was a child, and came crying. He (Hassan) said to him: "My son, what is wrong with you?" He said: "A little insect stung me, as if it were wrapped in two striped Yemeni garments" [Its wording "in two striped garments": *ḥibra*, like *ʿanaba*: a Yemeni cloth. (Ṣiḥāḥ)]. So he embraced him to his chest and said to him: "My son, you have composed poetry!"

*Al-rijs*: punishment, from *al-irtijās*, which is agitation/trembling.

﴿Names that you have named﴾: these are things which are merely names with no named realities beneath them, because you call them gods, while the meaning of divinity is non-existent in them and impossible for them to have. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿what you worship besides Him is nothing but names﴾. The meaning of ﴿you named them﴾ is "you named them with," as in "I named him Zayd."

*Qat' dabirahum*: their uprooting, their total annihilation down to the last of them.

The story of them is that the 'Ad had spread throughout the lands between 'Uman and Hadramawt. They had idols which they worshipped: Sada', Sammud, and al-Habba'. God sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was among the most noble and excellent of them in lineage. They denied him and increased in insolence and arrogance. So God withheld rain from them for three years until they were afflicted with hardship. Whenever calamity befell people, they would ask God for relief at His Sacred House, both Muslim and polytheist. At that time the people of Mecca were the 'Amalīq, descendants of 'Umlīq ibn Lāwadh ibn Sām ibn Nūh, and their chief was Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr. The 'Ad sent seventy of their notable men to Mecca, among them Qayl ibn 'Anz and Martha ibn Sa'd, who had been concealing his Islam. When they arrived, they stayed with Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca beyond the Sacred Precinct (*haram*). He lodged them and honoured them, as they were his maternal uncles and in-laws. They remained with him for a month, drinking wine while two singing girls, al-Jaradatān, who were Mu'āwiya's, sang to them. When he saw how long they stayed and how they were absorbed in amusement and had forgotten what they came for, it troubled him, and he said: "My maternal uncles and in-laws are perishing, and these people are as they are." He was too shy to speak to them, fearing they would think his hosting them had become a burden. So he mentioned that to the two girls. They said: "Compose a poem for them to sing, so they will not know who composed it." So Mu'āwiya said:

Ah, Qayl, woe to you, stand up and make a murmured supplication,
perhaps God will give us rain as clouds.

So that He waters the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad
have become unable to speak clearly,

From severe thirst; we do not hope for it
(for it), the old man nor the boy.

Their women were once in goodness,
but now their women have become widows (*ayāmā*),

And wild beasts come to them openly,
and do not fear the arrows of the 'Adites.

And you are here, in what you desire,
your day and your night in complete pleasure.

Evil is your delegation, of a people
who neither greet nor give salutation.

[This is what is said for Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr. It is reported that 'Ad sent from among their people: Qayl ibn 'Anz, Nu'aym ibn Hazāla, Martha ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, Julhuma ibn al-Hals, maternal uncle of Mu'āwiya ibn Bakr, and Luqmān ibn 'Ad, each with a group of their kin, to supplicate God for rain at the Ka'ba. So he composed this and ordered the two girls to sing it to them. *Al-hay'ama*: a faint sound that is not understood. Its meaning is supplication to God for rain. *Yasqīnā ghamāman*: meaning water of clouds. *Mā yubayyinūna al-kalām*: because of their weakness from thirst. "*Fa-laysa narjū*" means "we do not hope for her," that is, for 'Ad. It is also narrated as "*bihi*," meaning because of thirst. The correct transmission is "*bihā*," meaning in the land of 'Ad. *Al-shaykh wa-lā al-ghulām*: *al-'ayma* is intense desire for milk. Its meaning is absolute destitution. *Al-'ayāmā*: plural of *ʿayyim* (with shadda), meaning one of weak condition; its root is *ʿayāʾim*, changed to *ʿayāmā*, as *ayāmā* is reported, which is the plural of *ayyim*, originally *ayāʾim*, meaning women who have lost their husbands. The meaning is thus by way of comparison. It is also possible that the intended meaning is your women whom you left behind, as if they were without husbands there. The repetition of "women" is for the purpose of eliciting compassion for them. *Al-ʿādī*: a relative adjective from 'Ad, and they were the harsh and mighty. *Al-wahsh*: a collective noun of plurality, singular *wahshī*, like *kānis* and *insī*, *turk* and *turkī*. It is treated as masculine in terms of its form and as feminine in terms of its collectivity. It is also reported as "*bihimā*." *Nahārakum*: accusative as an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*). *Min wafd qawm*: the specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Al-salām* is conjoined to *al-taḥiyya*, and it contains a double meaning (*tawriya*), because it points to the cessation of speech, just as those who meet bring it at parting. He said: "As for the white, it is a sudden cloud (*jafl*); as for the red, it is a passing cloud (*ʿāriḍ*); as for the black, it is a heavy-pouring cloud (*hayṭal*)." **Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 73–74:**

It is read as *Wa-ilā Thamūda* with no nunation (*man' al-ṣarf*), by interpreting the name as a tribe, and as *Wa-ilā Thamūdin* with nunation, by interpreting it as a living group, or by considering the original name, since it is the name of their greatest ancestor, Thamūd ibn ʿĀbir ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ. It has also been said that Thamūd was named after the scarcity of its water, from *al-thamd*, meaning little water. Their dwellings were the rock-cut houses (*al-Ḥijr*) between al-Shām and al-Ḥijāz, extending to Wādī al-Qurā.

﴿قَدْ جَاءَتْكُم بَيِّنَةٌ﴾ "There has come to you a clear proof," meaning a manifest sign and evidence for the truth of my prophethood. It is as if it were asked: "What is this proof?" So he said: ﴿هَٰذِهِ نَاقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكُمْ آيَةً﴾ "This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you."

*Āya* (a sign) is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), and the element that governs it is the meaning of the verb implied by the demonstrative, as if it were said: "It is pointed to as a sign." *Lakum* (for you) explains for whom it is a sign that obligates belief specifically: they are Thamūd, because they witnessed it, whereas the rest of the people only received reports about it, and report is not like witnessing. It is as if he said: "For you specifically." It was attributed to the name of Allah only to magnify it and to exalt its status, and because it came from Him, created without a stallion and without mating, as a sign of His signs, just as you say "the sign of Allah."

It is related that when ʿĀd was destroyed, Thamūd rebuilt its lands and succeeded them on the earth. They multiplied and lived very long lives, so much so that a man would build a sturdy dwelling and it would collapse during his lifetime. They therefore carved houses out of the mountains. They lived in ease and plenty, but they transgressed against Allah, spread corruption on the earth, and worshipped idols. So Allah sent Ṣāliḥ (ʿalayhi al-salām) to them. They were an Arab people, and Ṣāliḥ was of the most noble lineage among them. He called them to Allah, but only a few of them followed him, and they were the weak. He warned them and admonished them. They asked him for a sign, and he said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "Come out with us to our festival on a known day of the year, and you call upon your god while we call upon our gods. If yours is answered for you, we will follow you, and if ours is answered for us, you will follow us." Ṣāliḥ said: "Yes." So he went out with them. They called upon their idols and asked them to respond, but they did not answer them. Then their chief, Jundaʿ ibn ʿAmr, said, pointing to a single rock on the side of the mountain called al-Kāthiba: "Bring forth for us from this rock a she-camel, pregnant and hollow-sided and crying out"—*al-mukhtarija* being the one that resembles the female camel in the *al-bakht* type—"and if you do, we will believe you and respond to you." Ṣāliḥ (ʿalayhi al-salām) took covenants from them that if he did that, they would certainly believe and certainly affirm. They said: "Yes." So he prayed to his Lord, and the rock writhed like a pregnant woman in labour, and it split open, bringing forth a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and crying out, just as they had described. No one knew what was between her two sides except Allah, while their nobles watched. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundaʿ and a group of his people believed, but some of their leaders prevented their descendants from believing.

The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing on the trees and drinking water. She used to come to water on alternate days, and on her day she would put her head into the well and not lift it until she had drunk all the water in it. Then she would spread her legs apart, and they would milk her as much as they wished until their vessels were full, and they would drink and store it.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said: "I came to the land of Thamūd and measured the watering place of the she-camel, and I found it to be sixty cubits."

When the heat came, the she-camel would take up residence on the top of the valley, and their livestock would flee from her and descend to its bottom. When the cold came, she would spread across the bottom of the valley, and their livestock would flee to its top. This was hard for them. Two women, ʿUnayza, the mother of Ghanam, and Ṣadaqa bint al-Mukhtār, made the slaughter of her attractive to them, because she harmed their livestock, and they both had many animals. So they slaughtered her, divided her meat, and cooked it. Her young one ran off until it climbed a mountain called Qāra and cried out three times. Ṣāliḥ had said to them: "Catch the young camel; perhaps it will lift the punishment from you," but they could not catch it. After its cry, the rock split open and it entered it.

Ṣāliḥ said to them: "You will wake up tomorrow with your faces yellow; the day after tomorrow your faces will be red; and on the third day your faces will be black. Then the punishment will overtake you in the morning." When they saw these signs, they sought to kill him. But Allah saved him and brought him to the land of Palestine. When the fourth day came and the forenoon had risen, they embalmed themselves with aloe and shrouded themselves in leather mats. Then a cry came to them from the sky, and their hearts were torn apart, and they perished.

﴿تَأْكُلْ فِي أَرْضِ اللَّهِ﴾ "that she may eat in the land of Allah." That is, the land is the land of Allah and the she-camel is the she-camel of Allah, so leave her to eat in the land of her Lord. The land does not belong to you, nor does the vegetation in it come from your growing it. ﴿وَلَا تَمَسُّوهَا بِسُوءٍ﴾ "and do not touch her with harm": do not strike her, do not drive her away, and do not disturb her with any kind of harm, out of honour for the sign of Allah.

It is related that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by the rock during the expedition to Tabūk, he said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people, unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." [Agreed upon from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, through several chains.]

He (ﷺ) also said: "O ʿAlī, do you know who is the most wretched of the first (generation)?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ. Do you know who is the most wretched of the last (generation)?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The one who will strike you." [This was related by Ibn Isḥāq in al-Maghāzī: Yazīd ibn Muḥammad ibn Khaythama narrated to me, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, from Muḥammad ibn Khaythama, the father of the aforementioned Yazīd, from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir who said: "I and ʿAlī were companions in the expedition of hardship," until he said: He said: "O ʿAlī, shall I not inform you of the most wretched of people, two men?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Thamūd, the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and the one who will strike you, O ʿAlī, on this"—and he pointed to his head—"until this becomes wet," and he placed his hand on his beard. From this route, al-Nasāʾī in al-Khaṣāʾiṣ, al-Ḥākim, al-Ṭabarī and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil also related it. On this subject there is also a report from Jābir ibn Samura related by al-Ṭabarānī, and from Ṣuhayb related by Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ṭabarānī, and from ʿAlī related by Ibn Mardawayh in his tafsir of "By the sun and its brightness."

Note: In the version of the aforementioned narrators, that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked ʿAlī, he said to him at first: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel." He said: "You have spoken the truth." In the second he said: "I have no knowledge." In the report of Jābir ibn Samura: "Allah knows best."]

Abū Jaʿfar recited in a reported reading *Ta'kulu fī arḍi Allāh* (with the verb in the form "eating in the land of Allah"), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, in the sense of *ākila* (eating).

﴿وَبَوَّأَكُمْ﴾ "and settled you," meaning: lodged you. *Al-mabāʾa* means the dwelling. ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ "in the land," in the land of Ḥijr between al-Ḥijāz and al-Shām. ﴿مِن سُهُولِهَا قُصُورًا﴾ "from its plains, palaces," meaning: you build them from the softness of the land, from what you make of it: *al-rahṣ* (the solid rock set at the base of a wall), clay bricks, and fired brick.

Al-Ḥasan recited *wa-tanḥitūna* with a fatḥa on the *ḥāʾ*, and *tanḥātūna* with the fatḥa lengthened, as in the verse of the poet:

*yunbāʿu min dhafrā asīlin ḥurratin*
*zayyāfatin mithla al-fanīqi al-mukarrami*

It is from the Muʿallaqa of ʿAntara ibn Shaddād al-ʿAbsī, describing the sweat of his she-camel from the journey. He likened it to *al-rubb* (concentrated must) and *al-ṭilāʾ* (boiled liquor), or to *al-kuḥayl*, which is tar that has been hardened by fire on the sides of a kettle. *Aʿqadtu al-dawāʾ* means: I boiled the medicine until it thickened. *Ḥashsha al-wuqūd* means: he kindled and lit the fire, and here it is in the passive voice. The original of *yunbāʿu* is *yanbaʿu*, and the alif was generated for lengthening. *Al-dhafrā* is the depressed hollow beside the ear; when the camel's journey is long, the skin in its middle swells and rises, and sweat flows out into the hollow, and this is the thing likened earlier to the kettle. It has been said that *al-dhafrā* is the root of the ear. *Al-asīl* is the she-camel of straight build, from their saying "a long cheek" and "a long palm." *Ḥurr* of everything means its purest part. *Zayyāfa* means: abundant in swaying, which is strutting in walking. *Al-fanīq* is the stallion camel that is honoured by being excused from work for the purpose of mating, so *al-mukarram* is an explanatory epithet. It is also reported as *al-mukaddam* with a *dāl*; one says *kaddamahu* when one bites him, and as for *akdamahu*, I have not found it, and it is probably a rare dialect form. *Al-mukaddam* is its passive participle, meaning the one the stallions have bitten and gnawed, so that it leaves marks on it from the saddle and the spurring. It is also reported: "from the *dhafrā* of a furious, firm, sturdy-built she-camel," meaning very angry, hard, and firmly built. It has been said that *yunbāʿu* is of the form *yanfaʿilu* from *al-buʿ*, which is covering a great distance, but there is no meaning for it in the verse.

If you ask: "What is *buyūtan* in the accusative?" I say: it is a circumstantial accusative, as you say: "sew this cloth as a shirt" and "sharpen this reed as a pen." It is among the *ḥāl muqaddara* (the anticipated circumstantial clause), because a mountain is not a house at the time of carving, nor is the cloth a shirt or the reed a pen at the time of sewing and sharpening.

It has also been said: they used to dwell in the plains in summer and in the mountains in winter.

Then their chief, Jundaʿ ibn ʿAmr, said, pointing to a single rock on the side of the mountain called al-Kāthiba: "Bring forth for us from this rock a she-camel, pregnant and hollow-sided and crying out"—*al-mukhtarija* being the one that resembles the female camel in the *al-bakht* type—"and if you do, we will believe you and respond to you." Ṣāliḥ (ʿalayhi al-salām) took covenants from them that if he did that, they would certainly believe and certainly affirm. They said: "Yes." So he prayed to his Lord, and the rock writhed like a pregnant woman in labour, and it split open, bringing forth a she-camel, pregnant, hollow-sided and crying out, just as they had described. No one knew what was between her two sides except Allah, while their nobles watched. Then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundaʿ and a group of his people believed, but some of their leaders prevented their descendants from believing.

The she-camel remained with her young one, grazing on the trees and drinking water. She used to come to water on alternate days, and on her day she would put her head into the well and not lift it until she had drunk all the water in it. Then she would spread her legs apart, and they would milk her as much as they wished until their vessels were full, and they would drink and store it.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī said: "I came to the land of Thamūd and measured the watering place of the she-camel, and I found it to be sixty cubits."

When the heat came, the she-camel would take up residence on the top of the valley, and their livestock would flee from her and descend to its bottom. When the cold came, she would spread across the bottom of the valley, and their livestock would flee to its top. This was hard for them. Two women, ʿUnayza, the mother of Ghanam, and Ṣadaqa bint al-Mukhtār, made the slaughter of her attractive to them, because she harmed their livestock, and they both had many animals. So they slaughtered her, divided her meat, and cooked it. Her young one ran off until it climbed a mountain called Qāra and cried out three times. Ṣāliḥ had said to them: "Catch the young camel; perhaps it will lift the punishment from you," but they could not catch it. After its cry, the rock split open and it entered it.

Ṣāliḥ said to them: "You will wake up tomorrow with your faces yellow; the day after tomorrow your faces will be red; and on the third day your faces will be black. Then the punishment will overtake you in the morning." When they saw these signs, they sought to kill him. But Allah saved him and brought him to the land of Palestine. When the fourth day came and the forenoon had risen, they embalmed themselves with aloe and shrouded themselves in leather mats. Then a cry came to them from the sky, and their hearts were torn apart, and they perished.

﴿تَأْكُلْ فِي أَرْضِ اللَّهِ﴾ "that she may eat in the land of Allah." That is, the land is the land of Allah and the she-camel is the she-camel of Allah, so leave her to eat in the land of her Lord. The land does not belong to you, nor does the vegetation in it come from your growing it. ﴿وَلَا تَمَسُّوهَا بِسُوءٍ﴾ "and do not touch her with harm": do not strike her, do not drive her away, and do not disturb her with any kind of harm, out of honour for the sign of Allah.

It is related that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by the rock during the expedition to Tabūk, he said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people, unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." [Agreed upon from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, through several chains.]

He (ﷺ) also said: "O ʿAlī, do you know who is the most wretched of the first (generation)?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ. Do you know who is the most wretched of the last (generation)?" He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The one who will strike you." [This was related by Ibn Isḥāq in al-Maghāzī: Yazīd ibn Muḥammad ibn Khaythama narrated to me, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, from Muḥammad ibn Khaythama, the father of the aforementioned Yazīd, from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir who said: "I and ʿAlī were companions in the expedition of hardship," until he said: He said: "O ʿAlī, shall I not inform you of the most wretched of people, two men?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Thamūd, the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and the one who will strike you, O ʿAlī, on this"—and he pointed to his head—"until this becomes wet," and he placed his hand on his beard. From this route, al-Nasāʾī in al-Khaṣāʾiṣ, al-Ḥākim, al-Ṭabarī and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil also related it. On this subject there is also a report from Jābir ibn Samura related by al-Ṭabarānī, and from Ṣuhayb related by Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ṭabarānī, and from ʿAlī related by Ibn Mardawayh in his tafsir of "By the sun and its brightness."

Note: In the version of the aforementioned narrators, that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked ʿAlī, he said to him at first: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel." He said: "You have spoken the truth." In the second he said: "I have no knowledge." In the report of Jābir ibn Samura: "Allah knows best."]

Abū Jaʿfar recited in a reported reading *Ta'kulu fī arḍi Allāh* (with the verb in the form "eating in the land of Allah"), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, in the sense of *ākila* (eating).

﴿وَبَوَّأَكُمْ﴾ "and settled you," meaning: lodged you. *Al-mabāʾa* means the dwelling. ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ "in the land," in the land of Ḥijr between al-Ḥijāz and al-Shām. ﴿مِن سُهُولِهَا قُصُورًا﴾ "from its plains, palaces," meaning: you build them from the softness of the land, from what you make of it: *al-rahṣ* (the solid rock set at the base of a wall), clay bricks, and fired brick.

Al-Ḥasan recited *wa-tanḥitūna* with a fatḥa on the *ḥāʾ*, and *tanḥātūna* with the fatḥa lengthened, as in the verse of the poet:

*yunbāʿu min dhafrā asīlin ḥurratin*
*zayyāfatin mithla al-fanīqi al-mukarrami*

It is from the Muʿallaqa of ʿAntara ibn Shaddād al-ʿAbsī, describing the sweat of his she-camel from the journey. He likened it to *al-rubb* (concentrated must) and *al-ṭilāʾ* (boiled liquor), or to *al-kuḥayl*, which is tar that has been hardened by fire on the sides of a kettle. *Aʿqadtu al-dawāʾ* means: I boiled the medicine until it thickened. *Ḥashsha al-wuqūd* means: he kindled and lit the fire, and here it is in the passive voice. The original of *yunbāʿu* is *yanbaʿu*, and the alif was generated for lengthening. *Al-dhafrā* is the depressed hollow beside the ear; when the camel's journey is long, the skin in its middle swells and rises, and sweat flows out into the hollow, and this is the thing likened earlier to the kettle. It has been said that *al-dhafrā* is the root of the ear. *Al-asīl* is the she-camel of straight build, from their saying "a long cheek" and "a long palm." *Ḥurr* of everything means its purest part. *Zayyāfa* means: abundant in swaying, which is strutting in walking. *Al-fanīq* is the stallion camel that is honoured by being excused from work for the purpose of mating, so *al-mukarram* is an explanatory epithet. It is also reported as *al-mukaddam* with a *dāl*; one says *kaddamahu* when one bites him, and as for *akdamahu*, I have not found it, and it is probably a rare dialect form. *Al-mukaddam* is its passive participle, meaning the one the stallions have bitten and gnawed, so that it leaves marks on it from the saddle and the spurring. It is also reported: "from the *dhafrā* of a furious, firm, sturdy-built she-camel," meaning very angry, hard, and firmly built. It has been said that *yunbāʿu* is of the form *yanfaʿilu* from *al-buʿ*, which is covering a great distance, but there is no meaning for it in the verse.

If you ask: "What is *buyūtan* in the accusative?" I say: it is a circumstantial accusative, as you say: "sew this cloth as a shirt" and "sharpen this reed as a pen." It is among the *ḥāl muqaddara* (the anticipated circumstantial clause), because a mountain is not a house at the time of carving, nor is the cloth a shirt or the reed a pen at the time of sewing and sharpening.

It has also been said: they used to dwell in the plains in summer and in the mountains in winter.

To those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed. This is a substitute (badal) for "those who were deemed weak." The pronoun in "minhum" refers back to whom? I say: to his people, or to "those who were deemed weak." If you ask whether the difference in the two antecedents makes any difference in meaning, I say yes. If it refers to his people, then "to those among them who believed" is an explanation of those among them who were oppressed, which shows that their oppression was limited to the believers. If it refers to "those who were deemed weak," then the oppression was not limited to them, and it shows that the oppressed were both believers and disbelievers.

﴿Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?﴾ This was said in mockery and derision, as you say to the anthropomorphists: "Do you know that God is above the Throne?"

If you ask how their saying ﴿We believe in what he has been sent with﴾ could be a reply to this, I say: they were asked about their knowledge of his being sent, so they treated his being sent as a known, uncovered, accepted matter that admits no doubt, as if they said: knowledge of his being sent and of what he was sent with is something beyond dispute and no doubt can enter it, owing to its clarity and manifestness. The dispute is only about the obligation to believe in it, so we inform you that we believe in it. For this reason the disbelievers' reply was ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you believed in﴾. They put "you believed in" in place of "he was sent with," in rejection of what the believers had taken as known and accepted.

﴿And they hamstrung the she-camel﴾. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because it occurred with their consent, even though only some of them carried it out. It is said of a large tribe: "You did such-and-such," though only one of them did it.

﴿And they defied the command of their Lord﴾, meaning they turned away from it and were arrogant in refusing to obey it. "Their Lord's command" is what was commanded through the tongue of Salih, peace be upon him, namely: ﴿Leave her to eat in God's land﴾; or it means the affair of their Lord, which is His religion. It is also possible that the meaning is: their defiance originated from their Lord's command, as if the command of their Lord to leave her was the cause of their defiance. A similar use of "from" is in His saying: ﴿What I did was not by my own command﴾, meaning the punishment they were promised. The usage is permissible because it was known.

Their urging for it [the punishment] was due to their denial of it, and for this reason they tied it to what they disbelieved in, namely his being one of the messengers.

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: the cry by which the earth was shaken and they were agitated. ﴿In their homes﴾: in their lands, or in their dwellings. ﴿Prostrate﴾: motionless, not moving, dead. It is said: "People are jathm," meaning they sit without movement and do not utter a sound. From this comes al-mujthamah (an animal tied up with its legs bound so that it may be shot at), which the Prophet forbade.

[Regarding the prohibition: Abu Dawud, Ibn Hayyan, and al-Hakim narrated it from the hadith of Qatadah, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: "The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade drinking from the mouth of a water-skin, riding a jalalah (a beast that eats filth), and al-mujthamah." Al-Bazzar narrated it through al-Warraq, from Qatadah, from Anas, with the same wording. Al-Bazzar also narrated it and said: its isnad is good. And from the hadith of al-Irbad ibn Sariyah: "The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade al-mujthamah," narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, through the narration of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab from Abu al-Darda, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade eating al-mujthamah, which is that which is struck with arrows."]

From Jabir: when the Prophet ﷺ passed by al-Hijr, he said: "Do not ask for signs, for the people of Salih asked for them and the cry seized them, and none of them remained except one man who was in the sanctuary of God." They said: "Who is he?" He said: "That is Abu Raghal. When he left the sanctuary, what had happened to his people befell him." [Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ishaq, and al-Tabari narrated it through Abd Allah ibn Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, with the addition "in the Battle of Tabuk," and he stood and addressed the people.]

It is related that Salih had sent him to a people, and he disobeyed his command. It is also related that the Prophet ﷺ passed by the grave of Abu Raghal and said: "Do you know who this is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He then mentioned the story of Abu Raghal, that he was buried here and a branch of gold was buried with him. So they rushed to it and searched for it with their swords and extracted the branch. [Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated it through Bujayr ibn Abi Bujayr, from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As, and its wording is: "So the people rushed to it and extracted the branch." As for his saying "they searched for it with their swords," it was narrated by Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar as mursal (with a missing companion in the chain).]

﴿So he turned away from them﴾. The apparent meaning is that he was present for what happened to them, and that he turned away from them after seeing them prostrate, turning away grieved and regretful over what he had missed of their faith, sorrowing for them and saying: ﴿O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not like those who give advice.﴾ It is also possible that "turned away from them" means he departed from them, disowning their persistence when he saw the signs before the punishment descended. It is related that their slaughter of the she-camel was on Wednesday, and the punishment descended on them on Saturday. It is related that he went out with a hundred and ten Muslims, weeping, and he turned and saw the smoke rising, and knew that they had perished; and they were fifteen hundred households. It is related that he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their homes.

If you ask how addressing the dead was valid, and his saying ﴿But you do not like those who give advice﴾: I say, a man may say to his companion, when the latter is dead, and he had advised him while alive but he did not listen until he threw himself into ruin: "O my brother, how often did I advise you, and how often did I tell you, and you did not accept from me?" And his saying ﴿But you do not like those who give advice﴾ is the report of a past state.

To those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed. This is a substitute (badal) for "those who were deemed weak." The pronoun in "minhum" refers back to whom? I say: to his people, or to "those who were deemed weak." If you ask whether the difference in the two antecedents makes any difference in meaning, I say yes. If it refers to his people, then "to those among them who believed" is an explanation of those among them who were oppressed, which shows that their oppression was limited to the believers. If it refers to "those who were deemed weak," then the oppression was not limited to them, and it shows that the oppressed were both believers and disbelievers.

If you ask how their saying ﴿We believe in what he has been sent with﴾ could be a reply to this, I say: they were asked about their knowledge of his being sent, so they treated his being sent as a known, uncovered, accepted matter that admits no doubt, as if they said: knowledge of his being sent and of what he was sent with is something beyond dispute and no doubt can enter it, owing to its clarity and manifestness. The dispute is only about the obligation to believe in it, so we inform you that we believe in it. For this reason the disbelievers' reply was ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you believed in﴾. They put "you believed in" in place of "he was sent with," in rejection of what the believers had taken as known and accepted.

"Their Lord's command" is what was commanded through the tongue of Salih, peace be upon him, namely: ﴿Leave her to eat in God's land﴾; or it means the affair of their Lord, which is His religion. A similar use of "from" is in His saying: ﴿What I did was not by my own command﴾, meaning the punishment they were promised. The usage is permissible because it was known.

Their urging for it [the punishment] was due to their denial of it, and for this reason they tied it to what they disbelieved in, namely his being one of the messengers.

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: the cry by which the earth was shaken and they were agitated. ﴿In their homes﴾: in their lands, or in their dwellings. ﴿Prostrate﴾: motionless, not moving, dead. It is said: "People are jathm," meaning they sit without movement and do not utter a sound. From this comes al-mujthamah (an animal tied up with its legs bound so that it may be shot at), which the Prophet forbade.

[Regarding the prohibition: Abu Dawud, Ibn Hayyan, and al-Hakim narrated it from the hadith of Qatadah, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: "The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade drinking from the mouth of a water-skin, riding a jalalah (a beast that eats filth), and al-mujthamah." It is related that Salih had sent him to a people, and he disobeyed his command. It is also related that the Prophet ﷺ passed by the grave of Abu Raghal and said: "Do you know who this is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He then mentioned the story of Abu Raghal, that he was buried here and a branch of gold was buried with him. It is related that he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their homes.

"From anyone in the worlds." The first "min" is extra, for emphasizing the negation and conveying comprehensiveness (istighraq). The second "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿid).

If you ask: what is the position of this sentence? I answer: it is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) sentence. It is also read "innakum," as a new statement: "you approach men." "Ataa al-mar'a" means he had intercourse with the woman when he covered her.

﴿Out of desire﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning for the sake of appetite, with no motive driving you to it except mere desire, without any other call. There is no greater reproach than this, because it describes them as animalistic: they have absolutely no motive from reason, such as seeking offspring or the like. Or it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: desiring, following appetite, not heeding its ugliness.

Hence they exceeded the limits in satisfying desire, until they passed the customary to the unusual. Similar is ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress.﴾

﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said﴾: that is, they did not answer him with a reply to what Lot, peace be upon him, had said to them, denouncing the lewdness, magnifying its matter, and branding them with the mark of excess, which is the root of all evil. Instead, they brought up something else unrelated to his speech and admonition: the command to expel him and those with him of the believers from their town, out of irritation with them and with what they heard of his exhortation and advice.

﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾: their saying is mockery of them and of their purity from immoralities, and boasting of the filth they were in, as the rogues among the debauchees say to some of the righteous when he admonishes them: "Get this ascetic away from us, and relieve us of this self-denier." [The phrase "get this ascetic away from us": "al-mutaqashshif" is one who subsists on bread and patched garments, from "al-qashf," which means being changed by the sun or poverty. (ʿ)]

It is also said: those who stayed among them were swallowed by the earth, and stones rained on those who traveled among them and were scattered. It is also said: He rained upon them and then swallowed them. It is narrated that a merchant among them was in the sacred precinct, and the stone stood still for him for forty days until he finished his trade and left the sacred precinct, whereupon it fell upon him.

So if Allah sent down from the sky kinds of goods and provisions, such as manna and quail, it would be correct to say: "the sky rained down goods," meaning it sent them down as rain is sent. Evil is not a particular quality of this quadriliteral form; it merely happened that the sky sent nothing but rain that was a punishment, so the one who observed this took it as intentional in the wording. He therefore points out the precise truth of the matter.]

I say: The path of truth is one, but it branches into many different knowledges, limits and rulings. So whenever they saw someone beginning any of them, they threatened him and barred him.

If you say: To what does the pronoun in ﴿believes in it﴾ refer? I say: To every path. Its implied meaning is: "You threaten those who believe in it and bar them from it." So the explicit noun, "the way of God," is placed in the position of the pronoun, to increase the ugliness of their conduct and to show the greatness of what they barred people from.

It is said: They would sit on roads and at watch-posts, and say to whoever passed by them: "Shu'ayb is a liar, so do not let him seduce you from your religion," as Quraysh used to do in Mecca. It is also said: they used to cut the roads.

It is said: They were tax-collectors. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: that is, seeking for the way of God to be crooked, describing it to people as a crooked, non-straight way, in order to bar them from traveling it and entering it. Or it is a mockery of them, that they seek for it what is impossible, because the way of truth does not bend.

It is said: Madyan ibn Ibrahim married the daughter of Lot, and she bore children. God placed blessing and growth in her descendants, so they multiplied and spread. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when you were poor and needy, so He made you rich. Or: you were few and weak, so He made you mighty through abundance of numbers.
