Or it refers to acting upon what He commanded them and forbade them. ﴿Better for you﴾ means better in humanity and in a good reputation, and in what you seek of gain and profit, because people are more eager to deal with you when they know your trustworthiness and fair dealing. ﴿If you are believers﴾: if you are truthful to me in my saying, "That is better for you."

﴿And do not sit at every path﴾: do not follow Satan in his saying, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, so that you sit at every path, that is, every method of the religion. The evidence that the "path" means the way of truth is His saying ﴿and bar from the way of God﴾. The position of ﴿threatening﴾ and what is conjoined to it is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). That is: ﴿do not sit threatening and barring from the way of God, and seeking to make it crooked.﴾

If you say: The path of truth is one, as in His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the other ways, lest they scatter you away from His way﴾. How then is it said ﴿at every path﴾?

I say: The path of truth is one, but it branches into many different knowledges, limits and rulings. So whenever they saw someone beginning any of them, they threatened him and barred him.

If you say: To what does the pronoun in ﴿believes in it﴾ refer? I say: To every path. Its implied meaning is: "You threaten those who believe in it and bar them from it." So the explicit noun, "the way of God," is placed in the position of the pronoun, to increase the ugliness of their conduct and to show the greatness of what they barred people from.

It is said: They would sit on roads and at watch-posts, and say to whoever passed by them: "Shu'ayb is a liar, so do not let him seduce you from your religion," as Quraysh used to do in Mecca. It is also said: they used to cut the roads.

It is said: They were tax-collectors. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: that is, seeking for the way of God to be crooked, describing it to people as a crooked, non-straight way, in order to bar them from traveling it and entering it. Or it is a mockery of them, that they seek for it what is impossible, because the way of truth does not bend.

﴿And remember when you were few﴾: idh here is an object-adverb (zarf), not a time-adverb (as in "when"). That is: remember with gratitude the state in which you were few in number, ﴿so He multiplied you﴾, increasing your numbers.

It is said: Madyan ibn Ibrahim married the daughter of Lot, and she bore children. God placed blessing and growth in her descendants, so they multiplied and spread. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when you were poor and needy, so He made you rich. Or: you were few and weak, so He made you mighty through abundance of numbers.

﴿And see the end of the corrupters﴾: the final outcome of those who corrupted before you among the nations, such as the people of Noah, Hud, Salih and Lot, whose time was close to what befell the overturned cities.

﴿So be patient﴾: wait and watch, ﴿until God judges between us﴾, that is, between the two parties, by making the righteous victorious over the falsifiers and making them prevail over them. This is a warning to the unbelievers of God's vengeance upon them, like His saying: ﴿So wait, for we are waiting with you.﴾ Or it is an admonition to the believers and an exhortation to patience and to bearing the harm that the polytheists inflicted on them, until God judges between them and avenges them upon the others.

It is also permissible that it is addressed to both parties: let the believers be patient over the harm of the unbelievers, and let the unbelievers be patient over what grieves them from the faith of those among them who believed, until God judges, distinguishing the wicked from the good. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, because His judgment is true and just, and there is no fear of injustice in it.

It was said of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, that he was the "orator of the prophets" (khatib al-anbiya'), because of the excellence of his argument with his people. They were people who cheated in measures and weights.

﴿A clear proof has come to you from your Lord﴾: a miracle (mu'jizah) bearing witness to the truth of my prophethood, which makes it obligatory for you to believe in me, to act on what I command you, and to refrain from what I forbid you. ﴿So give full measure and weight, and do not diminish people's goods.﴾

If you say: What was his miracle? I say: It is established that he had a miracle, by His saying: ﴿A clear proof has come to you from your Lord.﴾

Moreover, a claimant to prophethood must have a miracle that bears witness to him and confirms him; otherwise his claim is not valid, and he would be a pretender (mutanabbi), not a prophet. However, his miracle is not mentioned in the Qur'an, just as most of the miracles of our Prophet (ﷺ) are not mentioned in it.

Among the miracles of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, is what is related about the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, contending with the serpent (al-tinnin) when he gave him his flock. [Note: "al-tinnin" is a kind of snake, black-headed and white in the rest of its body. (ʿ)] Also the ewes giving birth to speckled offspring only, when he promised that the speckled ones would be his from their young; the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, coming into his hand seven times; and other signs. All of these occurred before Moses was commissioned as a prophet, so they were miracles for Shu'ayb.

I say: By al-kayl is meant the instrument of measuring, which is al-mikyal. Or the thing measured with it is named al-kayl, as al-ʿaysh is said of what one lives by. Or the meaning is: ﴿give full the measure and the weight of the scale.﴾

It is also permissible that al-mizan is like al-mi'ad and al-milad, in the sense of a verbal noun. One says: bakhastuhu haqqahu (I diminished his right for him) when you reduce it. From this comes al-bakhs, which is the term for an unjust levy.

Among their proverbs: "You think her a fool, while she is a cheat."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 88–89:

That is, one of the two things will certainly happen: either your expulsion, or your return to disbelief (al-kufr). If you ask: how did they address Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) with "return" [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, how did they address Shu'ayb with the form of 'return' ... etc." Ahmad said: Al-Zamakhshari built this discussion on the premise that the form "return" (al-'awd) requires that the one returning go back to a state he was in before. The verification in answering the said question, given that 'awd implies that, is this: although this verb is used in that way, it frequently occurs in the sense of "became" (sara). In that case it is permissible for it to be a sister of kana, and it does not require a return to a previous state, but rather the opposite, namely a transition from a previous state to a new state, like sara. It is as if they said—and God knows best—"We will certainly expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you, from our town, or you will certainly become disbelievers like us," and in that case the question is dispelled. Or the use of 'awd in the sense of return to a previous matter is granted, and the answer to it is like the answer to His saying, "God is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light, while those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut; they bring them out of the light into the darknesses" (2:257). Expulsion (al-ikhraj) requires a prior entry into that from which the expulsion occurs, yet we know that the believer who grew up in faith never entered the darkness of disbelief nor was in it, and likewise the original disbeliever never entered the light of faith nor was in it. But since faith and disbelief are voluntary acts, which God created the servant able to attain either of them and capable of it should he will it, He expressed the believer's capacity for disbelief and then his turning away from it to faith as a report of expulsion from darknesses into light, by way of divine success (tawfiq) for him and kindness (lutf) toward him, and the reverse regarding the disbeliever. A parallel to this consideration has already passed at His saying, "Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance" (2:16), and it is a figurative usage in which the cause is expressed by its effect. The benefit of choosing it in these places is to establish the capacity and the choice, so as to establish God's proof against His servants, and God knows best.]] in disbelief in their words "or you will certainly return to our religion" (aw la-ta'udunna fi millatina)? And how did he answer them with His saying, "If we return to your religion after God has delivered us from it, and it is not for us to return to it" (7:89)? And prophets (peace be upon them) may not be subject to any minor sins except those that involve no repulsion, let alone major sins, let alone disbelief? I say: when they said, "We will certainly expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you," they conjoined to his pronoun those among them who had entered faith after their disbelief, and then they said, "you will certainly return," so they gave precedence to the group over the individual, and made them all returners, applying the speech according to the rule of predominance (al-taghlib). Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) also framed his reply accordingly, saying, "If we return to your religion after God has delivered us from it," while he meant the return of his people, except that he included himself among them, though he was innocent of that, applying his speech according to the rule of predominance. If you ask: then what is the meaning of His saying, "It is not for us to return to it, unless God wills" (7:89), while God the Exalted is too exalted that He should will the apostasy of believers and their return to disbelief? [[His saying "God the Exalted is too exalted that He should will the apostasy of believers" means: He is exalted above willing ... etc., according to the Mu'tazilite doctrine that God does not will evil. As for the people of the Sunna, He wills it as He wills good. (Gh.)]] [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, God is sanctified above willing the apostasy of believers and their return to disbelief ... etc." Ahmad said: This question, as you see, is based on the corrupt premise of believing in the obligation to observe what is good and best (al-salah wa-al-aslah), and it is not directed at the principle of Sunna. The apparent meaning of the verse is what is relied upon; it may not be interpreted or altered. As for al-Zamakhshari's use of His saying, "Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge" (7:89) as proof for the soundness of his interpretation, it is one of his stratagems in false interpretations, supporting them and following doubts and fabricating them. The placement of His saying "Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge" is the acknowledgement of insufficiency regarding knowledge of the outcome and awareness of unseen matters, for return to disbelief is within God's power to occur from the servant, and if it occurs, it is by His power and will, which are hidden from His creation; so caution remains and fear is necessary, but for one whom God has granted success in sound belief and whole faith. And God is the Granter of success. A parallel is the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him), "And I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something; my Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge" (6:80). When he referred the matter to the will, which is concealed, bounded by God the Exalted through His sole knowledge of the unseen, God knows best.]]? I say: its meaning is: "unless God wills our abandonment and the withholding of His kindnesses from us, since He knows that they would not benefit us and would be futile." Futility is ugly, and the Wise does not do it. The proof of this is His saying, "Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge," that is, He knows everything that was and will be, so He knows how the states of His servants change, how their hearts turn about, how they harden after softness, sicken after health, and return to disbelief after faith. "In God have we put our trust" that He may keep us firm in faith and grant us increase in certainty. It is permissible that His saying "unless God wills" be a cutting off of their hope of return, because God's will for their return to disbelief is impossible, outside of wisdom [[His saying "impossible, outside of wisdom" is also based on the Mu'tazilite doctrine. (Gh.)]]. "Would you bring us back even though we were unwilling?" The hamza is interrogative, and the waw is the waw of circumstance; the sense is: "Would you return us to your religion while we are averse, and despite our being unwilling?" "It is not for us" means: "it is not proper for us, nor does it befit us, nor is it valid for us." "Our Lord, decide between us in truth" means: judge between us. Al-fataha means judgment; or make our matter manifest, so that what is between us and our people is opened and revealed, by sending down upon them a punishment through which it becomes clear that they are upon falsehood. "And You are the best of deciders," like His saying, "And He is the best of judges" (7:87 context / 10:109). If you ask: what is the construction of His saying "We have certainly fabricated against God a lie if we return to your religion"? I say: it is a report restricted by a condition, and it has two aspects. The first: that it be a new independent statement carrying the sense of wonder, as if they said: "How much we would have lied against God if we returned to disbelief after Islam," because the apostate is more abundant in fabrication than the disbeliever, since the disbeliever fabricates a lie against God when he claims that God has a rival, and God has no rival; the apostate is like him in that and beyond him, since he claims that what was hidden from him of the distinction between truth and falsehood has become clear to him. The second: that it be an oath with the lam omitted from its construction, meaning: "By God, we would indeed have fabricated against God a lie."

And the chieftains of those of his people who disbelieved said to those beneath them, who were being deterred from faith: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then indeed you will be losers" (لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُمْ شُعَيْباً إِنَّكُمْ إِذاً لَخاسِرُونَ), that is, in exchange for guidance you would have taken error. This is like His saying, ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, so their commerce has not profited﴾ (Qur'an 2:16). It was also said: "You would lose, by following him, the benefits of cheating and short-measuring, because he forbids you from them and commands you to give full measure and to be even-handed."

If you ask: what is the answer to the oath which the lam introduces in لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُمْ شُعَيْباً, and what is the answer to the conditional? I say: His saying إِنَّكُمْ إِذاً لَخاسِرُونَ ("indeed you would then be losers") serves in place of both answers.

الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا شُعَيْباً ("Those who denied Shu'ayb") is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is كَأَنْ لَمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا ("as if they had never dwelt therein"). Likewise: كانُوا هُمُ الْخاسِرِينَ ("they were the losers"). In this beginning (ibtida') there is the sense of restriction (ikhtisas), as if it were said: those who denied Shu'ayb are the ones singled out to be destroyed and uprooted, as though they had never lived in their homes, because those who followed Shu'ayb were rescued by God. Those who denied Shu'ayb are the ones singled out for the great loss, unlike his followers, for they are the winners.

In this resumption (istinaf), this beginning, and this repetition there is intensification in refuting the words of the chieftains to their followers, a condemnation of their opinion, a mockery of their advice to their people, and a magnification of what befell them.

الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا شُعَيْباً ("Those who denied Shu'ayb") is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is كَأَنْ لَمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا ("as if they had never dwelt therein"). Likewise: كانُوا هُمُ الْخاسِرِينَ ("they were the losers"). In this beginning (ibtida') there is the sense of restriction (ikhtisas), as if it were said: those who denied Shu'ayb are the ones singled out to be destroyed and uprooted, as though they had never lived in their homes, because those who followed Shu'ayb were rescued by God. Those who denied Shu'ayb are the ones singled out for the great loss, unlike his followers, for they are the winners.

In this resumption (istinaf), this beginning, and this repetition there is intensification in refuting the words of the chieftains to their followers, a condemnation of their opinion, a mockery of their advice to their people, and a magnification of what befell them.

Al-Asa: intense grief. Al-Ajjaj said:

"And his eyes flowed with milk from excess of grief" (the line as given is rendered here in the sense of his eyes overflowing with sorrow)

Note: the poetic line as it stands in the source is: وانحلبت عيناه من فرط الأسى, which I translate as: "And his eyes wept from the excess of grief."

He grieved intensely over his people, then rebuked himself, saying: "How should I grieve intensely over a people who do not deserve to be grieved over, because of their disbelief and their deserving of what befell them?" It is also possible that he means: "I have indeed given you full warning in conveying the message, offering sincere counsel, and warning you of what has come upon you, but you did not listen to my words and did not believe me. So how should I grieve over you?" meaning that he does not grieve over them, because they are not deserving of grief.

Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: فكيف إيسى (fa-kayfa iyasa), with a kasra on the hamza.

﴿Except that We seized its people with adversity,﴾ with misery and poverty, ﴿and affliction,﴾ with harm and sickness, ﴿so that they might humble themselves.﴾ This was because of their arrogance in following their prophet and their defiance toward him, so that they would submit humbly and abase themselves, and put down the cloaks of pride and might.

﴿Then We replaced the evil with good,﴾ meaning: We gave them, in place of what they had been in of trial, affliction, and hardship, ease, health, and plenty. This is like His saying: ﴿And We tested them with good and evil﴾ [Qur'an 7:168], ﴿until they multiplied﴾, meaning they increased and grew in their persons and their wealth. It comes from their saying: "The plants multiplied (ʿafā al-nabāt), and the fat and the wool multiplied (ʿafā al-shaḥm wa al-wabar)," when they became abundant. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Let the beards grow» [mentioned in al-Baqara].

Al-Ḥuṭay'a said:

*"When she glanced one day with the corner of her eye*
*toward a mountain landmark in the low ground, she said, 'Go away!'*

*In a land where the young hubara bird seems*
*to be a rider standing high atop a hillock.*

*With lush grass of the wadi-bank whose plants have multiplied,*
*she drops me, with my saddle, at the sound of a single hudhud bird."*

Mu'akhkhar al-ʿayn (the corner of the eye) is its side. Al-ʿalam is a mountain or a sign on the road. Al-ghawr is the sunken, low-lying place.

"Go away" (ubʿad) is a majāz (metaphor, a figurative usage) for her quickly leaving him, so that he moves away from her. The ḥubāra is a bird that loves mountains, and its young is called al-nahār. The young of the karawān (partridge) is called al-layl. Al-mūfī is the one who overlooks. Al-qardad, like hudhud, is a rough, high place. Al-mustaʾsid is a plant that is strong, coarse, and tall, just as the beast is called a lion (asad) for its strength. Al-qiryān, with a ḍamma, is the plural of qurā, a water channel that gathers water to the meadow. Al-ʿāfī means abundant. The poet describes his she-camel's swift pace; because of her fear on that road, she cannot fully see its landmarks, so when she glimpses a shape in it she hurries away from it in an unknown land, as if the young hubara there were a rider overlooking from a high place. His saying "with lush grass" (bi-mustaʾsid) is either a substitute for "in a land" or is connected to "she drops me." The meaning is that she sees no difference between the hard ground and the plain in the plants of the streambeds when they are abundant; she throws me off with my saddle, because of the speed of her pace out of fear at the sound of a single hudhud bird. On the first reading, "she drops me" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "she said," or it is the answer of the condition; "she said to him, 'Go away!'" is a descriptive clause (ṣifa) for "a landmark." The poet expressed it as "drops" because the meaning is: whenever her movement became strong, I nearly fell.

He also said:

*"But we bite the sword from them,*
*with fat-hump camels, well-fed in their shanks, and humped."*

*"When her milk does not suffice for a guest,*
*the fat of her humps is guaranteed to be his provision.*

*So the fine-fleshed ones do not pass by*
*to the young maiden camels that are lean, nor to the old ones."*

This is by Labīd ibn Rabīʿa al-ʿĀmirī. He says: when the milk of the she-camels is not enough for the guest's hospitality, their fat provides his meal. The ascribing of the provision to the she-camels' milk is by way of attributing the cause or instrument to the thing. Ascribing the guarantee to the she-camels is also a majāz, because they are the place of what is guaranteed; the two actions really belong to the owner of the camels. The meaning is that they are prepared for this, either by their milk or their fat. Al-ʿuḍla is the fine, fat one. Al-bakr is the young camel, male or female. Al-maʿāzib is the lean one, from ʿazaba (to be far away). Al-maʿzāba and al-maʿzāb are the one whose bachelorhood and distance from mates is long, either for lack of offspring or for being far from the tents; so it originally means "one who keeps away," and then it is used metaphorically for the lean one. Al-kazm (with a zāy) is the short one, and from it comes kazam (short-necked), with akzam and kuzūm, so al-kazūm, like ṣabūr, is a short female camel. It is said also that it is an aged one whose lower lip is shorter than the upper, or one who has no teeth left from old age. Kazamahu also means to break him with the front of the mouth. It is possible that al-maʿāzib, with a fatḥa, is the plural of maʿzāb or maʿzāba, so that al-bakr is used in the sense of a plural: that is, they do not leave the middle-aged fat camels to go to the young lean ones and the old ones who have reached extreme age. Rather, we make the sword bite from them, with shanks, the plural of sāq, ascribed to ʿāfiyāt, meaning abundant in fat because they were left from work for a year or two. Al-kawm is the plural of kawmāʾ, meaning those with greatly high humps.

And they said: ﴿Indeed, adversity and ease touched our fathers,﴾ meaning: their abundance made them haughty and insolent, so they said: "This is the custom of time; among people it alternates between hardship and ease. Our fathers were touched by something like this, and it is not a trial from God for His servants." So after they had been tested with evils and goods, nothing remained but that We seize them with punishment. ﴿So We seized them﴾ with the most severe and dreadful seizing, which was taking them suddenly, without any awareness on their part.

The definite article in "al-qura" (the villages/towns) refers to the villages indicated by His saying ﴿And We did not send into any town a prophet﴾, as if He said:

"Had the people of those villages, who denied and were destroyed, believed instead of disbelieving, and guarded against sins instead of committing them, ﴿We would surely have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾; We would have brought them good in every respect. It is also said that He meant rain and vegetation. ﴿But they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾"

It is also permissible for the article in "al-qura" to be the article of genus (al-jins). If you ask: what is the meaning of "opening blessings upon them"? I say: making them easy for them, just as the matter of closed doors is made easy by opening them. From this comes their saying: "I opened (the recitation) to the reciter" (fatahtu 'ala al-qari'), when he could not manage the recitation and you made it easy for him by prompting him (al-talqin).

The commentary on "bayat" (night attack) means "staying overnight" (al-baytutah). It is said: bāta bayātan. From this is the verse ﴿So Our punishment came upon them by night while they were sleeping, or while they were resting at midday﴾. It may also mean al-tabyīt (attacking by night), as al-salām means al-taslīm. It is said: the enemy attacked him by night (baytahu al-ʿadūwu bayātan). So it is permissible to take it to mean: that Our punishment comes upon them while they are spending the night (bā'itīn), or at a time of night (waqt bayāt), or as a night-stay (mabītan), or as those who spend the night (mabītīn); or it may mean tabyītan, as if it were said: that He attacks them with Our punishment by night (an yubayyitahum bi-ʾasinā bayātan).

And ḍuḥan is in the accusative as an adverbial of time (ẓarf). It is said: he came to us at ḍuḥan, ḍuḥayan, and ḍuḥāʾ. The ḍuḥā, originally, is the name for the light of the sun when it shines and rises high.

The fāʾ and the wāw in ﴿afa-amina﴾ and ﴿awa-amina﴾ are two conjunctions (ḥarfā ʿaṭf) which the interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkār) has entered upon. If you ask: what is the element being conjoined to (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayhi)? And why did you conjoin the first with fāʾ and the second with wāw? I say: the element conjoined to is His words ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾ (fa-akhadhnāhum baghtatan), and His words ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared God, We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾, which came as an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) between the conjoined and the element conjoined to. And He conjoined with fāʾ because the meaning is: they did and they made, so We seized them suddenly. Is it then that the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will come upon them by night (bayātan), and they feel secure that Our punishment will come upon them in the forenoon (ḍuḥan)?

It is also read ﴿awa-amina﴾ with the conjunction awa, by way of coordination with awa. ﴿While they are playing﴾ (wa-hum yalʿabūna): they occupy themselves with what does not benefit them, as if they were playing.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 99:

If you ask: why did he return and introduce with the particle fa' (then/so) the phrase "Do they then feel secure from the plan of Allah?" (afa-amina makra Allah)? I answer: it is a repetition of his words "Do the people of the cities feel secure...?" (afa-amina ahl al-qura), and the "plan of Allah" (makr Allah) is a metaphor (isti'arah) for His seizing the servant from where he does not perceive, and for His gradual leading (istidraj) of him. So it is incumbent upon the intelligent person that he be in fear of the plan of Allah, like the warrior who fears from his enemy an ambush (kamin), a night attack (bayat), and a surprise assault (ghilah).

And it is related from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym that his daughter said to him: "What is the matter with me? I see people sleeping and I do not see you sleeping." He said: "O my daughter, indeed your father fears a night attack," meaning His words: ﴿Or do they feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 100:

If it is read as أَوَلَمْ يَهْدِ with the letter yā' (yahdi, "does it not guide"), then أَنْ لَوْ نَشاءُ ("that if We willed") is in the nominative case, as its subject (fā'il). The meaning is: "Does it not make clear to those who inherit the earth after its previous people, in their dwellings, that this is the case: that if We willed, We would afflict them for their sins, as We afflicted those before them, and We would destroy the inheritors just as We destroyed the earlier inheritors?" If it is read with nūn (nahdi, "We guide"), then it is in the accusative case, as if it were said: "Has God not made clear to the inheritors this matter: that if We willed, We would afflict them for their sins, as We afflicted those before them?" The verb of guidance (hidāya) is construed with lām (li-) because it carries the sense of making clear (tabyīn).

If you ask: with what is the phrase وَنَطْبَعُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ ("and We seal upon their hearts") connected? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask with what the phrase 'and We seal upon their hearts' is connected..." Ahmad said: Indeed it is permissible, by God, that it be coordinated with it, and it does not follow that the addressees must be described as sealed, nor does it harm them if they were unbelievers or committers of sins, for sealing is not necessarily a consequence of committing sin. Sealing is persistence in unbelief, obstinacy, and extreme fixity of resolve, to the point that the one described by it is despaired of accepting the truth. It does not follow that every unbeliever is in this state. Rather, the unbeliever who persists in his disbelief is threatened that God will seal upon his heart, so that he never believes. This is what is required by the coordination with "We afflicted them." Thus the verse has threatened them with two things: first, affliction with some of their sins, and second, sealing upon their hearts. This second is more severe than the first, and it is also a kind of affliction by sins or punishment for them, but it is the most painful type of torment and the most grievous kind of punishment. God often punishes a sin by plunging one into a greater sin, and punishes unbelief by increasing the fixity of resolve in it and extremism in it, as He said: "So He increased them in filth upon their filth" (Qur'an 9:125), just as He increased the believers in faith upon their faith. This kind of reward and punishment is fitting to what was its cause and its recompense: the reward of faith is faith, and the reward of unbelief is unbelief. Zamakhshari, however, avoids from this aspect the inclusion of sealing within God's will, because that is, in his view, impossible, since it is ugly, and God is exalted above it. But how can escape from the truth be complete? How many verses have explicitly stated that sealing comes from God, let alone that His will is connected to it?]] ? I say: there are several possibilities. It may be coordinated with what is indicated by the meaning of "أَوَلَمْ يَهْدِ," as if it were said: "They are heedless of guidance, and We seal upon their hearts." Or it may be coordinated with "yarithūna al-arḍ" ("they inherit the earth"). Or it may be a separate clause, meaning: "And We seal upon their hearts." If you ask: is it permissible that وَنَطْبَعُ mean وطبعنا ("and We sealed"), just as لَوْ نَشاءُ means "if We willed," and be coordinated with "أصبناهم"? I say: the meaning does not support this, because those people were sealed upon their hearts and were described by the attribute of their predecessors, namely committing sins and being afflicted by them. This interpretation would lead to their being free of this attribute, and to God, had He willed, having caused them to be described by it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 101:

﴿Those are the cities whose tidings We relate to you.﴾ It is like His saying: ﴿This is my husband, an old man.﴾ As to its grammatical analysis: it is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar) and a circumstantial clause (hal). It is also permissible that al-Qura (the cities) be a qualifier (sifah) of tilka (those), with naqussu (We relate) as the predicate, and that al-Qura be the subject with naqussu as a predicate following a predicate.

If you say: What is the meaning of ﴿tilka al-qura﴾ such that it forms a meaningful sentence? I say: It is meaningful, but on condition of restriction by the circumstantial clause, just as it conveys meaning on condition of restriction by the qualifier in your saying: "He is the generous man." If you say: What is the meaning of the report about the cities as ﴿We relate to you some of their tidings﴾? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 106:

If it is said: How did he say to him "then bring it" after his saying "if you have come with a sign"? I say: its meaning is: if you have come from the One who sent you with a sign, then bring it and produce it before me so that your claim may be valid and your truthfulness established. ﴿A serpent, manifest﴾: its matter is plain, and no one doubts that it is a serpent. It is narrated that it was a male serpent, its hair bristling, gaping its mouth [[His saying "gaping its mouth" means opening its mouth. (Ibn ʿAbbad)]], between its jaws eighty cubits. It placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned toward Pharaoh to seize him, and Pharaoh leapt from his throne and fled, and he defecated, having never done so before. The people fled and shouted, and it charged at the people, and they were routed, and twenty-five thousand of them died, some of them killing others. Pharaoh entered the house and shouted: "O Musa, take it! I will believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you." So Musa took it, and it returned to being a staff.

If it is said: With what does ﴿to the onlookers﴾ relate? I say: it relates to "white." The meaning: ﴿then behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾. It would not be white to the onlookers unless its whiteness was a wondrous whiteness, beyond the usual, such that people gather to look at it as spectators gather for marvels. This is what is narrated: that he showed Pharaoh his hand and said: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand." Then he put it into his collar, and he was wearing a woollen cloak, and he took it out, and behold, it was white with a luminous whiteness whose radiance overcame the radiance of the sun. Musa, peace be upon him, was very dark-skinned.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 109–112:

"Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer (ʿalim)": that is, one who knows sorcery (ʿalim bi-l-sihr), proficient in it. He has seized the eyes of the people by one of his tricks (khud'ah), so that the staff appeared to them as a snake, and the rope as white.

If you say: this statement is attributed to Pharaoh in Surah al-Shuʿara', where it is said that he said it to the chiefs (al-mala'), and here it is attributed to them. I say: he said it and they said it, so the report gives his words first and then their words here. Or he said it at the outset, and the chiefs took it from him and said it to their subordinates. Or they said it on his behalf to the people by way of relaying (tabligh), as kings do: one of them holds an opinion and speaks it to those closest to him among the elite (khassah), then the elite relay it to the common people (ʿammah). The proof of this is that they answered him in their words: ﴿Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾. And it is read as sahhar, meaning they will bring you every sorcerer like him in knowledge and skill, or better than him.

This was a plot made with the Copts. Their words ﴿So what do you command?﴾ come from amartuhu, "I consulted him, and he advised me with such-and-such an opinion" (idha shawartahu fa-ashara ʿalayka bi-ra'y). It is also said that ﴿So what do you command?﴾ is part of Pharaoh's speech, which he addressed to the chiefs when they said to him: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer who wants to drive you out of your land." It is as if it were said: "So what do you command?" They said: ﴿Put him off and his brother﴾. The meaning of ﴿put him off and his brother﴾ is: delay them and send them away from you, until you see your opinion concerning them and plan their affair. It is also said: imprison them.

It is read as ʾarjiʾhu with a hamzah, and as arjihu, from arjaʾahu and arjaahu.

The proof of this is that they answered him in their words: ﴿Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾. And it is read as sahhar, meaning they will bring you every sorcerer like him in knowledge and skill, or better than him.

This was a plot made with the Copts. Their words ﴿So what do you command?﴾ come from amartuhu, "I consulted him, and he advised me with such-and-such an opinion" (idha shawartahu fa-ashara ʿalayka bi-ra'y). It is also said that ﴿So what do you command?﴾ is part of Pharaoh's speech, which he addressed to the chiefs when they said to him: "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer who wants to drive you out of your land." It is as if it were said: "So what do you command?" They said: ﴿Put him off and his brother﴾. The meaning of ﴿put him off and his brother﴾ is: delay them and send them away from you, until you see your opinion concerning them and plan their affair. It is also said: imprison them.

It is read as ʾarjiʾhu with a hamzah, and as arjihu, from arjaʾahu and arjaahu.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 113–114:

If you ask: why was it not said "wa-jā'a al-saḥaratu Firʿawna fa-qālū" (And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh and said)? I answer: it is in the sense of an implied questioner who asked: "What did they say when they came to him?" So the answer was given with His words: ﴿They said, "Indeed, for us there will surely be a reward"﴾, i.e., a fixed payment for victory. It was also read as "inna lanā la-ajran" (indeed for us there is a reward), in the declarative form, affirming and establishing a great reward, as if they said: "We must have a reward." The indefiniteness (of ajr) is for magnification, like the Arabs' saying: "Inna lahu la-ibilan, wa-inna lahu la-ghanaman" (indeed he has a great number of camels, and indeed he has a great number of sheep), meaning abundance.

If you ask: what is ﴿And indeed you will surely be among those brought near﴾ coordinated with? I answer: it is coordinated with an omitted element that the particle of affirmation took the place of. It is as if he said, affirming their statement "indeed for us there is a reward": "Yes, indeed for you there is a reward, and indeed you will be among those brought near." He meant: "I shall reward you with reward alone, and you will have along with the reward something that makes the reward seem small, namely nearness and honor, because the one rewarded only rejoices in what reaches him and is pleased with it when he attains honor and elevation along with it."

It is narrated that he said to them: "You will be the first to enter and the last to leave." It is also narrated that he summoned the chiefs of the sorcerers and their teachers and said to them: "What have you done?" They said: "We have learned a magic that no sorcerers on earth can match, unless it is a matter from heaven, for then we have no power against it." It is narrated that they were eighty thousand. It was said: seventy thousand; and it was said: some thirty-odd thousand. The reports differ, some giving fewer and some more. It was said: two Magians from the people of Nineveh were teaching them. It was said: Pharaoh said: "We will not contend with Moses except with what is from him," meaning magic.

The meaning is: what they fabricate, i.e., what they turn from truth to falsehood and falsify. Or their fabrication, calling the fabricated thing a fabrication. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 123–124:

"Did you believe in Him" is stated as a report, meaning: you committed this shameful act, as a rebuke and reproach to them. It is also read "Aa'amantum" (أآمنتم) with the interrogative particle, and its meaning is denial and disbelief in the matter. ﴿Indeed, this is a plot that you have plotted in the city﴾: indeed, your doing this is a stratagem that you and Musa devised in Egypt before you came out of it into this desert, having colluded in it for an aim of your own, namely that you should expel the Copts from it and settle the Children of Israel in it. This statement of Pharaoh was a deception of the people, lest they follow the magicians into faith. It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, said to the chief magician: "Will you believe in me if I defeat you?" He said: "I will bring a magic that magic cannot overcome." 

﴿And if you defeat us, we will surely believe in you﴾, and Pharaoh was listening, so he said what he said. ﴿Then you will know﴾ is a threat, summarised and then detailed by His saying ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾. It is also read "la-uqatti'anna" with the lightened form, and likewise ﴿then I will surely crucify you all﴾ (ﷺ not applicable), meaning: a part from each side. It was said: the first person to cut off (hands and feet) from opposite sides and to crucify was Pharaoh.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 125–126:

Innā ilā rabbinā munqalibūn (﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾) has several interpretations. They may mean: "We do not mind death, because our return is to the meeting with our Lord, His mercy, and our deliverance from you and from your meeting [i.e., your punishment]." Or: "We will return to Allah on the Day of Recompense, and He will reward us for the severe hardships of amputation and crucifixion." Or: "We (all together, meaning themselves and Pharaoh) will return to Allah, and He will judge between us." Or: "We are certainly going to die and return to Allah, so you can do to us only what we must endure anyway."

Wa mā tanqimu minnā illā an āmannā (﴿You do not resent us except that we believed﴾) and what you find fault with in us is only the belief in the signs of Allah. They meant: "What you find fault with in us is only that which is the root of all virtues and glories, namely faith." From this is the verse:

"There is no fault in them except that their swords, on the day of 'Arafat, are for battle, grim, bearing wounds, some fresh with blood and some dry and crusted over... When they are called down to fight, they hasten down, hurrying toward death like troubled camels [al-Ju­māl al-muṣā'ib]..."

"There is no fault in them except that their swords ... are notched from striking the battalions."

This is al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani describing horsemen on sweating, enduring, grim, and gaping steeds, with wounds on them, some moist with blood and others dry, covered with a crust (jalaba, meaning a crust). When the fighting becomes close and the situation requires them to dismount from their horses, they hurry down, selling their lives, like troubled camels (jamʿ muṣʿib). You say: "aṣʿabtu al-jamal" when you leave the camel from work until it becomes difficult and hard. Al-Fulul are notches in the edge of a sword. Al-Qirā' is striking. Al-Katā'ib are the groups. The verse is an example of "istitbā' al-madḥ bi-mā yushbih al-dhamm" (following praise with what resembles blame): if the notches in the sword were a fault, then affirm it, but they are not a fault, so there is no fault in them at all, and this is hyperbole in praise.

Afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabran (﴿Pour upon us patience﴾): grant us abundant patience and pour it over us, until it overflows and covers us, as water is poured out copiously. It is related from some of the early generation: "Indeed one of you pours a bucket over his brother and then says, 'I was only joking with you,'" meaning he overwhelms him with shame and embarrassment. Or it means: pour upon us what purifies us from the filth of sins, namely patience in the face of what Pharaoh threatened us with, because they knew that if they remained steadfast and patient, that would be a means of purification for them.

Wa tawaffanā muslimīn (﴿and cause us to die as Muslims﴾), steadfast upon Islam.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 127:

وَيَذَرَكَ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with لِيُفْسِدُوا, since if Pharaoh leaves them and does not prevent them, and that leads to what they call corruption, and to his abandoning worship of him and his gods, then it is as if he has left them for that reason. Or it is a response to the interrogative with the waw, as it is answered with the fa', as in the verse of al-Huṭay'a:

ألم أك جاركم ويكون بيني ... وبينكم المودّة والإخاء [[The explanation of this witness has been given earlier in the first volume, page 578, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

The accusative is by implied "an" (an-naṣb bi-iḍmār "an"), its meaning being: "Would it be that you leave Moses, and that he leaves you and your gods?"

It was also read: وَيَذَرَكَ وَآلِهَتَكَ in the nominative, as a coordination with أَتَذَرُ مُوسَى, with the meaning: "Do you leave him and he leaves you?", meaning: you allow him that.

Or it may be a new (resumptive) clause, or a circumstantial clause, in the sense of: "Do you leave him while he leaves you and your gods?"

Al-Hasan read: وَيَذَرَكَ with the jussive, as if it were said: "they corrupt," just as it was read: وَأَكُنْ مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ, as if it were said: "I would be sincere."

Anas (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) read: وَنَذَرَكَ with the nūn and the accusative, meaning: "He diverts us from your worship, so we leave it."

It was also read: وَيَذَرَكَ وَإِلَاهَتَكَ, meaning: your worship.

It is narrated that they said this to him because he had agreed with the sorcerers on faith, six hundred thousand souls, so they intended by corruption in the land this, and feared that they would be overpowered in the kingdom.

It was said: Pharaoh made idols for his people and commanded them to worship them as a means of drawing near to him, just as the worshippers of idols worship idols, saying: "They bring us near to God in closeness." That is why he said: "I am your lord, the most high."

سَنُقَتِّلُ أَبْنَاءَهُمْ: meaning, we will reinstate upon them what we had afflicted them with of killing the sons, so that they know that we are upon what we were upon of dominance and subjugation, and that they are subdued beneath our hands as they were, and that Moses' victory has no effect on our kingdom and our dominion, and lest the common people suppose that he is the boy whom the astrologers and soothsayers foretold would bring about the end of our kingdom at his hand, which would discourage them from obeying us and call them to follow him, and that he is awaited still.

Moses said to his people, "Seek help in God." He said this to them when Pharaoh had said, "We will kill their sons," and they had become anxious and impatient. He consoles them and strengthens them, promising them victory over the Copts and reminding them of what God had promised the Children of Israel: the destruction of the Copts and the inheritance of their land and dwellings.

If you ask: why is this sentence stripped of the conjunction "wa" (and) and attached to the one before it? I answer: it is an independent, newly begun sentence. As for "And the chiefs said" (wa-qāla al-malaʾu), it is coordinated with what precedes it, namely His words "The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said" and His words "Indeed, the earth belongs to God" (inna al-arḍa lillāhi). The lām in "lillāh" may be the lām of prior reference (al-ʿahd), meaning the land of Egypt specifically, as in His words "and We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the land" (Q. 7:137). It may also be the lām of genus (al-jins), so that it encompasses the land of Egypt because Egypt belongs to the genus "land," as the poet Ḍamra said: "A man is only [judged] by his two smaller parts," where he means "man" as a genus, and his purpose is that it encompass [Egypt] in its primary sense.

"And the final outcome is for the God-fearing" (wa-l-ʿāqibatu lil-muttaqīn) is good news that the praiseworthy end belongs to the God-fearing, both among them and among the Copts, and that the divine will encompasses them.

Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read wa-l-ʿāqibata lil-muttaqīn in the accusative (naṣb), coordinating it with "the land" (al-arḍ).

They said, "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us" (ūdhīnā min qabli an ta'tīnā wa-min baʿdi mā jiʾtanā). They mean the killing of their sons before Moses' birth until he was made a prophet, and its recurrence after that, and the various kinds of servitude and humiliation with which they were enslaved and degraded, such as various services and labors, and the torment they suffered.

"It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy" (ʿasā rabbukum an yuhlika ʿaduwwakum): this is an explicit statement of the good news previously alluded to, and it reveals it, namely the destruction of Pharaoh and their succession to him in the land of Egypt. "And He will see how you act" (fa-yanẓura kayfa taʿmalūn): He will see what each of you does, its goodness and its ugliness, and the gratitude for blessings and their denial, in order to repay you according to what is found in you.

It is related from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, may God have mercy on him, that he entered upon al-Manṣūr before the caliphate, and on his table there was one loaf or two loaves. He asked for more for ʿAmr, but none was found. ʿAmr then recited this verse. Later, after al-Manṣūr had become caliph, ʿAmr entered upon him and mentioned this to him, and said: "There remains [the phrase] 'so He will see how you act.'"

with the years of drought: the years of famine. "Sanah" (year) is one of the words that became dominant in a particular sense, like "dabbah" (beast) and "najm" (star), and similar words; they also derived from it and said "asannat al-qawm," meaning they suffered drought. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: As for the years, they were for their desert dwellers and the people of their livestock; and as for the loss of fruits, it was in their cities. And from Ka'b: There will come a time upon people when a palm tree will bear only one date.

"Perhaps they would take heed" — so that they would be alerted that this was because of their persistence in disbelief [[Mahmud said: "The meaning of 'perhaps they would take heed': they would be alerted, because that was due to their persistence ... etc." Ahmad said: The lam indicates their claim to deserve good. As for their claim that it is exclusively theirs, so that no one else shares in it, this is indicated by the estimation of the predicate, which is "lana" (for us), and you have known the method of the author in establishing restriction through placing what should be postponed before, such as the object, the predicate, and the like.]] and their denial of the signs of Allah, and because people in times of hardship are more humble of cheek, softer in their sides, and more tender of heart.

It was said: Pharaoh lived four hundred years and did not experience any hardship during three hundred and twenty years; had a pain, hunger, or fever afflicted him during that period, he would not have claimed lordship.

فَإِذا جاءَتْهُمُ الْحَسَنَةُ، أي من الخصب والرخاء، ﴿قالُوا لَنا هذِهِ﴾، أي: هذه مختصة بنا ونحن مستحقوها، ولم نزل في النعمة والرفاهية. واللام فيها مثلها في قولك: الجُلّ للفرس. ﴿وَإِنْ تُصِبْهُمْ سَيِّئَةٌ﴾، أي من ضيقة وجدب، ﴿يَطَّيَّرُوا بِمُوسى وَمَنْ مَعَهُ﴾، أي يتطيروا بهم ويتشاءموا ويقولوا: هذه بشؤمهم، ولولا مكانهم لما أصابتنا، كما قالت الكفرة لرسول الله (ﷺ): ﴿هذه من عندك﴾. فإن قلت: كيف قيل: ﴿فإذا جاءتهم الحسنة﴾ بإذا وتعريف الحسنة؟ [[عاد كلامه. قال: فإن قلت: «كيف قيل: فإذا جاءتهم الحسنة ... الخ» قال أحمد: وقد ورد: ﴿إِنْ تُصِبْهُمْ حَسَنَةٌ يَقُولُوا هذِهِ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ وَإِنْ تُصِبْهُمْ سَيِّئَةٌ يَقُولُوا هذِهِ مِنْ عِنْدِكَ﴾ فلم يراع فرق ما بينهما، ولعل بين سياق الآيتين اختلافا أوجب في كل واحد منهما ما ذكر فيه.]]، ﴿وإن تصبهم سيئة﴾ بإنّ وتنكير السيئة؟ قلت: لأنّ جنس الحسنة وقوعه كالواجب لكثرته واتساعه، وأما السيئة فلا تقع إلا في الندرة، ولا يقع إلا شيء منها. ومنه قول بعضهم:
قد عددتُ أيامَ البلاءِ فهل عددتَ أيامَ الرخاءِ

﴿طائِرُهُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾، أي سبب خيرهم وشرهم عند الله، وهو حكمه ومشيئته، ﴿والله هو الذي يشاء ما يصيبهم من الحسنة والسيئة﴾، وليس شؤم أحد ولا يمنه بسبب فيه، كقوله تعالى: ﴿قُلْ كُلٌّ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾. ويجوز أن يكون معناه: ألا إنما سبب شؤمهم عند الله، وهو عملهم المكتوب عنده الذي يجرى عليهم ما يسوءهم لأجله، ويعاقبون له بعد موتهم بما وعدهم الله في قوله سبحانه: ﴿النَّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ الآية. ولا طائر أشأم من هذا.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 132–133:**

*mahma* (مَهْما), in which *ma* (ما) carries the meaning of a conditional particle [[Ahmad said: Al-Zamakhshari said: "*mahma*, in which *ma* carries the meaning of the conditional, has joined to it the redundant *ma* that emphasises the conditional... etc." Ahmad said:

What he first attributed to Sibawayh's words, and which we will mention, is this. Sibawayh said: "I asked al-Khalil about *mahma*, and he said: it is *ma* with another *ma* added to it, a superfluous particle, like its use with *mata* (when), when you say: *mata ma ta'tini haddathtuka* (whenever you come to me, I will tell you)." End of Sibawayh's words. It seems that this speaker, and God knows best, was deceived by al-Khalil's comparison of it with *mata ma*, and thought that it has the same meaning. In fact, al-Khalil only compared the second part of *mahma*, in its attachment as a superfluous emphasising element to the first, with the *ma* attached to *mata*. Sibawayh's words continue: "But they disliked repeating one word, so they replaced the *ha'* for the *alif* that was in the first." End of his quotation from al-Khalil. Sibawayh said: "It is permissible that *kadha* be likewise joined to *ma*." End of his words.

Ahmad said: The meaning of Sibawayh's comparing it with *idhma* is that the conditional belongs to the whole word, not to its first part alone; otherwise it would be exactly al-Khalil's view. What confirms this is that Sibawayh said at the beginning of this chapter: "As for *haythu* and *idh*, they are not used as conditionals even when *ma* is added to them, so *idh* with *ma* becomes like *innama* and *ka'anama*, and the *ma* in them is not superfluous; rather each of them with *ma* is like a single letter." Note his words, "the *ma* in them is not superfluous," meaning it is not a redundant emphasising element, but that it has a share in producing the conditional, such that the word's meaning is achieved only by the union of its two parts. There remains a question about whether Sibawayh meant that *ma* was joined to *mah*, which is the sound, or to the conditional *ma*.

The apparent intent is that it is joined to the sound, because if it were joined to the conditional *ma*, the latter would independently convey the conditional before *ma* was joined to it, and it would not be like *idh* and *haythu*, and Sibawayh's analogy would not match. This is what Ibn Tahir understood, and his student Ibn Kharuf followed him. Ibn Kharuf attributed this view to Sibawayh and rejected the statement of Ibn Babshadh that this view belonged to al-Khalil alone. Ibn Babshadh and al-Zamakhshari agreed in denying this view to Sibawayh and attributing it to someone else.

The strongest evidence supporting al-Khalil's view, and God knows best, is that this word is used in interrogation as it is used in the conditional, and they recited:

*mahma li al-laylata mahma liyah*
*awdā bi-na'lī wa-sarra māliyah*

He meant: *mali al-layla* (what is with me tonight). There is no difficulty here: it is the interrogative *ma* that was repeated for emphasis, as they say *la la* (no no) and *na'am na'am* (yes yes). Then the repetition of the identical word was disliked, so the *alif* of the first became *ha'*. The change of the interrogative *ma* has occurred even without repetition, so it is more appropriate here. When it becomes clear that *mahma* used in interrogation originally was a repeated *ma*, this is a clearer proof that the conditional one is similar. The citing of parallels is the trustworthy proof in the Arabic sciences, and God knows best.

As for al-Zamakhshari's refutation of those who claim that it means *mata ma* (when), it is a correct refutation, and the verse is the most truthful witness to his refutation. The pronoun in *bihi* refers definitely to *mahma*, and what is attached to it as its explanation is *min ayatin* (a sign), which shows that the pronoun refers to the sign. Thus it is necessary that *mahma* refers to it, because a referent and its referred-to must correspond. Therefore the claim of this speaker that *mahma* refers to a time, claiming it means *mata ma*, is a departure from the truth.

Al-Zamakhshari's excuse is clear in responding to his reporting [of this view] and his harsh denunciation of it, and in directing the arrows of censure at him. So reflect on this section, for in it is light for the path and a cure for the thirst. God is the Granter of success.]] — [Ahmad's marginal comment ends]. The *ma* is the redundant emphatic *ma* that is added to it for the conditional, as in your saying *mata ma takhruj akhruj* (whenever you go out, I will go out), and in *ayna ma takunu yudrikkum al-mawt* (﴿Wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾), and *fa-imma nadhhabanna bika* (﴿Then, if We take you away﴾). However, the *alif* was changed into *ha'* to avoid the heaviness of repeating two similar sounds. This is the sound and correct Basran view. Some people claim that *mah* is the sound with which one tells a dog to stop, and *ma* is the conditional, as if it were said: "Stop, whatever sign you bring us with which to bewitch us, we will not believe you." If you ask: what is the grammatical position of *mahma*? I answer: it is in the nominative case, meaning: "whatever thing you bring us," or in the accusative, meaning: "whatever thing you bring us, whatever thing you bring to us." *Min ayatin* (from a sign) is an explanation of *mahma*. The two pronouns in *bihi* and *biha* refer back to *mahma*, except that one is masculine according to the wording, and the second is feminine according to the meaning, because it means *ayah* (sign). Similar to this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*wa-mahma yakun 'inda imri'in min khaliqatin*
*wa-in khalaha takhfa 'ala al-nasi ta'lami*

[This is from Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma's Mu'allaqa. *Mahma* is a conditional noun meaning "whatever thing," according to the preferred view, which is why the pronoun refers back to it. If the referent is feminine, as here, the pronoun sometimes refers back to it in the masculine according to the wording, as in his saying *yakun*, and sometimes in the feminine according to the meaning, as in his saying *wa-in khalaha*. He did not make this refer to *khaliqah* (disposition), because *mahma* is what is spoken about, and *min khaliqatin* is its explanation. Since it was explained with a feminine noun, it is proper to feminise the pronoun referring to it after explaining it. He says: whatever nature and disposition exists in a person, people will know it by its signs, even if he thinks it is hidden from them.]

This word belongs to the category of words that people who have no grasp of Arabic grammar distort: they place it in the wrong position, and think that *mahma* means *mata ma* (whenever), saying: "*mahma* you come to me, I will give you." This is their own invention and has nothing to do with the words of the Arabic lexicographer. Then they go on to interpret *mahma ta'tina bihi min ayatin* as meaning "a time," and thus they deviate from God's signs without realising it. This and similar errors make one kneel before whoever reads the book of Sibawayh. If you ask: how did they call it a sign, and then say "to bewitch us with it"? I answer: they did not call it a sign because they believed it was a sign, but they called it so only in imitation of Moses's naming, and they intended by this mockery and frivolity. *al-tufan* (the flood) is what overwhelmed and overcame them of rain or torrent. It is said: the water rose above their fields. They were rained on for eight days in deep darkness; they could not see sun or moon, and none of them could leave his house. It is also said: God sent upon them the sky until they nearly perished, and the houses of the Children of Israel and the houses of the Copts were intermingled; the Copts' houses filled with water until they stood in water up to their necks, and whoever sat down drowned, while not a drop entered the houses of the Children of Israel. The water overflowed over their land and stagnated, preventing them from farming, building, and dealing, and it lasted seven days over them.

From Abu Qilaba: *al-tufan* is the smallpox, which was the first punishment that befell them, and it remained in the land. It is also said that it is *al-mawtan* (a plague that strikes livestock), and it is also said that it is the *ta'un* (plague). They said to Moses: "Pray to your Lord to remove this from us, and we will believe in you." He prayed, and it was lifted from them, but they did not believe, so that year the grass and crops grew as never before. They lived for a month, then God sent upon them locusts, which ate most of their crops and fruits, then ate everything, even the doors, the roofs of their houses, and their clothes; but nothing entered the houses of the Children of Israel. They were terrified and went to Moses and promised to repent, so God removed it from them after seven days. Moses went out into the open, pointed with his staff toward east and west, and the locusts returned to the regions from which they had come. They said: "We will not abandon our religion." They remained a month, then God unleashed upon them *al-qummal* (lice), which according to Abu Ubayda is the large ticks. It is also said: *al-dabā* (the young locusts), which are the offspring of the locust, the wing-buds of locusts. It is also said: fleas. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: it is the weevil. It ate what the locusts had left, and licked the earth, and it used to enter between a man's garment and his skin and suck him; one of them would eat food and it would be full of lice; one of them would take ten sacks to the mill and only a little would come back. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: there was beside them a grey-dust mound; Moses struck it with his staff and it became lice, which fell upon their skin, their hair, the lids of their eyes, and their eyebrows, and clung to their skins like smallpox. They shouted, cried out, and went to Moses, who lifted it from them. They said: "Now we are certain that you are a sorcerer; by the might of Pharaoh, we will never believe you." God then sent upon them, after a month, the frogs. They entered their houses, filled their vessels and food. No one could uncover any cloth, food or drink without finding frogs in it. When a man wanted to speak, a frog would leap into his mouth; their beds were full of them so they could not sleep; the frogs threw themselves into pots boiling and into ovens blazing. They complained to Moses and said: "Have mercy on us this time, and we will truly repent and not return." They made covenants with him, he prayed, and God removed it from them. Then they broke the covenant, so God sent upon them blood, and their water became blood. They complained to Pharaoh, who said: "He has bewitched you." He used to gather a Copt and an Israelite at one vessel; what was on the Israelite's side was water, and what was on the Copt's side was blood, even though they drew from one water source: the Copt drew blood and the Israelite drew water. Even a Coptic woman would say to her Israelite neighbour: "Put water in your mouth, then spit it into mine," and the water in her mouth would become blood.

Pharaoh became so thirsty that he was near death, and he used to suck on moist trees, but when he chewed them, their sweet water turned into salty bitter water. From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: the Nile flowed over them as blood. It is also said: God sent upon them nosebleeds. It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, stayed among them after he overcame the magicians for twenty years, showing them these signs. It is also narrated that when he showed them the hand and the staff, and the loss of souls and fruits, he said: "O Lord, this servant of Yours has exalted himself in the land; so seize him with a punishment that You make a vengeance upon him and his people, a lesson for my people, and a sign for those after me." Then God sent upon them the flood, then the locusts, then what followed of the punishments.

Al-Hasan recited *wa-al-qamla* (and the lice) with a fatha on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *mim*, meaning the well-known lice. *Ayatin mufassalatin* (﴿clear signs﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The meaning of *mufassalat* is: explained and manifest, such that no sensible person would be confused that they are signs of God, which none other can produce, and that they are a lesson for them and a punishment for their disbelief. Or it means: there was a separation between some of them and others by a time in which their condition was tested, to see whether they would remain steadfast in what they had promised themselves, or would break their word, so as to establish the proof against them?

It is also narrated that when he showed them the hand and the staff, and the loss of souls and fruits, he said: "O Lord, this servant of Yours has exalted himself in the land; so seize him with a punishment that You make a vengeance upon him and his people, a lesson for my people, and a sign for those after me." Then God sent upon them the flood, then the locusts, then what followed of the punishments.

Al-Hasan recited *wa-al-qamla* (and the lice) with a fatha on the *qaf* and a sukun on the *mim*, meaning the well-known lice. *Ayatin mufassalatin* (﴿clear signs﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. The meaning of *mufassalat* is: explained and manifest, such that no sensible person would be confused that they are signs of God, which none other can produce, and that they are a lesson for them and a punishment for their disbelief. Or it means: there was a separation between some of them and others by a time in which their condition was tested, to see whether they would remain steadfast in what they had promised themselves, or would break their word, so as to establish the proof against them?

By what He has covenanted with you (ما عَهِدَ عِنْدَكَ): the "ما" is verbal-masdar (ما مصدرية), so the meaning is "by His covenant with you," that is, prophethood. The "bi" (ب) may be connected to His saying "Pray to your Lord for us" (ادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ), in two ways. The first: "Help us to what we ask of you, namely to pray for us, by the right of what you have of God's covenant and His honour in prophethood." Or: "Pray to God for us, seeking nearness to Him through His covenant with you." Or it may be an oath answered by "we will surely believe" (لَنُؤْمِنَنَّ), meaning: "We swear by God's covenant with you that, if you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe in you."

Until a term (إِلى أَجَلٍ) that they will reach: until a limit of time that they will certainly reach, that is, they will be punished in it without doubt, and the respite they were granted before and the removal of punishment will not benefit them until it befalls them.

Then, when (إِذا) they break their word (هُمْ يَنْكُثُونَ): this is the answer to "lamma" (لما), meaning: when We removed it from them, they immediately broke their word and hastened to it; they did not delay it, but as soon as it was removed from them, they broke their promise.

So We took retribution from them (فَانْتَقَمْنا مِنْهُمْ): We intended to take vengeance upon them, so We drowned them (فَأَغْرَقْناهُمْ) in the sea (اليم), which is the sea whose bottom cannot be reached. It is said: it is the deep part of the sea and its main body of water; its derivation is from "tayammum" (التيمم), because those who seek benefit from it aim for it.

Because they denied Our signs (بِأَنَّهُمْ كَذَّبُوا بِآياتِنا): that is, their drowning was due to their denial of the signs, their heedlessness of them, and their scant reflection upon them.

The people who were oppressed (al-qawm alladhina kanu yustad'afun): these are the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh and his people oppressed. "And the land" refers to the land of Egypt and Syria, which the Children of Israel possessed after the Pharaohs and the Amalekites. They disposed of its regions and its eastern and western parts as they willed. "Which We had blessed" means with fertility and abundance of provision. "Your Lord's good word" (kalimat rabbika al-husna) refers to His saying: "And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land," up to His saying "what they feared."

Al-husna is the feminine form of the elative al-ahsan, functioning as an adjective of al-kalima (the word). The meaning of "was fulfilled upon the Children of Israel" (tammat 'ala Bani Isra'il) is that it continued over them and remained in effect, from your saying tamma 'ala al-amr, meaning it passed over him. "For their patience" means because of their steadfastness. This is sufficient as an incitement to patience and as an indication that whoever meets affliction with impatience, God leaves him to it, while whoever meets it with patience and awaits victory, God guarantees him relief.

It is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri): "I am astonished at one who becomes light-headed, how he becomes light-headed when he has heard His saying." Then he recited the verse.

Khaffa (becomes light-headed) means he became agitated with impatience and lacked endurance, and he did not show the steadiness of those possessing patience.

Asim, in one narration, read: "Wa tammat kalimat rabbika al-husna" (in the plural, kalimat). A parallel to this is: "min ayati rabbihi al-kubra" (from the greatest of the signs of his Lord).

"What Pharaoh and his people used to make" (ma kana yasna'u Fir'awnu wa qawmuhu) means what they used to do, and "what they used to build" (ma kanu ya'rishun) refers to their constructing and building of palaces and buildings. "Of the trellised gardens" refers to: "It is He who produced gardens, both trellised and untrellised" (huwa alladhi ansha'a jannatin ma'rushatin). Alternatively, it means what they used to raise of lofty buildings in the sky, such as the tower of Haman and others.

Yа'rishun is also read with kasra and with damma (ya'rishun and ya'rushun). Al-Yazidi reported that the kasra is more eloquent. I have been told that some people read it as yaghrisun (they plant), from planting trees, but I do not think this is anything but a scribal error (tashif) on his part.

This is the final part of the account the Almighty has specified concerning Pharaoh, the Copts, their denial of God's signs, their wrongdoing, and their disobedience. Then he follows it with the account of the Children of Israel and what they introduced, after their deliverance from Pharaoh's dominion and enslavement, their witnessing of the great signs, and their crossing of the sea. This included worshipping a calf, asking to see God openly, and other kinds of disbelief and disobedience. The purpose is to show the state of the human being, that he is, as God described him, ﴿wrongdoing, ungrateful, ignorant, and ungrateful﴾, except for those whom God protects, ﴿and few of My servants are grateful﴾. It also serves to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he saw from the Children of Israel in Medina.

It is related that Moses led them across on the Day of 'Ashura', after God had destroyed Pharaoh and his people, and they fasted it out of gratitude to God. ﴿They came upon a people devoted to idols of theirs﴾, meaning they persisted in worshipping them and clung to their worship. Ibn Jurayj said: they were images of cows, and that was the beginning of the affair of the calf. It was also said that they were a people from Lakhm. It was said that they were from the Canaanites, whom Moses, peace be upon him, had been commanded to fight.

It is read as "wa-jawwaznā" (وجوّزنا), meaning "we caused to pass," from ajāza. It is said: ajāza al-makān, jawwazahu, and jāwazahu, all meaning "he crossed it," as in your saying: a'lāhu, 'alāhu, and 'ālāhu (أعلاه وعلاه وعالاه).

It is also read as "ya'kifūna" (يعكفون) with a damma and a kasra on the kāf. ﴿Make for us a god﴾, meaning an idol, ﴿just as they have gods﴾, meaning idols, ﴿that they devote themselves to.﴾ The "mā" (ما) in the phrase is a kāfah (كافة), i.e., a particle that detaches the kāf from governing the noun, and for this reason a full sentence follows it.

It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that a Jew said to him: "You differed after your Prophet before his water had dried." He said: "You said, ﴿Make for us a god﴾ before your feet had dried." ﴿Indeed, you are a people who act ignorantly.﴾ This is a expression of astonishment at their words, following what they had seen of the greatest sign and the greatest miracle. So He described them with absolute ignorance and emphasized it, because there is no ignorance greater than what they showed, nor more shameful.

﴿Indeed, these﴾, meaning the worshippers of those images, ﴿will be destroyed in what they are doing﴾, meaning shattered and broken to pieces in what they are engaged in. This comes from the phrase "a broken vessel" (إناء متبر), when it is crumbled into fragments (فضاضا). [[Note by the editor: "fadāḍā" means crushed fragments like rubble; this is from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] The word al-tibr (التبر) is used for broken gold. That is, God will destroy and ruin their religion, which they follow, at my hands, and will smash these idols of theirs and leave them as rubble. ﴿And what they were doing is void﴾, meaning whatever they did of their worship in the past was nothing but void and vanished, and of no benefit to them, even though they supposed it was a means of drawing near to God, as He said: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust.﴾

The use of "these" (هؤلاء) as the subject of "inna" (إنّ), and the placing of the predicate of the nominal sentence before the sentence that serves as its predicate, marks the worshippers of idols as those who are exposed to destruction, that it will not pass them at all, and that it is for them a binding decree. This is to warn them of the consequence of what they sought and to make hateful to them what they loved.

﴿Shall I seek for you a god other than God,﴾ meaning an object of worship other than the One who deserves worship? ﴿When He has favored you over all beings?﴾ This means: shall I seek for you a deity, when He alone has done for you what He has done, granting you a favor He has given to no one else, so that you may single Him out for worship and not associate anyone with Him. The interrogative hamza (الهمزة) here carries the sense of denial and astonishment at their request to worship other than God, despite being immersed in the blessings of God.
