Tafsir (commentary) of al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 7, verse 141:

﴿يَسُومُونَكُمْ سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ﴾ means: they seek to inflict upon you the severest torment, from "sama al-sil'ah" (he sought the commodity) when he asked for it. If it is asked: what is the place (i'rab) of "yasumunakum"? The answer: it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) with no grammatical position. It is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the addressees or from the family of Pharaoh.

﴿وَذَلِكُمْ﴾ is a reference to the deliverance or to the torment. "Al-bala'" means either a blessing or a trial. It has also been read as "yuqattilun" with the letters lightened (bi-al-takhfif).

It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel, while they were in Egypt, that if God destroyed their enemy, he would bring them a Book from God containing a clarification of what they should do and what they should avoid. When Pharaoh was destroyed, Moses asked his Lord for the Book, and He commanded him to fast thirty days, which was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty days, he disliked the odour of his mouth and used a miswak (tooth-stick). The angels said: "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you have spoiled it with the miswak." It has also been said: God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odour of the mouth of a fasting person is more pleasing to Me than the scent of musk?" So God commanded him to add ten days to them from Dhu al-Hijjah for this reason.

It has also been said: God commanded him to fast thirty days and to act in them with what brings him closer to God, and then the Torah was revealed to him during the ten days, and He spoke to him in it.

The forty (nights) were mentioned in summary in Surah al-Baqarah, and are detailed here.

"And the appointed time of his Lord" means the time that He set for him and fixed for him.

"Forty nights" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject), meaning that this number was fully completed.

"Harun" is in apposition to his brother, as an ʿaṭf al-bayān (explicative apposition, clarifying the preceding noun).

It was also read with a ḍamma (هارونُ) as a vocative (nidāʾ), so that the meaning is "O Harun."

"Take my place among my people" means: be my successor among them.

"And reform" means: be a reformer. Or: "reform what must be reformed of the affairs of the Children of Israel, and whoever among them calls you to corruption, do not follow him or obey him."

For Your appointed time: at the time We set and appointed for him. The lam here denotes specificity, as if it were said: his coming was singled out for Our appointed time, just as you say, "I came to him on the tenth of the month."

**And his Lord spoke to him** without an intermediary, **as a king speaks**, and His speaking means that He creates speech [[Al-Zamakhshari says: "His saying 'without an intermediary...' etc." Ahmad says: This is an explicit statement by him that God creates speech, as the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology) hold. What refutes this in this verse is that it is set in the context of favouring Moses, through God's choosing him and singling him out for speaking to Him. Likewise, after some verses, God says: "I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech; so take what I have given you and be among the grateful" (7:144). If God's speaking to him meant creating letters and sounds in some bodies and Moses hearing them, then everyone would be equal to Moses in that, and indeed the individual Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) would be more deserving of this distinction and more entitled to this particularity than Moses, because they heard speech in the aforementioned manner from the most excellent and purest of created bodies, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and their distinction would be more evident and their particularity more abundant. We know necessarily, from the context of this verse, that Moses (peace be upon him) was distinguished by this quality. Therefore nothing can be taken from it except the belief that he heard the eternal speech subsisting in the Essence of God, glorified and exalted, without an intermediary of letters or anything else. Just as we allow by reason that the Essence of the Creator, glorified and exalted, may be seen though He is not a body, so we allow that His speech may be heard though it is not a letter or a sound. The discussion of this creed is long, and the course is muddy. This point is the specific one for this verse, and Allah is the Granter of success.]]. Its meaning, speaking, is that He creates speech [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "and His speaking means that He creates speech" reflect the Mu'tazilite doctrine that the speech of God consists of words that God creates in some bodies. As for the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority), His speech is an eternal attribute subsisting in His Essence, so His speaking to His servant is that He reveals it to him, as is established in the science of tawhid (theology). (Ibn al-Munayyir)]] articulated in some bodies, just as He created it inscribed on the Tablet. It is related that Moses (peace be upon him) would hear that speech from every direction. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that He spoke to him for forty days and forty nights and wrote the Tablets for him. It is said that He spoke to him only at the beginning of the forty days.

**"Show me, that I may look upon You."** The second object of "show me" is omitted. [[He returns to his speech. He says: "His saying 'show me, that I may look upon You' has its first object omitted and its second mentioned; the implied meaning is: show me Yourself, that I may look upon You..." Ahmad says: How greatly his speech is confused in this verse, for his aim is to refute truth with error and to disfigure the face of the moon with his palm. Far-fetched! The dawn has become clear to one who has two eyes; the truth is bright, not mixed with doubt except in the eyes of one who has a blemish. As for the share of reason in permitting the vision of God, this is the task of ilm al-kalam (dialectical theology), and the most concise way to establish it is this: existence is what makes vision valid, as evidence that the permissibility of being seen is a judgement that requires something to validate it. Permissibility includes substance and accident, and there is no common feature between them that can be made the validator except existence. If existence is the validator, then His being seen, may He be exalted, is valid by virtue of His existence. As for the claim that it is improbable that what is not in a direction should be seen, this is an imaginary notion like that which afflicted the Mu'attilah (those who deny divine attributes), so their insight became blind, until they denied an existent that is not in a direction. Whoever follows fancies wanders in the deserts of error and is bewildered. If seeing depended on the direction of the seen, knowing would depend on the direction of the known; and there is no disagreement that He, glorified, is known without direction, so He is likewise seen without direction. The truth is that Moses (peace be upon him) asked for vision for himself, knowing that it is permissible for Allah. The Qadariyyah (a school that emphasised human free will) are driven by greed and emboldened so that they wish to make Moses (peace be upon him) hold their belief. But in that case they are only among those who harmed Moses, and God absolved him of what they said, and he was honourable in the sight of God. As for his (peace be upon him) saying: "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?" (7:155), it is a disavowal of their deeds, a declaration of their foolishness and a condemnation of their opinion. The Qadariyyah have no ease in citing it as evidence that Moses (peace be upon him) denied the permissibility of vision. The cause of their destruction, according to most exegetes, was the worship of the calf. If the cause was their asking for vision, it was not because it is impermissible for God, but because God informed them that it does not occur in this world, and the report is true. Their request came after Moses's request, and when they asked, having heard the report that it would not occur, their request was contrary to what was known, a denial of the report. For this reason Moses (peace be upon him) called them foolish and disavowed asking for what God had informed them would not occur at that time. If their request for vision was before God informed them that it would not occur, then Moses (peace be upon him) called them foolish for proposing to God this particular matter and for making belief conditional upon it, when they said: "We will not believe you until we see God plainly" (2:55). Do you not see that their saying "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us out of the earth" (17:90) was asking for something permissible, yet they were rebuked for proposing to God what belief does not depend upon? These three discussions clarify for you the bad judgement of al-Zamakhshari, who looks through the eye of desire and whose blindness keeps him from the path of guidance. Allah is the Granter of success.]], i.e. show me Yourself, that I may look upon You.

*If you say:* "Seeing is the same as looking; how then is it said, 'show me, that I may look upon You'?" *I say:* The meaning of "show me Yourself" is: make me able to see You, by manifesting Yourself to me, so that I may look upon You and see You.

*If you say:* "Then why did He say, 'You shall not see Me,' and not 'You shall not look upon Me,' given His words 'that I may look upon You'?" *I say:* When he said "show me," meaning "make me able to see," which is perception, He knew that what was sought was vision, which is perception, and not mere looking, which carries no perception. So He said "You shall not see Me" and did not say "You shall not look upon Me."

*If you say:* "How could Moses ask for that, when he is the one who knows God best, what is permissible for Him and what is not, and His exaltedness above being seen by some of the senses, which is valid only of what is in a direction? Whatever is neither a body nor an accident cannot possibly be in a direction. The Mujbirah (determinists, here meaning Ahl al-Sunnah) deny that this is impossible, but that denial is not necessarily accepted by reason, since it is not the first of their obstinacies and presumptions. And how could he ask for it, when he said, after the quake seized those who said 'Show us God plainly': 'Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?' up to 'You mislead by it whom You will' (7:155), disavowing their deed and calling them foolish and misguided?"

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words "the Mujbirah deny that this is impossible" mean Ahl al-Sunnah, who hold that seeing God is permissible and deny that the seen must be in a direction. He, exalted, says: "Faces that day shall be radiant, looking toward their Lord" (75:22–23). What is permissible may be absent at some times and occur at others. The hadith, as will come, is: "You will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon." The place of this discussion is the science of kalam. (Ibn al-Munayyir)]]

*I say:* He asked for it only to rebuke those whom he called foolish and misguided, and to disavow their deed, and to silence them. When they asked for vision, he denied it to them, informed them of their error and alerted them to the truth. They persisted and went on in their obstinacy, saying: "We will not, and we will never believe you until we see God plainly." So he wished them to hear the explicit text from God that this is impossible, namely His saying "You shall not see Me," so that they would be certain and the doubt that had entered them would be removed. Therefore he said: "My Lord, show me, that I may look upon You."

*If you say:* "Why did he not say, 'Show them, that they may look upon You'?"

[[He returns to his speech. He says: "If you say, why did he not say, 'Show them, that they may look upon You'?..." Ahmad says: This other speech is of the first rank, and the closest evidence against it is this: if the request for vision had been for them, so that when they heard God refuse it they would be certain that it was impossible, then asking for it would have been futile and would not serve this purpose. For these people were either believers in Moses or disbelievers in him. If they were believers in him, then his telling them that God is not seen and that this is not permissible for Him would have achieved the aim, without any need for Moses (peace be upon him) to ask God to show them His Essence, while knowing that this is impossible. If they were disbelievers in Moses (peace be upon him), the aim would not be achieved either, because when God refuses his request for vision, that refusal is established for them only by Moses's word that God refused it; and since they disbelieve in Moses, how would another's report from God of that impossibility benefit them? This is the clearest proof, for Moses (peace be upon him) asked for vision for himself, believing it permissible for God, and God informed him that it does not occur in this world, though it is permissible.]]

*I say:* Because Allah, glorified, spoke to Moses (peace be upon him) while they were listening. When they heard the speech of the Lord of Might, they wished Moses to see His Essence so that they would see it with him, just as He had made him hear His speech and they heard it with him. This wish was based on faulty analogy. Therefore Moses said: "Show me, that I may look upon You." Also, when he was rebuked for what he asked, and denied in his prophethood, his special standing and his nearness to God, and was told, "That will not be," then others were more deserving of denial. Also, the Messenger is the leader of his community, so whatever is addressed to him, or whatever he is addressed with, returns to them.

[[He returns to his speech. He says: "And His saying 'that I may look upon You,' and what it contains of the meaning of facing..." Ahmad says: His claim that looking entails corporeality has already been refuted. As for his exonerating Moses (peace be upon him) by attributing to him the belief that vision is impossible, that is unnecessary to him.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 143 (part 2 of 2):

As for his claim, in its detail, that he (peace be upon him) was superior to Wasil ibn 'Ata', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nazzam, Abu al-Hudhayl and the two Shaykhs in knowledge of God and His attributes, this is a diminishing of his exalted rank. The least of the common folk who follow the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) is superior in the sight of God to the people of innovation (bid'a) and of whims (ahwa'), even if they fill the earth with hypocrisy and crowd their books with obstinacy and enmity toward the People of the Sunna. How then could it be said of the one to whom God spoke (kalim Allah), upon him be the best of prayers and peace?

[...] which are pure likening (tashbih) and anthropomorphism (tajsim), are evidence that this is a rendering of their proposal and a relaying of their saying. The owner of the Jamal (al-Zamakhshari, whose commentary is al-Kashshaf) is too exalted to make God an object of sight, perceived by the faculty of vision. How then about one who has greater knowledge of God, exalted is He, than Wasil ibn 'Ata', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nazzam, Abu al-Hudhayl, the two Shaykhs, and all the theologians (mutakallimun)?

If you say: What is the meaning of "lan" (never)? I say: It is the emphasis of the negation that "la" (not) conveys.

[[He returned to his speech. He said: "If you say, what is the meaning of 'lan'? I say: it is the emphasis of the negation which 'la' conveys... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "Lan," as al-Zamakhshari said, shares with "la" in negation and is distinguished by the special feature of emphasizing it. As for al-Zamakhshari's deduction from this that the vision is incompatible with the state of the Creator, glorified and exalted, and then his application of the term "state" (hal) to God, which should be avoided, and his citing of it as proof that "lan" indicates the rational impossibility of what is negated by it, this is greatly refuted by many verses, such as His saying: ﴿Say: You will never (lan) go out with me, ever﴾, which does not render their going out rationally impossible; and ﴿Never (lan) will any of your people believe except those who have already believed﴾; ﴿You will never (lan) follow us﴾. All of these are rationally possible, were it not that the report prevents their occurrence. So too is the vision.]]

That is because "la" negates the future. You say: "I will not do it tomorrow (la af'alu ghadan)." When you emphasize its negation, you say: "I will never do it tomorrow (lan af'ala ghadan)." The meaning is that his doing it contradicts his state, as in His saying: ﴿They will never (lan) create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾. So His saying ﴿Vision does not reach Him (la tudriku-hu al-absar)﴾ is a negation of vision in the future. And ﴿You will never (lan) see Me﴾ is emphasis and clarification, because what is negated is incompatible with His attributes.

If you say: How is the exception (istidrak) in His saying ﴿But look (wa lakin unzur) at the mountain﴾ connected to what precedes it? I say: It is connected to it in the sense that seeing Me is impossible, so do not seek it; rather, have recourse to another sight: that you look at the mountain which trembles with you and with those on whose behalf you sought the vision, how I will deal with it and how I will make it crumble (dakk) because of your request for the vision. This is so that you may magnify what you have undertaken through the great effect that I show you. It is as if, exalted and majestic, He established at the time of the request for vision what is similar to the attribution of offspring to Him in His saying ﴿and the mountains fall down in ruin (wa takhirru al-jibalu hadda), that they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾.

[[He returned to his speech. He said: "And the meaning of 'if it remains in its place' (fa in istaqarra makanahu): if it stays firm as it was, moving..." Ahmad said: This is one of the tricks of the Qadariyya (the Mu'tazila, who deny divine predestination in the sense used here) in rejecting the vision. They say: God made it contingent upon an impossible condition, namely the mountain's remaining stable while it is crumbled; and what is contingent upon the impossible is impossible. This is a false trick. For what is made contingent is the mountain's remaining stable as stability, and that is possible and permissible. The knowledge that it will not remain stable does not remove the possibility of its remaining stable. The divine knowledge does not change the thing known, nor shift its ruling from possibility to impossibility or the reverse. At that point, it becomes a proof for the People of the Sunna. We say: the mountain's remaining stable is possible, and the occurrence of vision was made contingent upon it. What is contingent upon the possible is possible. The Mu'tazila believe that the opposite of what is known cannot be within God's power, while we say it is within His power, but His will has not been directed to bringing it into being. Our saying is more suited to courtesy (adab) and more fitting for honoring the address (al-khitab).]]

in its places, then ﴿you will see Me (fa sawfa tarani)﴾ is the making of the existence of vision contingent upon the existence of what does not happen, namely the mountain's remaining stable in its place when He crumbles it and levels it to the ground. This is speech interlocked, one part within another, delivered in a wondrous style and an original mode. Do you not see how he escaped from looking to looking through the word of exception? Then how did he build the threat of the trembling, which occurred because of the request to look, upon the condition for the existence of vision? I mean His saying ﴿if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾.

﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain (fa lamma tajalla rabbu-hu lil-jabal)﴾: i.e., when His power became manifest to it, and His command and will took charge of it, ﴿He made it crumble (ja'alahu dakkan)﴾: i.e., crumbled, a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, like "the ruler's striking (darb al-amir)." Al-dakk and al-dakk (both meaning crushing) are brothers, like al-shakk and al-shakk (both meaning piercing). It is also read as "dakla'" (diminutive form)... [note: the source reads "دكاء" as the reading]. Al-dakka': the name for a raised hillock of the earth, like a dakka, or a level flat land (ardan dakka'). From it comes their saying: "a she-camel with a humble hump (naqa dakka' mutawadi'at al-sanam)." It is reported from al-Sha'bi that al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym said to him: "Spread your hand flat (ibsut yadaka dakka')," i.e., extend it level. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "dakkan," meaning in pieces, crumbled, the plural of dakka'.

﴿And Musa fell down unconscious (wa kharra Musa sa'iqan)﴾ from the terror of what he saw. Sa'iqa is of the pattern "fa'ala-tu fa-fa'ala" (I did it and it became done): one says "sa'iqtu-hu fa-sa'iqa" (I struck him and he was struck). Its origin is from the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa), which is also called al-sa'iqa, from saqa'a-hu, when one strikes him on the head. Its meaning is: he fell down in a swoon, like death. It is reported that the angels passed by him while he was in a swoon.

[[He returned to his speech. He said: "And the meaning of 'Musa fell down unconscious': he fell in a swoon like death, and it is reported that the angels passed by him..." Ahmad said: This is a report which only one who forces it does so for the sake of rejecting the vision, taking it as support and backing for a corrupt doctrine. The proper course is to refute the one who transmitted it and to declare the angels, upon them be peace, free from humiliating Musa, the one to whom God spoke, by kicking him with the foot and insulting him in address.]]

So they began to kick him with their feet and say: "O son of the menstruating women! Did you covet seeing the Lord of Majesty?" ﴿When he recovered from his swoon, he said: Glory be to You (subhanaka)﴾: I declare You free from what is not permissible for You, including vision and other things. ﴿I have repented to You (tubtu ilayka)﴾ from seeking the vision. ﴿And I am the first of the believers (wa ana awwalu al-mu'minin)﴾: that You are not seen nor perceived by any of the senses.

If you say: If the request for vision was for the purpose you mentioned, then for what did he repent?

[[He returned to his speech. He said: "If you say: if the request for vision was for the purpose you mentioned, then for what did he repent?" Ahmad said: As for the crumbling of the mountain, its secret has already been discussed. As for Musa's glorification (tasbih), it was because it became clear to him that knowledge had already preceded that the vision would not occur in this world, and God, exalted is He, is sanctified above the occurrence of the opposite of what He knows, and above any reversal in His true report and His truthful word. So when it became clear that what he sought was contrary to what was known, he glorified God and declared His knowledge and His report free from reversal. As for repentance on the part of prophets, it does not imply that it was from a sin, because their noble station requires that they be pure and free from everything that would lower them. There is no doubt that refraining from asking for vision without permission would have been more perfect. It has been reported: "The misdeeds of those brought near are good deeds for the righteous."]]

I say: From his uttering that great statement upon his tongue, even though it was for a correct purpose and without permission from God, exalted is He. So look at God's magnification of the matter of vision in this verse: how He made the mountain tremble for those who asked for it and made it crumble; how He struck them with a swoon, and did not spare His interlocutor from the scattering [[His words "and did not spare His interlocutor from the scattering of that" — "nafayan" is what flies off from raindrops, from the bucket's drip, from sand when trodden, from wool when carded, and similar things. Thus in the commentary on the Mu'allaqat by the scholar al-Zawzani. (A)]] of that, as an exaggeration in magnifying the matter; how he glorified his Lord, seeking refuge in Him, and repented of letting that word pass upon his tongue, and said: "I am the first of the believers." Then he marveled at those who call themselves Muslims and who call themselves People of the Sunna and the Community (Ahl al-Sunna wa al-Jama'a), how they adopted this great matter as a doctrine.

[[He returned to his speech. He said: "Then he marveled at those who call themselves Muslims and who call themselves People of the Sunna and the Community..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari, in this section, moved to the mockery of the People of the Sunna which you hear. Were it not for relying on Hassan ibn Thabit al-Ansari, companion and poet of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), who defended him and with whom was the Holy Spirit, we would say to these who title themselves "the Just" (al-'Adliyya) and "the Saved" (al-Najiyya): peace. But just as Hassan defended the Messenger of God against his enemies, so we defend the companions of the Sunna of the Messenger of God against their enemies, and we say:

A group who disbelieved in seeing their Lord
truly, and God's promise He will not break:
They titled themselves "the Just." We said: Indeed!
They equated their Lord, so their folly is enough for them.
They titled themselves "the Saved." No indeed,
if they are not in the blaze, they are on its brink.]]

How they took this monstrous thing as a doctrine. Do not be deceived by their cover of "bila kayf" (without asking how), for it is one of the stratagems of their elders! The saying is what one of the "Just" said about them:

A group that named their desires "the Sunna,"
and a group, by my life, donkeys saddled.
They likened Him to His creation and feared
the people's censure, so they hid behind "balkafa."

[[Al-Zamakhshari on the People of the Sunna: that is, a group who named their own desires "Sunna." But whoever knows that the Mu'tazila's basis is reason, and the Community's basis is transmitted text, will recognize the desire from the guidance. "Hummar" (donkeys) means like donkeys. "Mawkafa" means with a pack-saddle placed upon them, as an exaggeration in the comparison. "They likened Him": i.e., God, exalted is He, to His creation, in that they said He is seen with the eye; so they feared the people's reproach, and hid behind their saying that He is seen "without modality" (bila kayf). Thus "balkafa" is coined from that.]]

Another interpretation: he means by His saying ﴿Show me (arini), that I may look at You (anzur ilayka)﴾: "Make Yourself known to me with a clear and manifest knowledge, as if he wanted a manifestation of Yourself through a sign like the signs of the Resurrection, which compel creation to know You: ﴿that I may look at You﴾, I would know You with a knowledge of necessity, as if I were looking at You." As in the hadith: "You will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon" [[Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayhi) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, who said: "We were sitting with the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon, and said: 'Indeed you will see your Lord as you see this moon'..." And al-Bukhari has, from another narration: "Indeed you will see your Lord plainly (ʿiyanan)." Both agreed upon it from the hadith of Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra with the same meaning.]], meaning: you will know Him with a clear knowledge, as clear as your sight of the moon when it is full and complete.

﴿He said: You will not see Me (lan tarani)﴾: i.e., you will not be able to bear knowing Me in this manner, and your strength will not endure that compelling sign. ﴿But look at the mountain﴾: I will manifest to it one of those signs, and if it remains firm at its manifestation and stays in its place without collapsing, then you will be able to bear it and endure it. ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾: when a sign of His power and greatness appeared to it, ﴿He made it crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious﴾ from the greatness of what he saw. ﴿When he recovered, he said: Glory be to You, I have repented to You﴾ from what I proposed and presumed, ﴿and I am the first of the believers﴾ in Your greatness and majesty, and that nothing can stand against Your might and Your force.

I have chosen you above the people: I selected you over the people of your time and preferred you over them ﴿with My messages﴾, which are the books of the Torah, ﴿and with My speech﴾, and with My speaking to you. ﴿So take what I have given you﴾, meaning what I have bestowed upon you of the honour of prophethood and wisdom, ﴿and be among the grateful﴾ for the blessing in that, for it is among the greatest blessings. It is said: Moses fainted (ṣaʿiq) on the Day of ʿArafah, and he was given the Torah on the Day of Sacrifice (al-Naḥr). If you say: how is it said "I have chosen you above the people" when Aaron was also chosen and a prophet like him? I say: Indeed, but he was a follower of his (tābiʿan lahu), a helper (wirdan) and a minister (wazīran). Al-Kalīm (the one who spoke with God) is Moses, peace be upon him, and the original bearer of the message (al-aṣīl fī ḥaml al-risālah).

They mentioned, regarding the number of the tablets and their substance and length, that they were ten tablets. It was also said: seven. It was said: two tablets, and that they were of emerald, brought by Jibril (peace be upon him). It was said: of green chrysolite and red ruby. It was said:

God commanded Musa to cut them from a hard rock which He made soft for him, so he cut them with his hand and split them with his fingers. From al-Hasan:

They were of wood that descended from the sky, and on them was the Torah, and their length was ten cubits. His words ﴿from every thing﴾ are in the accusative position as the object of *kataba* (We wrote). *Mawʿizatan* (as admonition) and *tafṣīlan* (as detailed explanation) are substitutes (*badal*) for it. The meaning is: We wrote for him everything that the Children of Israel needed in their religion, of admonitions and detailed rulings. It was also said that the Torah was sent down and it was seventy camel-loads, of which a portion was read in a year, and that only four persons read it: Musa, Yusha ibn Nun, Uzayr, and Isa, peace be upon them. From Muqatil: He wrote on the tablets: "I am God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. Do not associate anything with Me. Do not cut off the road. Do not swear by My name falsely, for whoever swears falsely by My name, I will not purify him. Do not kill, do not commit adultery, and do not disobey your parents." ﴿Take them﴾, so We said to him: take them, as a conjunction (*ʿatfan*) upon *kataba* (We wrote). It is permissible that it be a substitute for His words ﴿take what I have given you﴾. The pronoun in *fa-khudhha* refers to the tablets, or to "every thing," since it has the meaning of "things," or to the messages, or to the Torah. The meaning of *biquwwatin* (with strength) is with earnestness and resolve, the act of the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm). ﴿They should hold fast to the best of it﴾:

That is, in it there is what is good and what is better, such as retaliation, pardon, self-defense, and patience. So He commanded them to force themselves to take what is more included in goodness and more abundant in reward, like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. It was also said: they should take what is obligatory or recommended, because it is better than the permissible. It is also permissible that the meaning be: they should take what they were commanded, and not what they were forbidden, in the manner of your saying: "Summer is hotter than winter." ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ means the abode of Pharaoh and his people, which is Egypt, how it was emptied of them and they were destroyed for their defiance, so that you may take heed and not commit defiance like theirs, lest you be punished with a punishment like theirs. It was also said: the dwellings of ʿAd and Thamud and the generations whom God destroyed for their defiance, which you pass by on your journeys. It was also said: the abode of the defiantly disobedient is the Fire of Hell. Al-Hasan read *sa-uriyakum* (I will show you), and this is a widespread dialect in the Hijaz. It is said: *awarani kadha* and *awaraytuhu* (he showed me such-and-such). Its justification is that it may derive from *awrayta al-zand* (to strike the fire-drill so that it kindles), as if the meaning is: clarify it for me and illuminate it so that I may discern it. It was also read *sa-uwrithukum* (I will make you inherit), and this reading is sound, confirmed by His words: ﴿and We made the people who were oppressed inherit﴾. ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth﴾ by sealing upon their hearts and forsaking them, so they do not reflect upon them or take heed from them, out of heedlessness and immersion in what distracts them from them, namely their desires. From al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad: it was related to us from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "When my community magnifies the world, the awe of Islam will be removed from them, and when they abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil, the blessing of revelation will be withheld." [[I have not found it from this route. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported it in his *Nawadir* from the hadith of Abu Hurayra similarly, and he added: "And when my community reviles one another, they will fall from the eyes of people." He mentioned it in the seventy-fifth of the hundred and first chapters, and in its chain is al-Bakhtari ibn ʿUbayd.

And it is weak.]] It was also said: I will turn them away from nullifying them, even if they strive as Pharaoh strove to nullify the sign of Musa, by gathering the sorcerers against it, but God refused except the exaltation of the truth and the overturning of falsehood. It is also permissible:

I will turn them away from them, from disparaging them, and from belittling them. Calling them sorcery is in reference to their destruction. In this is a warning to the addressees about the end of those who turn away from the signs because of their arrogance and disbelief in them, lest they be like them and be made to follow their path. ﴿Without right﴾ has two possibilities: that it be a circumstantial state, meaning they are arrogant without being in the right, since arrogance with right belongs to God alone; and that it be a complement to the verb "to be arrogant," meaning they are arrogant with what is not right and with their religion, which they hold to. ﴿And if they see every sign﴾ among the signs sent down to them, ﴿they will not believe in it﴾. Malik ibn Dinar read *wa-in yarawu* with the *ya* vowelled with a *damma*. It was also read: *sabil al-rushd*, *al-rushd*, and *al-rushad*, like their saying: *al-siqm*, *al-siqm*, and *al-siqam* (sickness). How foolish is one who travels through a desert: if he sees a straight path he turns away from it and leaves it, and if he sees a crooked, deadly way he takes it and follows it. Whoever acts in this manner in his religion is more foolish. ﴿That﴾ is in the nominative or accusative position, meaning: that turning away is because of their denial, or that God turned them away in that manner because of it. ﴿And the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ may be an idafa of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: their meeting with the Hereafter and their witnessing its conditions; and it may be an idafa of the verbal noun to its time-frame, meaning: the meeting with what God promised in the Hereafter.

They mentioned, regarding the number of the tablets and their substance and length, that they were ten tablets. It was also said: seven. It was said: two tablets, and that they were of emerald, brought by Jibril (peace be upon him). It was said: of green chrysolite and red ruby. It was said:

God commanded Musa to cut them from a hard rock which He made soft for him, so he cut them with his hand and split them with his fingers. From al-Hasan:

They were of wood that descended from the sky, and on them was the Torah, and their length was ten cubits. His words ﴿from every thing﴾ are in the accusative position as the object of *kataba* (We wrote). *Mawʿizatan* (as admonition) and *tafṣīlan* (as detailed explanation) are substitutes (*badal*) for it. The meaning is: We wrote for him everything that the Children of Israel needed in their religion, of admonitions and detailed rulings. It was also said that the Torah was sent down and it was seventy camel-loads, of which a portion was read in a year, and that only four persons read it: Musa, Yusha ibn Nun, Uzayr, and Isa, peace be upon them. From Muqatil: He wrote on the tablets: "I am God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. Do not associate anything with Me. Do not cut off the road. Do not swear by My name falsely, for whoever swears falsely by My name, I will not purify him. Do not kill, do not commit adultery, and do not disobey your parents." ﴿Take them﴾, so We said to him: take them, as a conjunction (*ʿatfan*) upon *kataba* (We wrote). It is permissible that it be a substitute for His words ﴿take what I have given you﴾. The pronoun in *fa-khudhha* refers to the tablets, or to "every thing," since it has the meaning of "things," or to the messages, or to the Torah. The meaning of *biquwwatin* (with strength) is with earnestness and resolve, the act of the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm). ﴿They should hold fast to the best of it﴾:

That is, in it there is what is good and what is better, such as retaliation, pardon, self-defense, and patience. So He commanded them to force themselves to take what is more included in goodness and more abundant in reward, like His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. It was also said: they should take what is obligatory or recommended, because it is better than the permissible. It is also permissible that the meaning be: they should take what they were commanded, and not what they were forbidden, in the manner of your saying: "Summer is hotter than winter." ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ means the abode of Pharaoh and his people, which is Egypt, how it was emptied of them and they were destroyed for their defiance, so that you may take heed and not commit defiance like theirs, lest you be punished with a punishment like theirs. It was also said: the dwellings of ʿAd and Thamud and the generations whom God destroyed for their defiance, which you pass by on your journeys. It was also said: the abode of the defiantly disobedient is the Fire of Hell. Al-Hasan read *sa-uriyakum* (I will show you), and this is a widespread dialect in the Hijaz. It is said: *awarani kadha* and *awaraytuhu* (he showed me such-and-such). Its justification is that it may derive from *awrayta al-zand* (to strike the fire-drill so that it kindles), as if the meaning is: clarify it for me and illuminate it so that I may discern it. It was also read *sa-uwrithukum* (I will make you inherit), and this reading is sound, confirmed by His words: ﴿and We made the people who were oppressed inherit﴾. ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth﴾ by sealing upon their hearts and forsaking them, so they do not reflect upon them or take heed from them, out of heedlessness and immersion in what distracts them from them, namely their desires. From al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad: it was related to us from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "When my community magnifies the world, the awe of Islam will be removed from them, and when they abandon enjoining good and forbidding evil, the blessing of revelation will be withheld." [[I have not found it from this route. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi reported it in his *Nawadir* from the hadith of Abu Hurayra similarly, and he added: "And when my community reviles one another, they will fall from the eyes of people." He mentioned it in the seventy-fifth of the hundred and first chapters, and in its chain is al-Bakhtari ibn ʿUbayd.

And it is weak.]] It was also said: I will turn them away from nullifying them, even if they strive as Pharaoh strove to nullify the sign of Musa, by gathering the sorcerers against it, but God refused except the exaltation of the truth and the overturning of falsehood. It is also permissible:

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 148–149:

"From after him": from after his (Musa's) departure from them to Mount Tur (al-Tur). If you ask: why is it said, "And the people of Musa took a calf (ʿijl)," when the one who made it was the Samiri (al-Samiri)? I answer: there are two aspects. The first: the act is attributed to them, because a man from among them carried it out and it was found among them, just as it is said, "The Banu Tamim said such and such and did such and such," while the one who said and the one who did it is one person. Also, they were intent on making it and content with it, so it is as though they had all agreed upon it. The second: it is meant that they took it as a god and worshipped it.

It has been recited as "min huliyyihim" with a dammah on the ha' and a shaddah, the plural of hilan (ḥilan), like thady and thudiyy. It has also been recited "min hiliyyihim" with a kasrah, for harmony, like dili. And "min halyihim" in the singular. Al-hilyy (ḥilī): the name for whatever adorns a person of gold and silver. If you ask: why did He say "from their ornaments," when the ornaments were not theirs, but were borrowed items in their hands? I answer: the attribution (idafah) can be made on the basis of the slightest connection, and their being borrowed items in their hands suffices as a connection; moreover, they came to own them after the drowning of the destroyers, just as they came to own other of their possessions. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: "So We expelled them from gardens and springs and treasures and a noble station. Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them" (Qur'an 26:57–59)?

"A body (jasadan)": a body with flesh and blood like other bodies. "Al-khuwar": the sound of a cow. Al-Hasan said: the Samiri took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of Jibril (peace be upon him) on the day he crossed the sea, and threw it into the mouth of the calf, so it became a calf that had a lowing.

ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) recited "juʾar" with a jim and a hamzah, from ja'ara, meaning to cry out. The accusative of "jasadan" is in apposition (badal) to "ʿijlan."

"Did they not see" when they took it as a god, that it cannot speak or guide to a path? So they should not choose it over the One who, if the sea were ink for His words, the sea would be exhausted before His words were exhausted, and He is the One who guided the creation to the paths of truth and its methods, by what He placed in the minds of proofs, and by what He sent down in His books.

Then He began and said: "They took it" — that is, they went ahead with what they went ahead with of the reprehensible matter — "and they were wrongdoers," putting everything in other than its place. So the taking of the calf was not a novelty from them, nor was it the first of their abominations.

"And when they were overcome with remorse (suqita fi aydihim)": when their regret and anguish over the worship of the calf became intense, because it is the nature of one whose regret and anguish intensify to bite his hand in grief, so his hand becomes "fallen into," since his mouth has come to be in it. The verb "suqita" is attributed to "fi aydihim," and this is from the figurative mode (al-kinayah). Abu al-Sammaqʿ recited "saqata fi aydihim" with the active form of the verb, meaning the biting came to be in them. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that regret fell into their hands, that is, into their hearts and souls, just as it is said, "something undesirable happened in his hand," although it is impossible for it to be in the hand, as a likening of what occurs in the heart and soul to what occurs in the hand and is seen with the eye.

"And they saw that they had gone astray": they came to clearly recognize their misguidance, as though they had seen it with their own eyes.

It has been recited, "La-in lam tarhamna rabbuna wa-taghfir lana" with the ta' (in the second verb), and "rabbuna" in the accusative as a vocative. This is the speech of the penitent, just as Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them both) said: "And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us" (Qur'an 7:23).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 150–151:

Al-asaf (الأسِف): the one who is extremely angry. ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونَا انْتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("When they angered Us, We took vengeance on them"). It is also said that al-asif means the grieving one. ﴿خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾ ("you have replaced me") means you stood in my place and were my successors after me. This address is either to the worshippers of the calf, namely al-Samiri and his followers, or to the leaders of the Children of Israel, namely Harun (peace be upon him) and the believers among them. This is indicated by his words ﴿اخْلُفْنِي فِي قَوْمِي﴾ ("take my place among my people"). The meaning is: how evil is what you have done as my successors, in that you worshipped the calf in place of the worship of God, or in that you did not restrain those who worshipped other than God. If you ask: where is the subject (al-fa'il) and the object of blame (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm) that bi'sa (بئس, "how evil") requires? I answer: the subject is implied and is explained by ﴿مَا خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾, while the object of blame is omitted, its implied sense being: "how evil is the succession that you have succeeded to, after your own succession." If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِي﴾ ("after me") after ﴿خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾? I answer: its meaning is "after what you saw from me": from the affirmation of God's unity, the negation of partners from Him, and the sincere devotion of worship to Him. Or it means "after I used to guide the Children of Israel to monotheism and restrain them from what their eyes had yearned for, the worship of cows, when they said ﴿اجْعَلْ لَنَا إِلَٰهًا كَمَا لَهُمْ آلِهَةٌ﴾ ("make for us a god like they have gods"). It is the right of successors to follow the conduct of the one who appointed them and not to oppose him. A similar usage is ﴿فَخَلَفَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ﴾ ("then there succeeded them a generation"), meaning: after those described with praiseworthy qualities.

It is said: ʿajila ʿan al-amr (عجل عن الأمر) when one leaves a matter incomplete. Its opposite is tamma ʿalayhi (تم عليه), and "his being hastened away from it by another" is a form of the verb. It can be used with the sense of "to precede", so it takes the same construction, as in "ʿajjaltu al-amr" (عجلت الأمر). The meaning is: "you were hasty regarding your Lord's command," which was to await Musa while keeping his covenant and what he had enjoined upon you. You acted as though the appointed time had reached its end and I had not returned to you, so you spoke to yourselves about my death, and you changed as the nations changed after their prophets. It is narrated that al-Samiri said to them, when he brought out the calf and said, "This is your god and the god of Musa": "Musa will not return; he has died." It is also narrated that they counted twenty days with their nights and made them forty, and then they did what they did.

﴿وَأَلْقَى الْأَلْوَاحَ﴾ ("and he threw down the tablets"): he threw them down and let them fall because of the overwhelming astonishment and intense distress that overtook him when he heard the news of the calf, out of zeal for God and protectiveness of His religion. He was by nature harsh, extremely quick to anger, while Harun was gentler in disposition, and for that reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel than Musa. It is narrated that the Torah was in seven parts; when the tablets were thrown down they broke, so six parts were lifted up and one part remained. What was lifted up included the detailed explanation of everything, and what remained contained guidance and mercy.

﴿وَأَخَذَ بِرَأْسِ أَخِيهِ﴾ ("and he seized his brother by the head"): that is, by the hair of his head, drawing him toward himself by his forelock. This was because of the severity of the matter that had come upon him, which provoked him and took away his judgment, and because he suspected that his brother had been negligent in restraining them. ﴿ابْنَ أُمَّ﴾ ("son of my mother"): it is read with fath (فتح, the vowel "a") in imitation of khamsata ʿashar (خمسة عشر, fifteen), and with kasra (كسر, the vowel "i") by dropping the possessive yā' (ياء الإضافة). It is also read as "ibni ummi" (ابن أمي) with the yā', and as "ibn imm" (ابن إمّ) with kasra on the hamza and the mīm. It is said that he was his brother from the same father and mother. If that is correct, then he attributed him to the mother only to indicate that they were from the same womb. That is more likely to evoke tenderness and compassion, more serious in the binding claim of right, and because she was a believer, so he counted her lineage as a matter of honour, and because it was she who suffered fears and hardships on his account, so he reminded him of her right.

﴿إِنَّ الْقَوْمَ اسْتَضْعَفُونِي﴾ ("indeed the people overpowered me"): meaning that he spared no effort in restraining them by admonition and warning, and by exerting all the strength he could muster in opposing them, until they overpowered him and considered him weak, and nothing remained but that they should kill him. ﴿فَلَا تُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءَ﴾ ("so do not let the enemies gloat over me"): do not do to me what they wish, namely humiliating me and harming me. It is also read ﴿فَلَا يُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءُ﴾ ("so let the enemies not gloat over me"), with the enemies being forbidden from gloating. The meaning is that there should not befall him what they would gloat over on account of him. ﴿وَلَا تَجْعَلْنِي مَعَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ ("and do not place me with the wrongdoing people"): do not make me, in Your displeasure with me and Your punishment of me, a companion or partner to them. Or it means: do not consider me to be one of the wrongdoers, though I am innocent of them and of their wrongdoing.

When his brother made his excuse to him and mentioned the gloating of the enemies, he said, ﴿رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِأَخِي﴾ ("My Lord, forgive me and my brother"), in order to satisfy his brother and to show those who gloated that he was pleased with him, so that their gloating would not be complete. He also sought forgiveness for himself for what had been lacking on his part toward his brother, and for his brother, since perhaps he had been negligent in the good conduct of succession. He asked that they should not be separated from His mercy, and that it should remain encompassing them both, in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 150–151:

Al-asaf (الأسِف): the one who is extremely angry. ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونَا انْتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("When they angered Us, We took vengeance on them"). It is also said that al-asif means the grieving one. ﴿خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾ ("you have replaced me") means you stood in my place and were my successors after me. This address is either to the worshippers of the calf, namely al-Samiri and his followers, or to the leaders of the Children of Israel, namely Harun (peace be upon him) and the believers among them. This is indicated by his words ﴿اخْلُفْنِي فِي قَوْمِي﴾ ("take my place among my people"). The meaning is: how evil is what you have done as my successors, in that you worshipped the calf in place of the worship of God, or in that you did not restrain those who worshipped other than God. If you ask: where is the subject (al-fa'il) and the object of blame (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm) that bi'sa (بئس, "how evil") requires? I answer: the subject is implied and is explained by ﴿مَا خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾, while the object of blame is omitted, its implied sense being: "how evil is the succession that you have succeeded to, after your own succession." If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِي﴾ ("after me") after ﴿خَلَفْتُمُونِي﴾? I answer: its meaning is "after what you saw from me": from the affirmation of God's unity, the negation of partners from Him, and the sincere devotion of worship to Him. Or it means "after I used to guide the Children of Israel to monotheism and restrain them from what their eyes had yearned for, the worship of cows, when they said ﴿اجْعَلْ لَنَا إِلَٰهًا كَمَا لَهُمْ آلِهَةٌ﴾ ("make for us a god like they have gods"). It is the right of successors to follow the conduct of the one who appointed them and not to oppose him. A similar usage is ﴿فَخَلَفَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِمْ خَلْفٌ﴾ ("then there succeeded them a generation"), meaning: after those described with praiseworthy qualities.

It is said: ʿajila ʿan al-amr (عجل عن الأمر) when one leaves a matter incomplete. Its opposite is tamma ʿalayhi (تم عليه), and "his being hastened away from it by another" is a form of the verb. It can be used with the sense of "to precede", so it takes the same construction, as in "ʿajjaltu al-amr" (عجلت الأمر). The meaning is: "you were hasty regarding your Lord's command," which was to await Musa while keeping his covenant and what he had enjoined upon you. You acted as though the appointed time had reached its end and I had not returned to you, so you spoke to yourselves about my death, and you changed as the nations changed after their prophets. It is narrated that al-Samiri said to them, when he brought out the calf and said, "This is your god and the god of Musa": "Musa will not return; he has died." It is also narrated that they counted twenty days with their nights and made them forty, and then they did what they did.

﴿وَأَلْقَى الْأَلْوَاحَ﴾ ("and he threw down the tablets"): he threw them down and let them fall because of the overwhelming astonishment and intense distress that overtook him when he heard the news of the calf, out of zeal for God and protectiveness of His religion. He was by nature harsh, extremely quick to anger, while Harun was gentler in disposition, and for that reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel than Musa. It is narrated that the Torah was in seven parts; when the tablets were thrown down they broke, so six parts were lifted up and one part remained. What was lifted up included the detailed explanation of everything, and what remained contained guidance and mercy.

﴿وَأَخَذَ بِرَأْسِ أَخِيهِ﴾ ("and he seized his brother by the head"): that is, by the hair of his head, drawing him toward himself by his forelock. This was because of the severity of the matter that had come upon him, which provoked him and took away his judgment, and because he suspected that his brother had been negligent in restraining them. ﴿ابْنَ أُمَّ﴾ ("son of my mother"): it is read with fath (فتح, the vowel "a") in imitation of khamsata ʿashar (خمسة عشر, fifteen), and with kasra (كسر, the vowel "i") by dropping the possessive yā' (ياء الإضافة). It is also read as "ibni ummi" (ابن أمي) with the yā', and as "ibn imm" (ابن إمّ) with kasra on the hamza and the mīm. It is said that he was his brother from the same father and mother. If that is correct, then he attributed him to the mother only to indicate that they were from the same womb. That is more likely to evoke tenderness and compassion, more serious in the binding claim of right, and because she was a believer, so he counted her lineage as a matter of honour, and because it was she who suffered fears and hardships on his account, so he reminded him of her right.

﴿إِنَّ الْقَوْمَ اسْتَضْعَفُونِي﴾ ("indeed the people overpowered me"): meaning that he spared no effort in restraining them by admonition and warning, and by exerting all the strength he could muster in opposing them, until they overpowered him and considered him weak, and nothing remained but that they should kill him. ﴿فَلَا تُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءَ﴾ ("so do not let the enemies gloat over me"): do not do to me what they wish, namely humiliating me and harming me. It is also read ﴿فَلَا يُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءُ﴾ ("so let the enemies not gloat over me"), with the enemies being forbidden from gloating. The meaning is that there should not befall him what they would gloat over on account of him. ﴿وَلَا تَجْعَلْنِي مَعَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ ("and do not place me with the wrongdoing people"): do not make me, in Your displeasure with me and Your punishment of me, a companion or partner to them. Or it means: do not consider me to be one of the wrongdoers, though I am innocent of them and of their wrongdoing.

When his brother made his excuse to him and mentioned the gloating of the enemies, he said, ﴿رَبِّ اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِأَخِي﴾ ("My Lord, forgive me and my brother"), in order to satisfy his brother and to show those who gloated that he was pleased with him, so that their gloating would not be complete. He also sought forgiveness for himself for what had been lacking on his part toward his brother, and for his brother, since perhaps he had been negligent in the good conduct of succession. He asked that they should not be separated from His mercy, and that it should remain encompassing them both, in this world and in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 152:

﴿Wrath from their Lord and humiliation﴾ — The wrath (ghadab) is what they were commanded to do, namely killing themselves. The humiliation (dhillah) is their being driven out of their homes, for the humiliation of exile is a proverbial saying (mathal madrub). It has also been said: it is what befell their descendants, namely the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, of God the Exalted's wrath through killing and expulsion, and of humiliation through the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax). ﴿And thus We recompense those who fabricate﴾ — those who lie against God. There is no greater fabrication than the words of al-Samiri: ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾.

It is permissible for the phrase ﴿in the life of this world﴾ to be connected to humiliation alone, meaning: wrath will befall them in the Hereafter, and humiliation in the life of this world. And humiliation and destitution were stamped upon them, and they returned with wrath from God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 153:

Those who did evil deeds, including disbelief and all kinds of sins, then repented after them, returned to God, apologized to Him and believed, and purified their faith: indeed your Lord, after those [grave deeds], is Forgiving, [meaning] One who conceals their sins and erases what they had done, and Merciful, [meaning] One who bestows upon them the Garden. This is a general ruling that includes those who took the calf and others. [Mahmud] magnified their offence first, then followed it with a general ruling [[Mahmud said: "He magnified the offence of those who took the calf first, then followed it with a general ruling..." etc. Ahmad said: This alludes to the obligation of punishing sinners, and that forgiveness of a sin without repentance from it is impossible and inadmissible. This has already been counted among the heretical innovations. Rather, the truth is that forgiveness for anything other than polytheism is left to God's will, not rationally impossible, and it has in fact occurred according to transmission. And God is the Granter of success.]] in which He magnified His mercy, so that it is known that sins, however great and immense, are outweighed by His pardon and generosity, which are greater and more exalted. But the condition must be observed, namely the obligation of repentance [[His statement "the condition must be observed, namely the obligation of repentance": the Mu'tazila (a theological school holding that the grave sin is not forgiven except through repentance) hold this view. The Ahl al-Sunna (the majority Sunni school) hold that it may be forgiven by sheer grace alone. (Ga')]] and turning back to God. Anything beyond this is empty greed and cold Ash'abiyya, which a prudent person does not heed. [[His statement "cold Ash'abiyya": a trait attributed to Ash'ab, a man who was notably greedy, and who is proverbially cited for greed, as in al-Sihah (a lexicon by al-Jawhari). (Ga')]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 154:

"And when the anger subsided from Musa" — this is a figure of speech (mathal), as if the anger were urging him on to what he did and saying to him, "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and seize your brother by the head..." etc. [[Mahmud said: "This is a figure of speech, as if the anger were urging him on to what he did, saying to him, 'Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and seize your brother by the head...' etc." Ahmad said: This belongs to the type I mentioned earlier, the transfer from the reversal of the reality (qalb al-haqiqa) to metaphor (majaz). The original would be: "When Musa's anger subsided," and for this reason some of the grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya) counted it among the inverted constructions (maqlub), and placed it in the category of "piercing the cloth with the nail" (khurq al-thawb al-mismar). The verified view is that it is not of that kind, and that this inversion is nobler and more eloquent, because it carries an eloquent meaning, namely that anger had taken such firm hold of Musa that it seemed to direct his commands, and everything that proceeded from him at that time came from anger, to the point that it was as if anger itself had ordered it. A fine point like this is not found in "piercing the cloth with the nail"; rather it is present in His words, exalted is He, "It is fitting for me that I should not say about God anything but the truth" (ḥaqīq 'alā an lā aqūla 'alā Allāhi illā al-ḥaqq), according to the reading of Nafi'. This was mentioned just before, and God is the Granter of success.]] as though it urged him to do what he did and told him, "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and drag your brother toward you by the head." He therefore abandoned speech in that manner and cut off the urging. No sound-natured person of correct taste has found this phrase admirable or eloquent except for this reason, and because it belongs to the branches of eloquence. Otherwise, the reading of Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, "wa-lamma sakan 'an Musa al-ghadab," does not give the soul any of that hamza-like force or that splendour of effect.

It was also read as "wa-lamma sakata," and as "askata," meaning: God silenced it, or his brother silenced it by apologising to him and disclaiming responsibility. The meaning is: when his anger was extinguished, he took up the tablets that he had thrown down. "Wa-fi nuskhatiha" means: and in what was copied from them, i.e., what was written. "Nuskha" is on the pattern fi'la in the sense of maf'ul, like "khutba." "Li-rabbihim yarhabun" — the lam has entered because the object has been placed first, since the verb coming after its object gives it weakness. Its like is "li-l-ru'ya ta'burun," and you say: "laka darabtu" (I struck you).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 155–157:**

﴿وَاخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ meaning: from among his people. The preposition is dropped and the verb is connected directly to its object, as in the verse of the poet:

*"Among us is the one chosen among men for generosity ... and for bounty when the fierce winds blow."*

The meaning is: among us is the one whom people have chosen from among men. Al-rijal (men) is in the accusative because the preposition has been removed (naz' al-khafid, removal of the governing preposition). Samaha (generosity) is a tamyiz (specifying accusative) that identifies the respect in which he was chosen. Wujudan (bounty) is coordinated with it. "When the winds blow" is a kinaya (metonymy) for the arrival of winter, when the fierce winds that stir up everything blow, and when the time of cutting off supplies comes. So how much more so in summer.

It is said that he chose from twelve tribes, six from each tribe, until they reached seventy-two. He then said: "Let two of you remain behind." They disputed over this, so he said: "Whoever of you stays behind will have a reward like that of the one who goes out." So Caleb and Joshua stayed behind.

It is also reported that only sixty elders were found, so God revealed to him that he should choose ten young men. He chose them, and they became elders. It is also said that they were the sons of those who were under twenty and had not exceeded forty, from whom ignorance and youthfulness had departed. Moses commanded them to fast, purify themselves, and wash their garments. Then he set out with them to Mount Sinai for the appointment with his Lord. His Lord had commanded him to come with seventy of the Children of Israel. When Moses approached the mountain, a pillar of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain. Moses drew near and entered into it, and he said to the people: "Draw near." They drew near, until, when they entered the cloud, they fell prostrate. They heard Him speaking to Moses, commanding and forbidding him: "Do this, and do not do that."

Then the cloud cleared, and they came to Him and asked to see God. He admonished them, rebuked them, and denounced them. They said: "O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God openly." He said: "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You," meaning that they should hear the refusal and denial from Him. He was answered: ﴿You will not see Me﴾, and the mountain shook beneath them, and they fell unconscious. When they returned to consciousness, Moses said: ﴿My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me as well﴾. This is a wish on his part for destruction before he saw what he saw of the consequence of asking to see God, just as a man who regrets a matter says when he sees its bad outcome: "If God had willed, He would have destroyed me before this." ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?﴾ That is, will You destroy us all, himself and them, because he had only asked to see God in order to rebuke the foolish, whereas they asked out of folly and ignorance. ﴿It is only Your trial﴾, that is, Your test and affliction, when You spoke to me and they heard Your speech. They reasoned from speech to vision by faulty reasoning, until they were led astray. ﴿You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will﴾: through the trial You lead astray those ignorant ones who are not steadfast in knowing You, and You guide those who know You and stand firm by the firm word.

He treated this as misguidance from God and guidance from Him, because His trial was the cause of their going astray and being guided. It is as though He led them astray through it and guided them through it, by way of extended usage. (Note: his statement "because His trial was the cause" turns the meaning away from its outward sense, since in their view He does not create evil. As for the position of ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni tradition), there is no need for this. (ʿA.))

﴿You are our Guardian﴾, our Master who manages our affairs. ﴿Ordain for us﴾ and decree for us, ﴿in this world a good [state]﴾, that is, well-being, a good life, and success in obedience, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, that is, Paradise. ﴿We have turned to You﴾, that is, we have repented to You. Hāda ilayhi yahūdu means he returned and repented. Al-hūd is the plural of hā'id, which means a penitent. One of them said:

*"O rider of sin, return and repent, and prostrate yourself like a hoopoe."*

(Al-Zamakhshari: he likened his persistence in sin to a rider's persistence on his mount. Hādā yahūdu means he repented and returned. Hud is the imperative of this verb, repeated for emphasis. Then he said: "and prostrate yourself like a hoopoe," likening him to it because of how often it lowers its head to the ground, not because of speed. The meaning is: prostrate yourself much.)

Abu Wajza al-Sa'di read hadnā ilayka with a kasra on the ha', from hādahu yahīduhu, meaning when he moved and inclined it. This may have two senses: it may be active and passive, meaning "We moved ourselves toward You and inclined ourselves," or "We were moved toward You and inclined," on the assumption of fa'alnā (we did). This is like your saying "'adtu yā marīḍ" with a kasra on the 'ayn, from fa'alta (you did) of al-'iyāda (visiting the sick). It is also permissible to say "'adtu" with ishmām (a faint hint of the vowel). And "'udtu" with pure damma, for those who say "'ūd al-marīḍ" (visit the sick) and "qūl al-qawl" (say the saying). On this dialect it is also permissible that hudnā with a damma be fa'alnā from hādahu yahīduhu.

﴿My punishment﴾: its condition and attribute is that ﴿I afflict with it whom I will﴾, that is, those for whom punishment is obligatory in wisdom. There was no room for pardoning them, because it would be corruption. (Note: his statement "those for whom punishment is obligatory in wisdom" is the position of the Mu'tazila. As for ahl al-Sunna, nothing is obligatory upon God Most High. (ʿA.))

﴿My mercy﴾: its condition and attribute is that it is vast and reaches everything. There is no Muslim or unbeliever, obedient or disobedient, but he is enveloped in My blessings.

Al-Hasan read man asā'a (whoever does evil), from al-isā'a (evil-doing).

﴿So I will prescribe this mercy﴾ by a special prescription for you, O Children of Israel, for those who will be at the end of time from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who ﴿believe in all Our signs and Our books﴾, and do not disbelieve in any of them, ﴿those who follow the Messenger﴾ who is ﴿the Prophet, the unlettered﴾, the possessor of miracles, ﴿whom they find described﴾, whose description they find, ﴿those who follow him from the Children of Israel, written with them in the Torah and the Gospel......﴾ ﴿and he makes lawful for them the good things﴾, what was forbidden to them of good things, such as fats and others; or what is good in the Shari'a and in judgment, such as the slaughtered animals over which God's name has been mentioned, and earnings free of unlawful gain. ﴿And he forbids them the vile things﴾, what is considered vile, such as blood, carrion, and the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God; or what is vile in judgment, such as usury, bribery, and other vile gains. ﴿Their burden﴾: al-iṣr is the heavy load that binds its bearer, that is, prevents him from moving because of its weight. It is a metaphor for the heaviness and difficulty of their obligations, such as the requirement of killing oneself for the validity of their repentance. Likewise ﴿the shackles﴾ are a metaphor for the hard things in their laws, such as: the judgment of retaliation, whether intentional or unintentional, without the law of blood-money; cutting off the sinful limbs; and cutting out the place of impurity from the skin and the garment. Also: burning the spoils of war; forbidding the veins in meat; and forbidding the Sabbath.

It is reported from 'Ata': when the Children of Israel stood to pray, they wore hair shirts and bound their hands to their necks. A man might pierce his collarbone, insert the end of a chain into it, and fasten it to a pillar, restraining himself for worship.

﴿And honoured him﴾, meaning they prevented him, so that no enemy could overpower him. It is also read with tashdid (doubling), and the root meaning of al-'azr is prevention. From it comes ta'zir (discretionary punishment) for beating short of the hadd (the prescribed punishment), because it prevents a return to the ugly act. Do you not see how the hadd is named after it, and the hadd is prevention?

﴿The light﴾ is the Qur'an.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿أُنْزِلَ مَعَهُ (was sent down with him)﴾, when it was sent down with Gabriel?

I answer: its meaning is that it was sent down with his prophethood, because his being sent as a prophet was accompanied by the Qur'an and joined to it. It is also permissible that it be connected to "they followed," meaning: and they followed the Qur'an sent down with him, by following the Prophet, acting on his sunna, and doing what he commanded and abstaining from what he forbade. Or: and they followed the Qur'an as they followed it, as companions in its following.

If you ask: how does this answer correspond to Moses's peace be upon him and his supplication? I answer: when he prayed for himself and for the Children of Israel, he was answered with something that contains a rebuke to the Children of Israel for considering it permissible to ask to see God, and for their disbelief in the great signs of God that were performed at the hand of Moses. This is implied in His words ﴿and those who believe in Our signs﴾. It is intended that they hear the description of their descendants who believed in the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what he brought, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others from the People of the Two Books, as a kindness to them and an encouragement to sincere faith and righteous action, and so that they may be gathered with them and not separated from their descendants by the mercy of God, which encompasses everything.

(Note: his phrase "by the mercy of God" is perhaps "in the mercy of God." Or the separation carries the sense of exclusion, so it is followed by "from." (ʿA.))

As for ahl al-Sunna, nothing is obligatory upon God Most High. (ʿA.))

﴿My mercy﴾: its condition and attribute is that it is vast and reaches everything. There is no Muslim or unbeliever, obedient or disobedient, but he is enveloped in My blessings.

Al-Hasan read man asā'a (whoever does evil), from al-isā'a (evil-doing).

﴿So I will prescribe this mercy﴾ by a special prescription for you, O Children of Israel, for those who will be at the end of time from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who ﴿believe in all Our signs and Our books﴾, and do not disbelieve in any of them, ﴿those who follow the Messenger﴾ who is ﴿the Prophet, the unlettered﴾, the possessor of miracles, ﴿whom they find described﴾, whose description they find, ﴿those who follow him from the Children of Israel, written with them in the Torah and the Gospel......﴾ ﴿and he makes lawful for them the good things﴾, what was forbidden to them of good things, such as fats and others; or what is good in the Shari'a and in judgment, such as the slaughtered animals over which God's name has been mentioned, and earnings free of unlawful gain. ﴿And he forbids them the vile things﴾, what is considered vile, such as blood, carrion, and the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God; or what is vile in judgment, such as usury, bribery, and other vile gains. ﴿Their burden﴾: al-iṣr is the heavy load that binds its bearer, that is, prevents him from moving because of its weight. It is reported from 'Ata': when the Children of Israel stood to pray, they wore hair shirts and bound their hands to their necks. A man might pierce his collarbone, insert the end of a chain into it, and fasten it to a pillar, restraining himself for worship.

(Note: his phrase "by the mercy of God" is perhaps "in the mercy of God." Or the separation carries the sense of exclusion, so it is followed by "from." (ʿA.))

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 155–157:**
