*"Among us is the one chosen among men for generosity ... and for bounty when the fierce winds blow."*

The meaning is: among us is the one whom people have chosen from among men. Al-rijal (men) is in the accusative because the preposition has been removed (naz' al-khafid, removal of the governing preposition). Samaha (generosity) is a tamyiz (specifying accusative) that identifies the respect in which he was chosen. Wujudan (bounty) is coordinated with it. "When the winds blow" is a kinaya (metonymy) for the arrival of winter, when the fierce winds that stir up everything blow, and when the time of cutting off supplies comes. So how much more so in summer.

It is said that he chose from twelve tribes, six from each tribe, until they reached seventy-two. He then said: "Let two of you remain behind." They disputed over this, so he said: "Whoever of you stays behind will have a reward like that of the one who goes out." So Caleb and Joshua stayed behind.

It is also reported that only sixty elders were found, so God revealed to him that he should choose ten young men. He chose them, and they became elders. It is also said that they were the sons of those who were under twenty and had not exceeded forty, from whom ignorance and youthfulness had departed. Moses commanded them to fast, purify themselves, and wash their garments. Then he set out with them to Mount Sinai for the appointment with his Lord. His Lord had commanded him to come with seventy of the Children of Israel. When Moses approached the mountain, a pillar of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain. Moses drew near and entered into it, and he said to the people: "Draw near." They drew near, until, when they entered the cloud, they fell prostrate. They heard Him speaking to Moses, commanding and forbidding him: "Do this, and do not do that."

Then the cloud cleared, and they came to Him and asked to see God. He admonished them, rebuked them, and denounced them. They said: "O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God openly." He said: "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You," meaning that they should hear the refusal and denial from Him. He was answered: ﴿You will not see Me﴾, and the mountain shook beneath them, and they fell unconscious. When they returned to consciousness, Moses said: ﴿My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me as well﴾. This is a wish on his part for destruction before he saw what he saw of the consequence of asking to see God, just as a man who regrets a matter says when he sees its bad outcome: "If God had willed, He would have destroyed me before this." ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done?﴾ That is, will You destroy us all, himself and them, because he had only asked to see God in order to rebuke the foolish, whereas they asked out of folly and ignorance. ﴿It is only Your trial﴾, that is, Your test and affliction, when You spoke to me and they heard Your speech. They reasoned from speech to vision by faulty reasoning, until they were led astray. ﴿You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will﴾: through the trial You lead astray those ignorant ones who are not steadfast in knowing You, and You guide those who know You and stand firm by the firm word.

He treated this as misguidance from God and guidance from Him, because His trial was the cause of their going astray and being guided. It is as though He led them astray through it and guided them through it, by way of extended usage. (Note: his statement "because His trial was the cause" turns the meaning away from its outward sense, since in their view He does not create evil. As for the position of ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni tradition), there is no need for this. (ʿA.))

﴿You are our Guardian﴾, our Master who manages our affairs. ﴿Ordain for us﴾ and decree for us, ﴿in this world a good [state]﴾, that is, well-being, a good life, and success in obedience, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, that is, Paradise. ﴿We have turned to You﴾, that is, we have repented to You. Hāda ilayhi yahūdu means he returned and repented. Al-hūd is the plural of hā'id, which means a penitent. One of them said:

*"O rider of sin, return and repent, and prostrate yourself like a hoopoe."*

(Al-Zamakhshari: he likened his persistence in sin to a rider's persistence on his mount. Hādā yahūdu means he repented and returned. Hud is the imperative of this verb, repeated for emphasis. Then he said: "and prostrate yourself like a hoopoe," likening him to it because of how often it lowers its head to the ground, not because of speed. The meaning is: prostrate yourself much.)

Abu Wajza al-Sa'di read hadnā ilayka with a kasra on the ha', from hādahu yahīduhu, meaning when he moved and inclined it. This may have two senses: it may be active and passive, meaning "We moved ourselves toward You and inclined ourselves," or "We were moved toward You and inclined," on the assumption of fa'alnā (we did). This is like your saying "'adtu yā marīḍ" with a kasra on the 'ayn, from fa'alta (you did) of al-'iyāda (visiting the sick). It is also permissible to say "'adtu" with ishmām (a faint hint of the vowel). And "'udtu" with pure damma, for those who say "'ūd al-marīḍ" (visit the sick) and "qūl al-qawl" (say the saying). On this dialect it is also permissible that hudnā with a damma be fa'alnā from hādahu yahīduhu.

(Note: his phrase "by the mercy of God" is perhaps "in the mercy of God." Or the separation carries the sense of exclusion, so it is followed by "from." (ʿA.))

"I am the Messenger of Allah to you all." It is said: every messenger was sent only to his own people, but Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to all of mankind and all of the jinn. "Jamīʿan" (all together) is an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative) relating to "ilaykum" (to you).

If you ask: what is the position of "alladhī lahu mulku al-samawāti wal-arḍ" (the One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth)? The answer: the best view is that it is in the accusative, by an implied verb "aʿnī" (I mean), which is what is called the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ). It may also be in the genitive as a qualifier (ṣifah), even though the qualifier and the thing qualified are separated by the phrase "ilaykum jamīʿan."

The phrase "lā ilāha illā huwa" (there is no god but He) is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause "lahu mulku al-samawāti wal-arḍ," and likewise "yuḥyī wa yumītu" (He gives life and causes death). "Lā ilāha illā huwa" is an explanatory clarification (bayān) of the sentence before it, because whoever owns the world is, in truth, the God. "Yuḥyī wa yumītu" is a clarification of His exclusive right to divinity, since none other than Him can give life or cause death.

"Wa kalimātihi" (and His words): this refers to what was revealed to him and to those messengers before him, of His books and His revelation. It was also read as "wa kalimatihi" in the singular, meaning the Qur'an. Or it may mean the category of what He spoke. It is reported from Mujāhid that it refers to Jesus, son of Mary.

It is also said: it is the word by which Jesus and all of creation came into being, namely His saying "kun" (be). Jesus is called "the word of Allah" specifically because he had no cause other than that word, and he was not from a drop of semen that is poured out. "La-ʿallakum tahtadūn" (so that you may be guided) means: in the hope that you will be guided.

If you ask: why was it not said, after "innī rasūlu Allāhi ilaykum," "fa-āminū billāhi wa bī" (so believe in Allah and in me)? The answer: he turned from the pronoun to the explicit noun so that the attributes applied to him could apply to him, and because of the eloquence of the shift of discourse (iltifāt, a shift in grammatical person). It also shows that what is obligatory to believe in and follow is this particular individual, who is independently the unlettered Prophet who believes in Allah and His words, whoever he may be, whether I or someone else. This is a demonstration of fairness and a guard against partisanship for oneself.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 159:

﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide with the truth and by it deal justly.﴾ They are the believing, repentant ones from the Children of Israel. When he mentioned those among them who wavered in their religion and doubted, to the point that they committed the two great sins of worshipping the calf and deeming it permissible to see Allah, he mentioned that among them there is a community who are certain and steadfast, who guide people with the word of truth, point them to uprightness, and lead them aright. And by the truth they judge justly among them, never deviating. Or he meant those he described from among those who reached the Prophet ﷺ and believed in him from their descendants. It was also said: when the Children of Israel killed their prophets and disbelieved, and they were twelve tribes, one tribe disassociated itself from what they had done and made excuses, and asked Allah to separate them from their brethren. So Allah opened for them a tunnel in the earth, and they travelled through it for a year and a half until they emerged from behind China, and there they are, upright monotheists (ḥunafāʾ) submitting to Allah, facing our qibla. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that Jibril took him, on the night of the Isra', toward them, and he spoke with them. Jibril said to them: "Do you know whom you are speaking to?" They said: "No." He said: "This is Muhammad, the Unlettered Prophet." So they believed in him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Musa instructed us that whoever of you reaches Ahmad should convey my greeting to him." So Muhammad returned the greeting of Musa, peace be upon them both. Then he recited to them ten surahs of the Qur'an that had been revealed in Makkah, and no obligation had been revealed other than the prayer and the zakat. He commanded them to remain in their place, and they used to observe the Sabbath, so he commanded them to gather together and abandon the Sabbath. And from Masruq: it was recited in the presence of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), and a man said: "I am one of them." ʿAbd Allah said, meaning to those believers present in his assembly: "Do your righteous ones add anything over them: those who guide by the truth and by it deal justly?" It was also said: even if they were in a remote part of the world, adhering to a sharia and the abrogation of it had not reached them, they would be excused.

This is by way of supposition and hypothesis; otherwise the news of the sharia of Muhammad ﷺ has spread to every horizon and penetrated every hidden place, and Allah has left no people of settlement or of desert, no plain or mountain, no land or sea, in the eastern and western regions of the earth, except that He has conveyed it to them, filled their ears with it, established the proof against them with it, and He will question them about it on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 163–166:

﴿Ask them﴾ means: ask the Jews. It is also read as "wa-as'alhum." This question is meant as a reproach and a reminder of their old disbelief and their transgression of Allah's limits, and as an indication that this is part of their knowledge, which can only be known through a Book or revelation. When someone who did not read their scripture informs them of it, it is known that it comes from revelation. Its parallel is the interrogative hamza (alif of questioning) used for affirmation in your saying: "Did you transgress on the Sabbath?" The town (al-qarya) is Ayla. It has also been said: Madyan. It has also been said: Tiberias. The Arabs call a city "qarya." It is reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': "I have not seen any villagers more eloquent than al-Hasan and al-Hajjaj," meaning two men from city people. ﴿Hadirat al-bahr﴾ (the town by the sea) is near it, riding its shore. ﴿When they transgressed on the Sabbath﴾ means: when they exceeded Allah's limit regarding it, which was their hunting on Saturday, though they had been forbidden from it. It is read as "ya'addun," meaning "ya'tadun" (they transgress), with the ta' assimilated into the dal and its vowel moved onto the 'ayn. It is also read as "yu'iddun" (from i'dad, preparing), since they used to prepare hunting equipment on Saturday, though they were commanded not to occupy themselves on that day with anything other than worship. Al-sabt (the Sabbath) is a verbal noun of "sabatat al-yahud," when the Jews magnified their Sabbath by abstaining from hunting and by occupying themselves with devotion. So its meaning is: they transgress in magnifying this day. Similarly, His saying ﴿on their Sabbath day﴾ means the day of their magnifying the matter of the Sabbath. This is confirmed by His saying ﴿and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath﴾. The reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz is "yawm isbatihim" (the day of their observance). It is also read as "la yasbutun" with a dammah on the ba'.

It is also read by 'Ali as "la yusbitun" with a dammah on the ya', from asbatu (to observe the Sabbath). It is reported from al-Hasan: "la yusbatun," in the passive form, meaning the Sabbath is not imposed upon them, and they are not commanded to observe it.

If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical position) of ﴿when they transgress﴾ and ﴿when there came to them﴾? I say: the first is in the genitive as a badal (substitution) for "the town," and the intended meaning of "the town" is its people, as if it were said: "Ask them about the people of the town at the time of their transgression on the Sabbath." This is badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative, governed by "kanat" (was), or by "hadira." As for the second, it is in the accusative, governed by "ya'dun." It may also be a badal after a badal.

﴿Fish﴾ means the hitan (fish). The Arabs most often use "hut" to mean a single fish. ﴿Appearing openly upon the surface of the water﴾. It is reported from al-Hasan: "they come to their doorways, as if they were white rams." It is said: "shara'a 'alayna fulan" means "he approached us and came near to us." And "shari'tu 'ala fulan fi baytihi fa-ra'aytahu yaf'alu kadha" (I came upon so-and-so in his house and saw him doing such-and-such).

﴿Thus We test them﴾, that is, like that severe trial, We test them because of their immorality. ﴿And when a group among them said﴾ is coordinated with ﴿when they transgressed﴾, and its i'rab is the same. ﴿A community among them﴾ means a group of people from the town, from its righteous ones, who went to great lengths in their admonition until they despaired of their acceptance, to others who did not cease admonishing them. ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ That is, will exterminate them and purify the land of them, ﴿or punish them with a severe punishment﴾ because of their persistence in evil. They only said this because they knew the admonition would not benefit them. ﴿They said: as an excuse to your Lord﴾, that is, our admonition is to clear ourselves before Allah, and so that we may not be blamed for some negligence in forbidding the wrong. ﴿And perhaps they will become righteous﴾, and in hope that they will attain some measure of righteousness. It is also read as "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative, meaning: we admonished them as an excuse to your Lord, or we made an excuse with an excuse.

﴿So when they forgot﴾ refers to the people of the town. So when they abandoned what the righteous reminded them of, they were like one who forgets what he has forgotten. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾, ﴿and seized the wrongdoers who committed the wrong﴾. If you ask: the community who said ﴿why do you admonish﴾, which of the two groups were they? Were they from the saved group or the punished group? I say: they were from the saved group, because they were from the group who forbade. They did not say what they said except as those asking about the reason for the admonition and its purpose, since they saw no sound purpose in it, knowing the condition of the people. When the one who forbids knows the condition of the one forbidden, and that forbidding will not affect him, the obligation to forbid falls from him. Sometimes abandonment becomes obligatory because it falls under the category of futility. It is read as "ya'addun," meaning "ya'tadun" (they transgress), with the ta' assimilated into the dal and its vowel moved onto the 'ayn. It is also read as "yu'iddun" (from i'dad, preparing), since they used to prepare hunting equipment on Saturday, though they were commanded not to occupy themselves on that day with anything other than worship. It is also read as "la yasbutun" with a dammah on the ba'.

It is also read by 'Ali as "la yusbitun" with a dammah on the ya', from asbatu (to observe the Sabbath). It is reported from al-Hasan: "la yusbatun," in the passive form, meaning the Sabbath is not imposed upon them, and they are not commanded to observe it.

If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical position) of ﴿when they transgress﴾ and ﴿when there came to them﴾? I say: the first is in the genitive as a badal (substitution) for "the town," and the intended meaning of "the town" is its people, as if it were said: "Ask them about the people of the town at the time of their transgression on the Sabbath." This is badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion). It may also be in the accusative, governed by "kanat" (was), or by "hadira." As for the second, it is in the accusative, governed by "ya'dun." It may also be a badal after a badal.

﴿Fish﴾ means the hitan (fish). The Arabs most often use "hut" to mean a single fish. ﴿Appearing openly upon the surface of the water﴾. It is reported from al-Hasan: "they come to their doorways, as if they were white rams." It is said: "shara'a 'alayna fulan" means "he approached us and came near to us." And "shari'tu 'ala fulan fi baytihi fa-ra'aytahu yaf'alu kadha" (I came upon so-and-so in his house and saw him doing such-and-such).

﴿Thus We test them﴾, that is, like that severe trial, We test them because of their immorality. ﴿And when a group among them said﴾ is coordinated with ﴿when they transgressed﴾, and its i'rab is the same. ﴿A community among them﴾ means a group of people from the town, from its righteous ones, who went to great lengths in their admonition until they despaired of their acceptance, to others who did not cease admonishing them. ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ That is, will exterminate them and purify the land of them, ﴿or punish them with a severe punishment﴾ because of their persistence in evil. They only said this because they knew the admonition would not benefit them. ﴿They said: as an excuse to your Lord﴾, that is, our admonition is to clear ourselves before Allah, and so that we may not be blamed for some negligence in forbidding the wrong. ﴿And perhaps they will become righteous﴾, and in hope that they will attain some measure of righteousness. It is also read as "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative, meaning: we admonished them as an excuse to your Lord, or we made an excuse with an excuse.

﴿So when they forgot﴾ refers to the people of the town. So when they abandoned what the righteous reminded them of, they were like one who forgets what he has forgotten. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾, ﴿and seized the wrongdoers who committed the wrong﴾. If you ask: the community who said ﴿why do you admonish﴾, which of the two groups were they? Were they from the saved group or the punished group? I say: they were from the saved group, because they were from the group who forbade. They did not say what they said except as those asking about the reason for the admonition and its purpose, since they saw no sound purpose in it, knowing the condition of the people. When the one who forbids knows the condition of the one forbidden, and that forbidding will not affect him, the obligation to forbid falls from him. Sometimes abandonment becomes obligatory because it falls under the category of futility. Do you not see that if you went to the tax collectors sitting at the customs posts (al-ma'sir; the editor's note: al-ma'sir are the places of detention, from "asarahu Allah," meaning Allah detained him; as in al-Sihah) and the executioners appointed for torment, in order to admonish them and restrain them from what they are in, that would be futile on your part, and would be nothing but a cause for them to amuse themselves with you? As for the others, they did not turn away from them either because their despair had not yet become firm as the despair of the first group had, and they did not inform them as they had informed them, or because of their extreme eagerness and zeal in the matter, as Allah the Exalted described His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) in His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾.

It has been said: the community are the ones being admonished. When they were admonished, they said to the admonishers: why do you admonish among us a people whom you claim Allah will destroy or punish? It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "I wish I knew what became of those who said: why do you admonish a people?" 'Ikrimah said: I said, "May Allah make me your ransom, do you not see that they disliked what they were doing and opposed them, and said: why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?" I kept at it until I made him understand that they had been saved. It is reported from al-Hasan: two groups were saved and one group perished, and they were the ones who seized the fish.

It is reported that the Jews were commanded regarding the day that we were commanded about, which is Friday, but they abandoned it and chose Saturday. So they were tested with it, and hunting was forbidden to them on it, and they were commanded to magnify it. The fish used to come to them on Saturday, openly, white and fat, as if they were pregnant she-camels, so that the water could not be seen because of their abundance. On a day when they did not observe the Sabbath, they would not come to them. They remained in this state for a period of time. Then Iblis came to them and said: you were only forbidden from taking them on Saturday, so make pools for yourselves into which you drive the fish on Saturday, so that they cannot leave them, and you take them on Sunday. A man among them took a fish and tied a thread to its tail and to a piece of wood on the shore, then he roasted it on Sunday. His neighbor smelled the scent of the fish and looked into his oven, and said to him: "I see that Allah will punish you." When he was not punished, he took two fish the following Saturday. When they saw that the punishment did not hasten upon them, they hunted, ate, salted and sold. They numbered about seventy thousand, so the people of the town became three groups: one group forbade, and they numbered about twelve thousand; one group said: "why do you admonish a people?"; and one group were the people of the sin. When they did not desist, the Muslims said: "We will not live alongside you," so they divided the town with a wall: there was a door for the Muslims and a door for the transgressors. Dawud (peace be upon him) cursed them. One day the forbidders woke up in their gathering places, and none of the transgressors came out. They said: "Something has happened to the people." They climbed the wall and looked, and behold, they were apes. They opened the door and entered upon them, and the apes recognized their relatives among the humans, while the humans did not recognize their relatives among the apes. A monkey would come to its relative, sniff its clothes, and weep, and he would say: "Did we not forbid you?" and it would nod its head: "Yes." It has also been said: the young became apes, and the old became pigs.

It is reported from al-Hasan: "By Allah, they ate a meal, one of the worst meals eaten by any people, the heaviest in disgrace in this world and the longest in punishment in the Hereafter. Hah, by Allah, the taking of a fish by a people and their eating of it is greater in the sight of Allah than the killing of a Muslim man. But Allah has set an appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter." ﴿A severe punishment﴾ (ba'is shadid). It is said: "ba'isa yab'asu ba'san" when he became severe, so he is ba'is. It is read as "bi'sa," in the pattern of "hadhir" (cautious). And "bi's," with the 'ayn lightened and its vowel moved to the fa', as one says "kabid" for "kabid" (liver). And "bay's," with the hamza changed to ya', as "dhib" for "dhi'b" (wolf). And "bay'is," in the pattern of "fay'al," with the hamza vowelled with kasra and fatha. And "bays," in the pattern of "rays," by changing the hamza of "bay'is" into ya' and assimilating the ya' into it. And "bays," as a lightening of "bays," like "hayn" for "hayn" (humble). And "ba'is," in the pattern of "fa'il."

﴿So when they became arrogant regarding what they had been forbidden﴾, that is, when they became too proud to give up what they had been forbidden, like His saying: ﴿and they rebelled against the command of their Lord﴾. ﴿We said to them: "Be apes, despised"﴾ is an expression of their transformation into apes, like His saying: ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. The meaning is: Allah the Exalted first punished them with a severe punishment, then they rebelled after that, so He transformed them. It has also been said: "fa-lamma 'ataw" is a repetition of His saying "fa-lamma nasu" (when they forgot). And the "ba'is" punishment is the transformation (maskh).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 167:

*Ta'adhdhana Rabbuka* (تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكَ): "'azama Rabbuka" (عزم ربك), meaning your Lord resolved. It is the form *ta'affala* from *al-iidhan* (الإيذان), which means informing. This is because one who resolves upon a matter speaks to himself about it and informs his own self of its doing. It is treated as operating in the manner of an oath-verb, like *'alima Allahu* (علم الله, "God knows") and *shahida Allahu* (شهد الله, "God bears witness"). For this reason it receives the answer that an oath receives, which is His statement *la-yab'athanna* (لَيَبْعَثَنَّ, "He will surely send").

The meaning is: "And when your Lord decreed and prescribed for Himself that He would surely send against the Jews, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst of torment." So they used to pay the poll-tax (*al-jizya*, the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects) to the Magians, until God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) and he imposed it upon them, and it remains imposed upon them until the end of time.

The meaning of *la-yab'athanna 'alayhim* (ليبعثنّ عليهم) is *la-yusallatanna 'alayhim*, "He will surely give power over them," like His statement: *"Ba'athna 'alaykum 'ibadan lana uli ba's shadid"* (بعثنا عليكم عبادا لنا أولي بأس شديد), "We sent against you servants of Ours possessing great might."

I'll translate the passage as it stands.

And We divided them into groups (ummaman) upon the earth and scattered them within it, so that hardly any land is free of a group of them. Among them are the righteous who believed, among them those in Medina, or those beyond China (wara' al-Sin); and among them are others (wa-minhum duna dhalika), people below that standard, who fall short of it, namely the disbelievers and the transgressors. If you ask: what is the grammatical position (mahall) of duna dhalika? I answer:

It is in the nominative case (raf'), being an adjective (sifah) of a deleted noun (mawsuf mahdhuf), meaning: "and among them are people who fall short of righteousness," like His saying ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ (37:164), in the sense of: "And there is none of us but has a known station."

﴿And We tested them with good things and bad﴾ with blessings and calamities, ﴿so that perhaps they would turn back﴾, repenting and returning.

﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾ — these were the people who lived at the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — ﴿who inherited the Book﴾, the Torah, which remained in their hands after their predecessors. They read it and become acquainted with what it contains of commands, prohibitions, permissions and prohibitions, yet they did not act upon it. ﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾, that is, the trappings of this lowly thing, meaning the world and what is enjoyed from it. In His saying "this lower life" (hadha al-adna) there is belittling and contempt. Al-adna (lower) may derive either from dunuww (nearness), because it is immediate and near, or from dunuww in the sense of the condition's lowliness, decline and scarcity. What is meant is what they used to take in bribes in judgments, by distorting the words, to make things easy for the common people. ﴿And they say: "It will be forgiven us"﴾, that Allah will not hold us accountable for what we took. The subject (fa'il) of "will be forgiven" is the prepositional phrase "for us" (lana). It is also permissible that the subject be the act of taking, which is the verbal noun of "they take."

﴿And if goods like it come to them, they will take them again﴾. The waw is for the circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they hope for forgiveness while they persist, returning to the like of their deeds, not repenting. Forgiveness of sins is not valid except with repentance, and the persistent one has no forgiveness.

﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾, meaning His saying in the Torah: whoever commits a great sin, he will not be forgiven except through repentance. ﴿And they studied what is in it﴾, in the Book, concerning the condition of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. What the Mujbira [[His saying "in the forgiveness of sins, and what the Mujbira hold" means the People of the Sunna, whose doctrine is permitting forgiveness by sheer grace, not by hoping for it while persisting in disobedience. (ʿ)]] hold is the very doctrine of the Jews, as you see.

It is related from Malik ibn Dinar, may Allah have mercy on him: "There will come upon people a time when, if they fall short of what they were commanded, they will say, 'It will be forgiven us, for we did not associate anything with Allah.' All their affairs turn to hope; their best people among them are compromising. These people of this community are the likenesses of those whom Allah mentioned," and he recited the verse.

﴿And the Last Abode is better than that lowly goods﴾ for ﴿those who are mindful (of Allah)﴾, who guard against bribery and the things Allah has forbidden.

Also read: "wa-warrathu al-Kitab" (ورّثوا), and "wa-an la taqulu" with the ta' (تقولوا), and "wa-idarasu" (وادّارسوا), in the sense of tadarasu. And "afala ta'qilun" with the ya' and the ta'. If you ask: what is the position of His saying ﴿that they not say about Allah except the truth﴾? I answer: it is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the covenant of the Book." The meaning of "covenant of the Book" is the covenant mentioned in the Book. In it, the assertion that forgiveness is granted without repentance is a departure from the covenant of the Book and a fabrication against Allah, and a speaking against Him what is not true. If "the covenant of the Book" is explained as what was mentioned earlier, then "an la yaqulu" is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: lest they say. It is also permissible that "an" be explanatory, and "la yaqulu" be a prohibition, as if it were said: Did He not tell them, "Do not say about Allah except the truth"? If you ask: on what is the clause "and they studied what is in it" coordinated? I answer: upon "Was not the covenant taken from them," because it is an affirmation (taqrir), as if it were said: "The covenant of the Book was taken from them, and they studied what is in it."

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 170:

"And those who hold fast to the Book" has two possible readings. The first: it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿Indeed, We do not allow the reward of the reformers to be lost﴾. The meaning is: indeed We do not lose their reward, because "the reformers" (al-muslihun) carry the same sense as "those who hold fast to the Book," like His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed We do not allow the reward of whoever is best in deed to be lost﴾.

The second: it is in the genitive (majrur), coordinated (ma'tuf) with "those who are God-fearing" (alladhina yattaquna), and His saying ﴿indeed We do not allow to be lost﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh).

It is also read as "yumassikuna" with the doubled letter (tashdid), and the reading of Ubayy supports this: "wa-alladhina massaku bil-kitab" ("and those who have held fast to the Book"). If you say: holding fast to the Book includes every act of worship, among them the establishment of prayer, so why is prayer singled out? I say: to show the distinction of prayer, because it is the pillar of religion and the dividing line between disbelief and faith. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "wa-alladhina istamsaku bil-kitab" ("and those who have firmly held fast to the Book").

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 171:

﴿And [remember] when We uprooted the mountain above them⦗as if it were a canopy⦘﴾ [We] tore it up and lifted it, like His saying: ﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾. From it [comes the expression] nataqa al-siqa' (nataqa the waterskin), when he shakes it to dislodge the butter from it. Al-zulla (the canopy): everything that shades you, such as a roof or a cloud. It is also read with a ṭāʾ (aẓẓalla), from ahalla ʿalayhi, when he rose above it. ﴿And they thought that it would fall upon them﴾, and they knew that it was about to fall upon them. That was because they refused

to accept the rulings of the Torah, due to its severity and weight. So God raised the mountain above their heads to the size of their army, and it was a farsakh by a farsakh. It was said to them: "If you accept it with what is in it, [good]; otherwise it will certainly fall upon you." When they looked at the mountain, each man fell down prostrating on his left eyebrow, while looking with his right eye at the mountain, out of fear of its falling. For this reason you will not see a Jew prostrate except on his left eyebrow, and they say: "This is the prostration by which the punishment was lifted from us." When Moses displayed the tablets, in which was the Book of God, no mountain, tree, or stone remained but that it trembled, and for this reason you will not see a Jew reading the Torah over whom it is recited but that he trembles and shakes his head in response to it. [His saying "wa-anghaḍa lahā raʾsah" means he moved his head like one who is astonished, as explained in the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)] ﴿Take what We have given you⦗with determination⦘﴾, on the presumption of a saying: that is, "And We said: Take what We have given you," or "saying: take what We have given you from the Book with strength and resolve, to bear its hardships and obligations, and ﴿remember what is in it﴾, its commands and prohibitions, and do not forget it."

Or [it means]: "remember what is in it of the summons to the great reward, so desire it." It is also permissible that what is meant is: take what We have given you of the great sign with strength, if you are able to bear it, like His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through﴾. ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ of the indication of the overwhelming power and the warning, ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾ regarding what you are upon. Ibn Masʿud read: ﴿and you may remember﴾ (tadhakkarū). It is also read: wa-ndhakarū (wa-dhdhakarū), with the same meaning as tadhakkarū.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 172–174:

﴿from their loins﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the children of Adam," a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). The meaning of "taking their offspring from their loins" is: bringing them forth from their backs as offspring, and making them witness against themselves. And His saying ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes, we testify﴾ is by way of figure of speech and imagination (tamthil wa-takhyil) [[Mahmud said: "This is by way of figure of speech and imagination... etc." Ahmad says: The use of the term tamthil (figurative representation) is better, and the Shari'ah has come with it. As for his use of the term takhyil (imaginative representation) for the speech of God Most High, it is rejected, no revelation has been transmitted with it, and we have frequently objected to him over this term. Furthermore, the principle is established that the apparent meaning, so long as it does not contradict reason, must be upheld as it is; therefore the majority upheld it according to its apparent and literal sense and did not treat it as a parable. As for the manner of the bringing forth and the address, God knows best about that.]]! The meaning of this is that He set out for them the proofs of His lordship and His oneness, and their intellects and insights, which He had placed within them and made the means of distinguishing error from guidance, bore witness to these. It is as though He made them witness against themselves, established them in acknowledgment, and said to them: "Am I not your Lord?" And it is as though they said: "Yes, You are our Lord; we bear witness against ourselves and acknowledge Your oneness." The figurative mode is broad in the speech of God Most High and of His Messenger (ﷺ), and in the speech of the Arabs.

Its parallel is His saying Most High: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [41:11] ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ [41:11] And the verse of the poet:

﴿When the joints said to the belly: "Hurry"﴾ [[The explanation of this evidence has passed in the first part, p. 181, so refer to it there if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

﴿The eastern wind said to it: "Qarqar"...﴾ [[The line "The eastern wind said to it: 'Qarqar'... and the known and the denied became confused" is by Abu al-Najm al-'Ijli. "Qarqar" is an imperative verb meaning "rumble": a command to the clouds, treating them as rational beings, i.e., "make a sound with thunder."

This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad, following al-Mazini, said: it is an imitation of the sound of thunder. In either case it is built on kasr, on the principle of avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters. But on the first view it bears a pronoun, so it is compound; on the second there is no pronoun, so it is simple. However, an onomatopoeic sound does not convey urging or prohibition, whereas here it conveys urging by the context, and it has no verb of its own. This one has a verb: one says "qarqarat al-dajajah" when the hen clucks, unless it is said that the meaning is: "Make a sound, O thunder, qarqar." Their saying "qarqarat al-dajajah" is derived from "qarqar," just as they derived "al-'iyat" from "'iyt" with two kasras between which there is a sukun, imitating the sound of those who play. "Ikhtalata" may be imperative, which is more fitting to what precedes it, or it may be past. "Al-munkar" means the denied thing, and the wind has no speech. He likened the wind, in driving the clouds, to one who is capable of speech, by way of metaphor (al-makniyyah), and the speech is imaginative representation. It is also permissible that speech be borrowed for the pouring of the clouds, by way of explicit metaphor (al-tasrih). It is also permissible that it is from the category of kinayah. In this manner is His saying about the she-camel of Salih: "Then there came to her a reddish one like the brother of the arrow, with anger, and he said, 'Be still, O barren one.'" Necessity permitted the unwounded to be treated as the cause, and he attributed the act of wounding to one not wounded, to show the connection to the aspect of likeness of the barren one with the ambiguous. That is: the eastern wind said to the clouds, "Rumble with thunder." And "ikhtalata" means: the places which it had been accustomed to water mixed with those it did not reach by irrigation, meaning it equalized them all in it. It may be that "the known" is rain and "the denied" is thunder, lightning and thunderbolts, i.e., do all of them, taking it as a past verb, so it is conjoined to "qalat." **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 7, verses 175–176:**

﴿And recite to them, [O Muhammad], the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them.﴾ He was a scholar from among the scholars of the Children of Israel. It is also said that he was from the Canaanites. His name was Bal'am ibn Ba'ura' (Balaam son of Beor). He was given knowledge of some of the Books of God. ﴿But he detached himself from them﴾ from the signs, by disbelieving in them and casting them behind his back. ﴿So Satan pursued him﴾ Satan caught up with him, overtook him, and became his companion. Or, [it means] ﴿he followed his footsteps﴾. It is also read *fa-atba'ahu* (فاتبعه), with the meaning of *fa-tabi'ahu* (فتبعه). ﴿And he became of the misguided﴾ he became one of the astray and the disbelievers.

It is reported that his people asked him to invoke [God's curse] upon Musa and those with him. He refused and said: "How can I invoke [a curse] upon one who has the angels with him?" They pressed him insistently and did not cease to urge him until he did it.

﴿And had We willed, We would have elevated him thereby﴾ We would have exalted him and raised him to the ranks of the righteous scholars who act upon those signs. ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾ he inclined toward this world and desired it. It is also said: he inclined toward baseness.

If you ask: How did He make his elevation contingent upon God's will and not upon his own action, by which he would deserve elevation?

I answer: The meaning is: "Had he remained committed to acting upon the signs and not detached himself from them, We would have elevated him by them." God's will to elevate him was consequent upon his adherence to the signs, so the will was mentioned while what was meant is what follows from it and is caused by it, as if it were said: "Had he adhered to them, We would have elevated him by them." Do you not see His saying ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾? It counters the [supposed] will with his clinging, which is his own act. Therefore ﴿And had We willed﴾ must mean what is his own act. Had the statement been taken literally, it would have had to be said: "Had We willed, We would have elevated him, but We did not will [it]."

﴿So his likeness is like that of a dog﴾ his attribute, which is a likeness of lowliness and abjectness, is like the attribute of the dog in its most despicable and humiliating state, namely the state of constant panting (*al-lahath*) and its continuation. [[Its saying "constant panting" (dawam al-lahath): In al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari), *lahatha al-kalb* means the dog's tongue comes out from exhaustion or thirst. And God's saying: ﴿If you pursue it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾, because when you pursue a dog it barks and flees, and if you leave it, it charges at you and barks, so it exhausts itself in both cases; thus at that point it experiences what it experiences when thirsty, namely the protrusion of the tongue. (Editor's note: ʿ)]] whether it is pursued, that is, attacked and provoked and driven away, or left without being provoked. This is because the panting of other animals occurs only when they are provoked and stirred; otherwise they do not pant, whereas the dog's panting continues in both states.

The proper wording of the statement should have been: "Had We willed, We would have elevated him by them, but he clung to the earth, so We brought him low and lowered his rank." Placing ﴿So his likeness is like that of a dog﴾ in place of "We brought him low" is a more eloquent degradation, because likening him to the dog in its most despicable and humiliating state carries the meaning of such a debasement.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, that the dog is one whose heart is cut off, panting whether it is pursued or not pursued. It is also said: its meaning is: if you admonish him, he is astray, and if you do not admonish him, he is astray, like the dog: if you chase it, it runs and pants, and if you leave it in its state, it pants.

If you ask: What is the place of the conditional clause? I answer: It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if it were said: "Like the likeness of a dog, humbled, constantly abased, panting in both states."

It is also said: when Bal'am invoked [a curse] upon Musa, peace be upon him, his tongue came out and fell upon his chest, and he began to pant as a dog pants.

﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs﴾ from among the Jews, after they had read the description of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the Torah, and had heard the mention of the inimitable Qur'an and what it contains, and had given the people good news of the imminent coming of his mission, and used to seek victory through him.

﴿So relate the narrative﴾ narrate the story of Bal'am, which is similar to their own story, ﴿perhaps they will reflect﴾ so that they may take warning and guard against his end, since they have followed his way, and deviated in a manner similar to his deviation; and so that they may know that you learned it through revelation, whereupon their certainty in you increases and the proof becomes more binding upon them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 179:

"Many of the jinn and humankind" are those upon whose hearts a seal has been set, those whom God knew would receive no kindness (lutf). He made them such that they do not direct their minds toward knowing the truth, nor do they look with their eyes at what God has created with the look of consideration, nor do they listen to what is recited to them of God's signs with the listening of reflection. It is as though they lacked the understanding of hearts, the sight of eyes, and the hearing of ears. And He made them, owing to their being deeply rooted [[The note on "li-i'rāqihim": one says a tree is "a'raqa" when its roots have extended far into the ground; and "aghraqa al-nāzi‘ fi al-qaws" (with the dotted letter) means he drew the bowstring to its full extent, as stated in al-Sihah. (Ed.)]] in disbelief and the severity of their obstinacy in it, and because nothing comes from them except the deeds of the people of the Fire, as though they were created for the Fire. This indicates their deep immersion in the things that necessitate it and their firm establishment in what qualifies them to enter the Fire. From this is the letter of ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, to Khalid ibn al-Walid: "It has reached me that the people of Syria have prepared for you a dalūk [[The note on "dalūk": in al-Sihah, the dalūk is what one rubs on the body of perfume or other things. (Ed.)] kneaded with wine, and I think you are the family of al-Mughira, a seed of the Fire." [[Abu ʿUbayd related it in his Gharib: Isma‘il ibn ʿAyyash related to me from Humayd ibn Rabi‘a from Sulayman ibn Musa: that ʿUmar wrote to Khalid, and he mentioned it, as a broken (munqati‘) report.]] It is said of one who is deeply rooted in certain matters: "So-and-so was created only for such-and-such." The intended meaning is a description of the state of the Jews [[The note "and the intended meaning is a description of the state of the Jews": he interpreted it this way because, according to the Mu‘tazila, it is obligatory for God to do what is best (al-aslah) for the servant, and creating him for Hell is not best for him. According to Ahl al-Sunna, nothing is obligatory upon Him. (Ed.)]] in the gravity of what they undertook of denying the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while knowing that he is the promised Prophet, and that they are among the multitude for whom faith scarcely comes about. It is as though they were created for the Fire. "Those are like cattle" in lacking understanding, consideration for lesson, and listening for reflection. "Nay, they are more astray than cattle" in understanding, lesson, and reflection. "Those are the heedless," the perfect in heedlessness. It is said: cattle perceive their benefits and harms, so they keep to some of what they perceive; but these, most of them know that they are stubborn, yet they rush into the Fire.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verse 180:

"And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them" [[Mahmud said: "The meaning of 'the most beautiful names' ... etc." Ahmad said: That is, [names] that are permissible for Him even if their application is not reported in the Shari'ah, such as al-Sharif (the Noble) and al-'Arif (the Knowing), and the like.]], because they indicate good meanings of glorification, sanctification and other things. "So call upon Him by them" (fasma'uhu bi-tilka al-asma'), i.e., name Him by those names. "And leave those who deviate concerning His names" (wa dharu alladhina yulhidun fi asma'ihi), i.e., abandon the naming of those who incline away from truth and correctness in them, so that they name Him by other than the most beautiful names. This is that they name Him by what is not permissible for Him, as we have heard the Bedouins say in their ignorance: "O Abu al-Makarim! O white-faced one! O Nakhi!" Or [it is that] they refuse to name Him by some of His most beautiful names, such as saying "O Allah" but not saying "O Merciful (ya Rahman)." And Allah the Exalted has said: "Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names" [[Mahmud said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: and to Allah belong the most beautiful attributes (al-awsaf al-husna), which are describing Him with justice, goodness and beneficence and the negation of resemblance to creation, so describe Him with them, and leave those who deviate concerning His attributes..." etc. Ahmad said:

He does not forgo stuffing corrupt creeds into every place that can contain them. If what is meant is the attributes, then among the most beautiful ones is describing Allah with comprehensive power and singularity in creating the creatures, so that He does not associate His servants with Him in the creation of their actions. He is also magnified by being not questioned about what He does, that all His decree is just, and that it is not obligatory upon Him to observe what the creatures imagine to be a benefit by their intellects. And that His promise is true and His word is the truth, and He has promised the vision [of Him], so its occurrence is necessary, along with His other majestic attributes. "And leave those who deviate concerning His attributes" by denying them, then claim that His power does not encompass the creatures, but rather they are divided between Him and His servants, and they obligate Him to observe what they imagine to be a benefit, and they restrict a vast part of His forgiveness, pardon and generosity from the sinners among His monotheists, along with other deviations known for the sect that titles itself "the Just" (al-'adliyya), praising themselves; and He knows best who is pious.]], and it means describing Him with justice, goodness, beneficence and the negation of resemblance to creation, so describe Him with them. "And leave those who deviate" [[His saying "And leave those who deviate" means the People of the Sunnah, who say: every existent is willed and created by Him, the Exalted, even if it be evil, and His vision is possible, in contrast to the Mu'tazila in all of that, as is established in its proper place. (Gh.)]] "concerning His attributes", so they describe Him with the willing of ugliness and the creating of indecency and wrong, and with what enters into anthropomorphism, such as vision and the like. It is also said: their deviation concerning His names is their naming of the idols as gods, and their deriving al-Lat from Allah and al-'Uzza from al-'Aziz. [[Mahmud said: "And it is said: their deviation concerning His names is naming the idols..." etc. Ahmad said: This is a good and fitting interpretation, and Allah knows best.]]

When he said, ﴿And We have certainly created many of the jinn and humankind for Hell﴾, and so informed us that many of the two weighty creatures (al-thaqalan, jinn and humankind) act by the deeds of the people of the Fire, he followed it with his words: ﴿And among those We have created is a community that guides by the truth﴾. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he recited it he would say: "This is for you, and the people before you were given something like it." [Al-Tha'labi related it from Qatada and Ibn Jurayj, and his chain of transmission to them is mentioned at the beginning of his book.] And ﴿Among the people of Musa is a community that guides by the truth﴾. And from him (ﷺ): "Among my community there will be a people upon the truth until Isa (peace be upon him) descends." [Al-Tha'labi related it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and his chain to him is mentioned at the beginning of his book. Ahmad related it from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn with the wording: "A group of my community will not cease to be upon the truth until the command of Allah comes, and Isa ibn Maryam descends." In the Tarikh of al-Bukhari, from Abd al-Taghawi, from Jabir, there is something similar. Abu Ya'la related it through another route, and added: "Their imam will say, 'Come forward, O Spirit of Allah,' and he will say, 'You are more entitled to it; Allah has honoured this community with it.'"] And from al-Kalbi:

They are those among the People of the Book who believed. It was also said: they are the scholars and the callers to the religion.

Al-istidraj (gradual drawing-on): an verbal noun of the form istif'al from al-daraja (degree, step), in the sense of ascending step by step, or of bringing someone down degree after degree.

The poet al-A'sha said:

"Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep, and you climbed the ropes of the sky by a ladder,
Your speech would draw you on until you are bewildered, and you would know that I am not one to be silenced before you."

[[The explanation of this evidence is in the first volume, page 395; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

From the same root: "daraja al-sabiyy" (the child walked) when he brought his steps close together. "Adraja al-kitab" means he folded the book bit by bit. "Daraja al-qawm" means some of them died one after another.

The meaning of "sanastadrijuhum" (We will draw them on gradually) is: We will bring them nearer little by little to that which destroys them and multiplies their punishment, "from where they do not know" what is intended for them. This is that God continually showers His blessings upon them while they are immersed in error. Whenever He renews a blessing for them, they grow more insolent and renew their disobedience, so they advance step by step in sins through the succession of blessings, thinking that the continuous blessings are a favour from God and a drawing near, while in truth they are abandonment by Him and removal far away. This is the istidraj of God, Exalted; we seek refuge in God from it.

"Wa umli lahum" (And I give them respite) is coordinated with "sanastadrijuhum" and falls under the same governing particle (the sin). "Inna kaydi matin" (Indeed, My plan is firm): He called it a plan because it resembles a plan, in that outwardly it is a kindness and in reality it is abandonment.

"Ma bi-sahibihim" (There is no madness in their companion) refers to Muhammad (ﷺ): "min jinnah" means from madness. They used to say, "He is a poet, a madman." It is related from Qatada that the Prophet (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa and called them clan by clan, warning them of the punishment of God. One of them said: "Indeed, this companion of yours is a madman; he has been crying out until morning." [[The phrase "bat yuhawwit" means he was shouting. (Its corrector.)]] [[al-Tabari related it with a sound chain to Qatada, who said, "It was mentioned to us," and so on. Then God revealed: "Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion," and so on.]]

"Awa lam yanzuru" (Have they not looked): a look of inference "fi malakut al-samawat wal-ard" (into the dominion of the heavens and the earth), in what the two indicate of the greatness of the sovereignty. Al-malakut: the great kingdom. "Wa ma khalaqa Allahu min shay'" (and what God has created of anything): in what God created of things that fall under the name "thing," of kinds that number cannot count and description cannot encompass.

"Wa an 'asa" (and that perhaps): "an" is the light form of the heavy one, and the original is "wa annahu 'asa," where the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter. The meaning: "Or have they not looked into the matter, that perhaps their term has drawn near" "an yakuna qad iqtaraba ajaluhum" (that their term has already drawn near), and that they may die soon, so that they would hasten to reflection, to seeking the truth, and to what would save them, "before the sudden seizure of the term" [[The phrase "before the sudden seizure of the term" means its seizing them unawares. From al-Sihah. (Its corrector.)]] and the arrival of punishment.

It is permissible that the approach of the term be understood as the approach of the Hour, and the "kana" here would then contain the pronoun of the matter.

If you ask: With what does "fa-bi-ayyi hadithin ba'dahu yu'minun" (then in what discourse after this will they believe?) connect? I say: It connects with "'asa an yakuna qad iqtaraba ajaluhum," as if it were said: "Perhaps their term has drawn near, so why do they not hasten to believe in the Qur'an before it is too late? What are they waiting for after the clarity of the truth, and which discourse is more worthy than it that they wish to believe in?"

Translation:

It is recited as "wa-yadharuhum" with the ya' (the third person) and with the nun (the first person plural). The raf' (nominative vowelling) is on the basis of istiʾnaf (resumptive new clause), "wa-yadharuhum." And "wa-yadharuhum" with the ya' and the jazm (apocopate vowelling) is in ʿatf (conjunction) upon the place (maḥall) of "fa-lā hādiya lahu," as if it were said: "Whoever Allah leads astray, none guides him, and He leaves them."

They ask you about the Hour: when will be its landing? Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord." It was said: a group of the Jews said, "O Muhammad, tell us when the Hour is, if you are a prophet, for we know when it is." This was a test from them, while they knew that God, exalted is He, had reserved its knowledge for Himself. It was also said: the ones asking were the Quraysh. "As-Sa'a (the Hour)" is among the names that became dominant, like "an-najm" for the Pleiades (ath-Thurayya). The Resurrection was called "the Hour" because its coming is sudden, or because its reckoning is swift, or on the contrary because it is long, or because with God it is as long as an hour is to creatures. "Ayyan" means "when." It was said: its derivation is from "ayy" with the form fa'lan, because its meaning is "what time" and "what act," from "awaytu ilayhi" (I took refuge in him), because the part takes refuge in the whole, relying on it. This was said by Ibn Jinni, who rejected that it derives from "ayna" (where), since this is time and "ayna" is place. As-Sulami read "iyan" with a kasra on the hamza. [[Your phrase "as-Sulami read iyan with a kasra on the hamza": in al-Sihah, "ayyan" is a question about time, and "iyan" with a kasra on the hamza is the dialect of Sulaym. As-Sulami also read "ayyana yub'athun" with it. (A)]] "Mursaha" means its landing, or the time of its landing, that is its establishment and settling. Everything heavy settles and becomes stable. From this: "rasa al-jabal" (the mountain settled) and "arsa as-safina" (he anchored the ship). "Al-mursa" is the anchor by which a ship is moored. Nothing is heavier than the Hour, as shown by His saying: ﴿Heavy it is in the heavens and the earth﴾. The meaning: when will God settle it? ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾, that is, the knowledge of the time of its landing is with Him, and He has reserved it, not informing anyone of it, neither an angel brought near nor a sent prophet. He almost conceals it even from Himself, so that this is a stronger call to obedience and a stronger deterrent from disobedience, just as He concealed the specific term, which is the time of death. Therefore ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾, that is, it remains hidden; its matter does not appear and the obscurity of its knowledge is not lifted except by Him alone, when He brings it at its time suddenly. None of His creation reveals it by informing of it before it comes, because its concealment continues for others until the time of its occurrence. ﴿Heavy it is in the heavens and the earth﴾: every one of its inhabitants, from the angels and the two species (jinn and humankind), is concerned with the matter of the Hour, and wishes that its knowledge be made manifest to him, and its concealment is hard and burdensome on him. Or: it is heavy in them because its inhabitants expect it and fear its hardships and terrors. Or: because everything cannot bear it or stand up to it, so it is heavy upon them. ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾: except by surprise while you are heedless. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Hour will come upon people while a man is repairing his pool, and a man is watering his livestock, and a man is displaying his merchandise in his market, and a man is lowering and raising his scale." [[In al-Bukhari: "yaliṭu hawdahu" (he is plastering his pool). It is also narrated as "yulawwitu," meaning he repairs it. (A)]] [[Al-Tabari transmitted it with the chain mentioned to Qatada, who said, "It was mentioned to us," and then he related it. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "The Hour will surely come while two men have spread their garment between them and they neither sell it nor fold it, and the Hour will surely come while a man has departed with milk from his she-camel and he does not drink it," and so on.]] ﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾: as if you were knowing of it. Its real meaning: as if you were deep in asking about it. [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is as if you were insistent in asking about it..." Ahmad said: In this type of repetition there is a subtlety found only in the Mighty Book, and it is too exalted to be shared in. The usual pattern of such repetition is that when speech is built on an aim and an obstacle arises in its midst, and one wishes to return to complete the first aim after its memory has grown distant, one revives the first aim by mentioning it again, so that its end connects to its beginning. Examples of this occur in the Mighty Book, and more will come, and this is one of them. When the speech began with ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will be its landing?﴾, then the answer embedded in ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ up to ﴿suddenly﴾ intervened, it was intended to complete their question with a kind of rebuke, which is embedded in ﴿as if you were well-informed about it﴾, and this is strongly tied to the question. Its memory had grown distant, so it was revived with a general reviving, and we never find it revived except with some brevity, as a reminder of the first, needing no detail because of what came before. Hence it was said ﴿They ask you﴾ without naming the one asked about, which is the Hour, being content with what preceded. When the question was repeated for this benefit, the answer was also repeated briefly, saying ﴿Say: its knowledge is only with God﴾. This is observed in the summarizing of speech after its expansion. Among the finest things the Arabs noticed in this pattern of repetition, because the memory was distant and to revive the mention, is his saying:

"Hasten this for us and join us to that, the fat, for we have grown weary of it, Yajal."

That is, only. He mentioned the alif and lam as the closing of the first of the two verses, then when he began the second verse, the memory of the first seemed distant, so he revived it and kept the first in its place. For this reason Ibn Jinni argued that a verse of rajaz with three parts is a complete line, not a half, as Abu al-Hasan held. He said: If it were a single line, the memory of the first would not have been distant, so there would be no need to repeat it. Do you not see that Ubayd, when he came with a long qasida of lines and made the end of the first hemistich "al," did not repeat it at the start of the second hemistich, because it was a single line, so he did not see its memory as distant? That is his saying:

"O my two companions, halt and inquire of the dilapidated dwelling among the people of al-Halal,
like the wiping away of the frost by your absence, its rain-shelter and the sweeping of the north wind."

Then he continued in that manner for about a dozen more lines. Consider how the Arabs strove to observe this subtlety, to the point of making the near seem distant and the short seem long. Reflect upon it, for it is a treasure that circulates only among the skilled elite in the arts of Arabic and eloquence, and God is the one sought for help.]] , for whoever persists in asking about a thing and searching it out, his knowledge of it becomes firm and established. This structure means exaggeration. From it: "ihfa' ash-shaarib" (shaving the moustache closely), and "ihtifa' al-baql" (uprooting the herbs). "Ahfa fi al-mas'ala" means he pressed hard in the question, [[That is, he insisted and was forceful. (A)]] and "hafiya bi-fulan" and "tahaffa bihi" means he exceeded in kindness to him. It is reported from Mujahid: "I persisted in asking about it until I knew." Ibn Mas'ud read: "ka'annaka hafiyyun bihā," meaning you are knowing of it, deeply informed in knowing it. It was also said: "'anha" is attached to "yas'alunaka," meaning they ask you about it as if you were knowing of it. It was said: the Quraysh said to him, "Between us and you there is kinship, so tell us when the Hour is." It was said: "They ask you about it as if you were well-informed about it," meaning you favor them and single them out with teaching its time because of kinship, and you withhold its knowledge from others. Had you been told its time for a benefit that God knew in your informing of it, you would have conveyed it to near and far without distinction, like all that was revealed to you.

It was also said: "as if you were eager for the question about it, loving it and preferring it," meaning that you dislike the question about it, because it is among the knowledge of the unseen which God has reserved and has not granted to any of His creation. If you say: why was "they ask you" repeated when its knowledge is only with God? I say: for emphasis, and for the addition brought by "as if you were well-informed about it." On this basis, the skilled scholars in their books do not leave the repeated element without an added benefit; among them Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, the companion of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on them both. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that He is the one who knows it, and that He is the one singled out with knowledge of it.

Say, "I hold no power to benefit myself or to ward off harm, except as God wills. Were I to know the unseen, I would have chosen abundance of good and abundance of benefits, and I would have avoided all evil and harm, so that nothing of it would touch me. I would not have been victorious at one time and defeated at another in wars, nor profited and lost in trade, nor been right and wrong in my plans. I am only a servant, a messenger, a warner and a bringer of good tidings for a people who believe."

This is a manifestation of servitude and a disavowal of what is specific to Lordship, namely knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb). That is: I am a weak servant, like slaves and bondsmen, who holds no power to bring about benefit or to repel harm for himself, except what my Lord and Master wills of benefit to me and protection from me. "Were I to know the unseen, my condition would be other than what it is": for I would have sought much good and abundant benefits, and avoided evil and harms so that none of them would touch me. I would not have been a conqueror at one time and conquered at another in wars, nor a winner and a loser in commerce, nor correct and mistaken in my arrangements. "I am only a servant, a messenger, a warner and a bringer of good tidings" — and it is not my place to know the unseen — "for a people who believe."

The phrase "for a people who believe" may be connected to both the warner and the bringer of good tidings together, since warning and good tidings benefit only them.

Or it may be connected to the bringer of good tidings alone, with the object of the warner omitted, meaning: "a warner to the disbelievers, and a bringer of good tidings to a people who believe."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 189–190:**

*min nafsin wahidatin*: from a single soul, and that is the soul of Adam (ﷺ)... *wa-ja'ala minha zawjaha*: and made from it its mate, and she is Hawwa' (Eve). He created her from the body of Adam, from one of his ribs. Or [it means] from her own kind, as in His saying: ﴿He made for you mates from among yourselves﴾ [16:72].

*li-yaskuna ilayha*: that he might find rest in her, that he might be at ease with her, incline to her and not shun her, because one kind inclines more to its own kind and feels comfort with it. And when she is part of him, the rest and the love are more complete, just as a person finds rest in his child and loves him with the love of his own self, because the child is a piece of him. He said *li-yaskuna* in the masculine after having used the feminine in *wahidatin*, [and then] *minha zawjaha* [where the feminine returns], going by the sense of "soul," to show that what is meant by it is Adam. Also, because it is the male who finds rest in the female and covers her, so the masculine is the better fit for the meaning (*tibaq*, correspondence). *Al-taghshi* is a metaphor for intercourse, and likewise *al-ghayashan* and *al-ityan*.

*hamalat hamlan khafifan*: she carried a light burden, one that was light for her, and she did not suffer from it what some pregnant women suffer from their pregnancies of distress and harm, and she did not find it heavy as they do. You may hear some of them say about their child: "How light it was on my liver when I carried it!"

*fa-marrat bihi*: she went on with it, continuing with it until the time of its birth, without miscarriage (*ikhdaj*) or premature expulsion (*izlaq*).¹

It was also said: *hamalat hamlan khafifan* means the drop of semen, *fa-marrat bihi* meaning she stood with it and sat with it.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read: *fa-istamarrat bihi* (she continued with it). Yahya ibn Ya'mar read: *fa-marrat bihi*, with light pronunciation. Others read: *fa-mara't bihi* (she doubted it), from *al-miyah*, like His saying: ﴿Will you dispute with him about what he saw?﴾ [53:12]. Its meaning: a suspicion of pregnancy came into her mind, so she doubted it.

*falamma athqalat*: when the time of the weight of her burden came, as you say: "She drew near [to birth]."²

It is also recited *uthqalat*, in the passive form, meaning: the burden made her heavy.

*da'awa Allaha rabbahuma*: they called on Allah, their Lord and the Owner of their affair, who truly deserves to be called upon and sought for refuge, and they said: *la-in ataytana*, "If You give us," if You grant us, *salihan*, a child, *sawiyyan*, one who is sound in body and free of defects.³ It was also said: a male child, because maleness is part of soundness and excellence.

The pronoun in *ataytana* and *la-nakunanna* refers to both of them and to everyone who descends from their offspring.⁴

*falamma atahuma ma talaba*: when He gave them what they asked for, the sound and healthy child, *ja'ala lahu shurakaa*: they made for Him partners, that is, their children made for Him partners. This is by omitting the governing noun and placing the noun in the genitive in its place. Likewise *fima atahuma*, that is, what He gave their children. This is shown by His words *fa-ta'ala Allahu 'amma yushrikun*, where the pronoun is in the plural. Adam and Hawwa' are free of shirk. The meaning of their associating others with Him in what He gave them is their naming their children *'Abd al-'Uzza*, *'Abd Manat*,⁵ *'Abd Shams* and the like, in place of *'Abd Allah*, *'Abd al-Rahman* and *'Abd al-Rahim*.

Another interpretation is that the address is to the Quraysh who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who were the descendants of Qusayy. Do you not see His words in the story of Umm Ma'bad:⁶

*fa-ya li-Qusayyin ma zawa Allahu 'ankum*
*bihi min fakharin la yubara wa-sudadi*

[Translator's note: the poem is quoted in the commentary as: "May Allah, Lord of mankind, reward with the best reward / the two companions who stayed in the tents of Umm Ma'bad / They alighted in the land of goodness, then departed; / O happiness of him who became a companion of Muhammad! / O the Qusayy, what Allah has withheld from you / of glory unequalled and nobility! / Let the Banu Sa'd be glad of their maiden's abode, / and her seat is for the believers an ambush-place."]

These verses were said by a jinn whose voice the people of Mecca heard but whose person they did not see, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left Mecca with Abu Bakr as an emigrant, and its people did not know their news after they left the cave. It is also narrated as *jaza'iyyah* with a *ta'* like *hidayah*. It is narrated as *qala* instead of *hall*, and the meaning is close, except that the second is specific to resting at midday. *Khaymatay* is in the accusative by way of expansion, with the preposition omitted. *Umm Ma'bad* was a woman of the Banu Sa'd with whom they stayed in al-Bar and goodness. Some have mentioned that her name was 'Atika bint Khalid al-Khuza'iyya. *Ya li-Qusayy* originally was *ya Al Qusayy* and was lightened. Its nature has been disputed: it was said that its origin is also *ya Al Qusayy*; it was said that it is a particle of the genitive, and that it is either redundant, or original and governed by *ya*, according to Sibawayh, or by the verb it replaces, according to Ibn Jinni. *Ma* is interrogative, and the meaning is: O family of Qusayy, do you know what Allah has seized and withheld from you by the departure of the Messenger of Allah from among you, of glory which cannot be matched and of great nobility?

In this question there is the sense of wonder and magnification, as if the one asked about does not know its reality. It is permissible that the *lam* is for wonder, and *ma* is a relative pronoun in apposition to *Qusayy*. It is permissible that the *lam* is for invocation of help, as if he called on them for aid, so that perhaps they might make up what they had missed. *Sada fi qawmihi*: he was noble among his people; its verbal noun is *al-su'dud*, with the hamza and a *damma* on the *dal*, and with the *waw* and a *fatha* on the *dal* as here. The original is *al-sawad*, with a *damma*, like *al-husn*, and the *dal* was added for assimilation to *yarfa'* and *jundab*. *Li-yahanna* is jussive by the imperative *lam*, and the intention is supplication. *Maqam* is the subject, and *Bani* is the object. It is said: *hana'ahu al-ta'am* and the like, with the hamza, when it benefited him and its outcome pleased him; it is from the pattern of *nafa'a* and *darraba*, and its hamza is replaced by what suits what precedes it; and the replacement may be dropped, as here, as if it were original, but dropping it is colloquial. *Al-marsad* and *al-mirsad* is the road where watchers are posted. His saying *lil-mu'minin* contains an encouragement to emigrate.

And the meaning is: He is the One who created you from the soul of Qusayy, and made from its kind his mate, an Arab Qurashiyya, so that he might find rest in her. Then, when He gave them what they asked for, the sound and healthy child, they made for Him partners in what He had given them, in that they named their four children *'Abd Manaf*, *'Abd al-'Uzza*, *'Abd Qusayy* and *'Abd al-Dar*. The pronoun in *yushrikun* refers to both of them and to their descendants who followed them in shirk. This is a good interpretation, with no difficulty in it.

It is also recited *shurakaa'*, meaning: possessors of partnership, and they are the partners; or Allah caused partnership in the child.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 7, verses 191–193:

The idols were treated as if they were beings of intellect (ulu al-'ilm) in His words "and they are created (wa-hum yukhlaqun)", based on the belief of the idolaters about them and their naming them gods (alihah). The meaning is: Do they associate with Him what cannot create anything as Allah creates, while they themselves are created? Because Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, is their Creator. Or: it cannot create anything, because it is inanimate, while they are created, because their worshippers fashion them. So they are weaker than their worshippers. ﴿And they cannot give them help﴾, that is, to their worshippers, ﴿nor can they help themselves﴾, so that they could ward off from themselves the calamities that befall them. Rather, their worshippers are the ones who ward off harm from them and defend them. ﴿And if you call them to guidance﴾, that is, if you call these idols to guidance (hudan), namely to what is right guidance and rectitude, and to guide you. The meaning: if you seek from them, as you seek from Allah, good and guidance, they will not follow you to what you desire and seek, nor will they answer you as Allah answers you. This is indicated by His words: ﴿So let them answer you, if you are truthful. It is the same for you whether you call them or remain silent about calling on them﴾, meaning there is no success with them. If you say: why was it not said "or you are silent" and why was the nominal sentence placed in the position of the verbal one? I say: because whenever a matter distressed them, they called upon Allah rather than their idols, as in His words ﴿and when harm touches people﴾. So their constant state was to be silent about calling on them. Hence it was said: whether you call on them or not, the state does not differ between your act of calling on them and your habitual silence about calling on them.
